consecutively for the eight year.
 
5.7       DISCUSSIONS WITH THE MANAGEMENT OF HAL
 
5.7.1    During the course of discussions on the performance of HAL, Dr. B.B. Ramiah appreciated HAL for its
excellent performance over the past several years. HAL Chairman  Shri N.R. Mohanty was asked to spell out the vision
of the company in the future so as to enable it to withstand the pressures of changing times. Shri Mohanty informed  that
HAL was making efforts to diversify into other areas. He added that, at the moment the Indian Air force was its main
customer but HAL was now trying to enter the international market through the export route. In this context HAL has
begun making components for several international aircraft manufacturers and has also begun servicing of aircrafts.
HAL was also developing a multi-role aircraft with a seating capacity of hundred passengers and a capacity to carry 15-
20 tonnes of cargo. This multirole aircraft will enable HAL to make a significant presence in the International market.
Besides, Shri Mohanty informed that HAL has been doing sub-contract jobs from ISRO and HAL had substantial
expertise in this area. Work from ISRO has enabled HAL to generate additional revenue. Besides HAL is also trying to
involve the private sector in the development of several components on sub-contract basis with HAL acting as the
nucleus. When asked about the problems being faced by HAL, Shri Mohanty informed that Government should resort to
imports only in cases where indigenous production is not possible. Besides Government should also provide incentive
for exports so that products manufactured by HAL are competitive in the international market. In this context
Government may provide some sort of subsidy to encourage exports, as HAL would make money out of after sales
service and repair.
5.8                   OBERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
 
5.8.1    The Committee was pleased to note that HAL had been showing profits since its inception. In addition, the
Committee felt that HAL needs to make adequate efforts to expand its market base as well as its product and services
base. In this context, the Committee asked the management to outline the vision of the HAL over a 20-year period. The

VI.       NUCLEAR POWER CORPORATION OF INDIA LTD.
 
            Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL) is a public sector enterprise under the Department of Atomic
Energy (DAE), Government of India. It was registered on 17 September 1987 with the objective of operating the atomic
power stations and implementing the atomic power projects for generation of electricity in pursuance with the schemes
and programmes of the GOI under atomic energy act 1962.
 
6.1       Background Prior To Formation of NPCIL

Prior to the formation of NPCIL, the design, construction and operation of the nuclear power plants were carried out as
a departmental activity under DAE. In 1967, Power Projects Engineering Division (PPED), a unit of DAE,  was formed
with the responsibility of design, construction and operation  of the Nuclear Power Plants. PPED was converted into
Nuclear Power Board (NPB) in the year 1984 which was again a governmental unit of DAB with increased delegation
of  powers to the unit. In September 1987, NPB was converted into NPCIL and the assets of  NPB  except the first unit
of Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS-l ) were transferred to NPCIL.
 
6.2       Authorized Share Capital
 
The authorised share capital of the company is Rs. 100,000 million, of  which Rs.63,826.70 million is paid up as on
March 31, 2002 and is fully subscribed by the Government of India.
 
6.3       Major Activities of NPCIL
 
6.3.1    The main activities of the company are design construction, commissioning and operation of nuclear power
plants. The company is operating six nuclear power stations with 14 units and is implementing, construction of four
ongoing nuclear power projects. The existing operating power stations of the Company are Tarapur Atomic Power
Station Units-l&2 (TAPS-l&2-2X160 MWe) Maharashtra, Rajasthan Atomic Power Station Unit-2 to 4 (RAPS-2-, 3&4-
lX200 + 2X220 MWe), Madras Atomic Power Station Units-1 &2 (MAPS-1&2- 2X170 MWe) Tamil Nadu, Narora
Atomic Power Station Units-l &2 ( NAPS-1&2-2X220 MWe) UP, Kakrapar Atomic Station LTnits-l&2 (IT..APS-l&2-
2X220 MWe) Gujarat and Kaiga Atomic Power station (Kaiga-l&2- 2X220 MWe),  Karnataka  RAPS-l- 100 MWe
Rajasthan is managed by  NPCIL on behalf of DAE.   The aggregate nuclear capacity  in operation in the country,
including RAPS-1, is 2720 MWe.
 
6.3.2    The projects currently under execution are 2X54O  MWe PHWRs  at Tarapur, Maharashtra (TAPP-3&4), 2X220
MWe PHWRs at   Kaiga, Karnataka,   2X220 MWe PHWRs at Rawatbhata, Rajasthan and  2X1000 MWe  VVERs  at
Kudankulam, Tamilnadu   (KK-1&2) .  The  project at Kudankulam is being set up in  co-operation with Russian
Federation.
 
6.4       Development Phase of Nuclear Power in India
 
6.4.1    The basic research in the nuclear field commenced about four decades ago in units of DAE. The initial R&D and
the experience in setting up and operations of  research reactors provided the core competence for the nuclear power
programme.  DAE, the Administrative Ministry, has  established over the years  comprehensive .capability in the entire
spectrum of nuclear fuel cycle in terms of fuel, special materials for nuclear power plants and nuclear waste
management facilities etc.
 
6.4.2    NPCIL has acquired comprehensive capability for designing, constructing, commissioning and operating nuclear
power plants. PHWRs of 220 MWe -unit size developed indigenously have reached a significant level of maturity.
Development of 540 MWe PIIWR has also been carried out indigenously and the  first  two  units are being set up at
Tarapur (TAPP-3&4). The 540 MWe unit rating of PHWR.s is also being updated to about 680 MWe with minimal
design changes and partial , boiling in the coolant channels for setting up PHWRs beyond TAPP-3&4.
 
6.4.3    The path of self- reliance has been chosen from the very beginning of the programme. Cost of generation from
nuclear power plants is comparable to contemporary coal thermal power plants located away from coal-mines. Nuclear
power is also associated with the advantage of being devoid of carbon-dioxide releases. The indigenous industries have
gained intense experience and are now in a position to take up the manufacture of critical nuclear components with high
precision.
 
With this background, nuclear power programme is now poised for rapid growth.
 
6.5       Potential of Nuclear Energy in India
 
6.5.1    With the approach of three-stage nuclear power progrmnme of DAE with pressurized heavy water reactors

(PHWRs) using natural uranium in the first stage, fast breeder reactors (FBRs) in the second stage and reactors using
U233 in thorium-U233 cycle in the third stage, the potential for electricity generation in the long-term is significant.
India's uranium resources are modest, but thorium resources are large, and the three-stage programme as above  will
enable utilising the full energy potential of uranium by  recycling pollution in the  second stage and ultimately utilize
thorium in third stage for electricity generation. The first stage programme of PHWRs with 220 ~1Vle and 540 MWe
unit sizes is well underway. As an additionally a 2X 1000 MWe Light Water Reactor  (LWR) units have also been
approved for construction at Kudankulam, Tamil nadu  in  co-operation with the Russian  Federation.
 
6.5.2    The Indira Gandhi1Center  for Atomic Research of DAE has embarked  upon  design of 500 MWe protype  
Fast  Breeder Reactor (PFBR) .  Construction of PFBR is  planned  to commence in X Plan.  PFBR being prototype 
commercial scale fast reactor,   will be front   runner of FBR  technology.
 
6.5.3    An Advanced Heavy water Reactor (AHWR), as technology demonstrator   for large-scale  utilisation of thorium
for power production, is also planned for commencement of  construction in the X plan by BARC.
 
6.6     Safety & Environmental Protection
 
6.6.1    NPCIL accords the highest priority on Quality Assurance (QA) and safety and environmental protection at all
stages of the nuclear power programme. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) which is an independent and
statutory body in terms of the Atomic Energy Act 1962, monitors, prescribes and enforces safety review at NPCIL.
Well-known design safety principles like defence-in-depth, multiple barriers, release of radioactivity and fail safe
designs are adopted in the engineering of the plants so that  releases from the plants will be well within the prescribed
limits stipulated by AERB.
 
 
During safety review at operational stage, release from the plants are monitored and regulated to be within the stipulated
limits. Environment Survey Laboratories are set up at each operating nuclear power station, which monitor a number of
samples of air, water, road and other products in the environment around the power station for radioactivity and the
reports of these laboratories are reviewed by AERB. Nuclear power is one of the environmentally clean sources for bulk
generation of electricity. It is very relevant in protection of the environment from greenhouse gases, acid rain and smog.
6.7          Human Resource Development
 
Human resource development has been given the required priority from the  early stages of nuclear power development
consistent with knowledge, expertise  and skill   required for setting up and operating the nuclear power stations. 
Specialised training units like BARC Training School and NPCIl Nuclear Training Centre and well designed
programmes like in-plant induction training, qualification of operation staff to different positions as per requirements of
AERB, on the job training and training in specific specialised in the human resource development in NPCIL.

Step up renovation and plant life extension programmes for the nuclear Power station
Sustain excellence in safety performance
Move towards financing capability through internal resource generation
Obtain financial resources required to set up the projects to achieve enhanced growth rate of nuclear power.
 
            NPCIL is taking action on all fronts to complete the above tasks
 
6.9           MISSION
            To develop nuclear power technology and produce in a self-reliant manner nuclear power as a safe,
environmentally benign, economically viable source of electrical energy to meet the growing electricity needs of the
country.

6.11     HISTORY OF MOU SYSTEM IN NPCL
 
6.11.1    The company, after its formation in September, 1987 studied the MOU system which a few Public Sector
Enterprises (PSEs) had adopted them,.  Seeing the advantages of the system for performance  improvement of the
company, NPCIL   for the first time entered into MOU with the Administrative Ministry i.e. Department of Atomic
Energy for the year 1991-92.  Since then, every year, MOU has been  signed between NPCIL and DAE.   The
performance evaluation is carried out based   on the stated commitments in the MOU.
 
6.11.2     The process of arriving at MOU is as follows:
 
(i)         Compiling comprehensive set of criteria for company’s performance evaluation.  These criteria broadly cover
the Generating Performance, profitability, Project milestones, quality assurance, Human Resource Development,
Research & Development, Environment Protection & Public Awareness, etc.  This   fulfills one of the objectives of the
industrial policy resolution of  1956 that the performance of all PSE’s should be judged by their over-all results.
 
(ii)        NPCIL assigns weightages to different criteria of the MOU based on the relative importance of the indicators
and priorities between different objectives of the company.The aspects stated above are evolved through a process of
participation by respective functional Directorates. The target values for, each parameter are fixed, based on the
commitment of executing agencies. The process of involvement is complemented by other documents like performance
budget, annual plan or capital budget and revenue budget generated by the company. After in-house deliberations and
finalisation, the details are reviewed at DAE, before the MOU is proposed for consideration of DPE. The institutional
arrangement for MOU facilitates the third party vetting by Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). The industry
specific Adhoc Task Force (ATF) of DPE vigorously examines the MOU and gives clearance for entering into
performance contract of MOU of NPCIL and DAE.

6.12     DISCUSSIONS WITH THE MANAGEMENT OF NPCIL
 
6.12.1    Shri V.K. Sharma, the acting CMD of NPCIL, made a presentation on the history of the corporation since its
incorporation in 1987 till today, including its ongoing projects and thereafter, the Committee deliberated with officers of
the NPCIL and the following points emanated from the discussions.
 
6.12.2   Since 1987 additional capacity of 1760 MWE has been created through commencement of commercial
operation at NAPS-1&2, KAPS and kaiga
 
6.12.3    The present Nuclear power capacity in the country is 2720 Mwe and projection for enhancement of this
capacity is 6680 Mwe by 2008 in the light of additional capacity enhancement of 3960 Mwe through completion of
ongoing projects at TAPP, KAIga and Rapp and Kudankulam. Overall contribution of Nuclear energy in the total
energy component of the country being a meagre three percent it was informed that Nuclear energy is highly cost
intensive and it has also to be seen in the context of energy contribution growing in other traditional sector through
capacity creation. Nuclear energy generation involves higher iterative process due to high order risk to ensure reduction
of occurrence of risk or to ensure improbability of occurrence of risk.  Incidentally the Nuclear power sector in the
country has zero accident record since 1968. In addition, availability of raw material uranium of 238 category is scarce
and India has deposits of U235 only and conversion of U 235 to 238 is also a cost intensive process.
 
6.12.4    The committee also sought an assurance against occurrence of a Chernobyl type accidents.  In this context, the
Committee was reassured that Chernobyl type technology is not licensable, and the NPCIL follows an extremely
transparent policy besides, having a sound system of in built periodic safety audits and stock taking.
 
6.12.5   In addition, the NPCIL is also learning from accidents in other countries.Moreover, as a member of IAEC India
is bound by their safety and other provision of Nuclear Power use and hence accidents are near improbable.
 
6.12.6    The Committee was also informed that the capacity utilization is about 87 percent  and there is a continuous
improvement of capacity factors.
           
6.12.7   The Committee was informed that one of the reasons for the slow growth of nuclear power in our country has
been the indigenous technology development phase that the nuclear power programme had to go through. Nuclear
power plants are very complex and require millions of smaller and bigger items/components to be designed, fabricated
and assembled. The licensing of nuclear power plants involves a complex regulatory process in which all the safety
aspects are checked. The nuclear power plants have been installed in advanced countries by sharing of technology
developed by different countries and using their fabrication capabilities. On account of the restrictive trade barriers and
technology denial regime prevalent for India, all the development had to be done within the country and this took time
initially.
 
6.12.8     The Committee was also apprised that Nuclear power has no significant avenues for overseas financing. It has
to rely on Government budgetary support in combination with domestic borrowing and internal surplus. A programme
of setting up of 10,000 MWe of nuclear power capacity by 2000 was formulated. There were problems on the
availability of financial resources during the VIII Five-Year Plan. Therefore, this programme could not be implemented
as envisaged.

manufacture all such components/equipments should be given.
(5.8.8)
              The Committee was pleased to note that NPCIL had been performing extremely well since its inception.
(6.13.1)
 
   The Committee also observed that having regard to the vital sector in which the unit is operating the structure of the
MOU should be more appropriately geared to this factor.  It was observed the focus on financial performance being
iterated in the MOU should be altered to shift the focus on more important factors of national interest. Hence the MoU
should accord higher weightage to performance parameters relating R&D, contribution to defense, contribution to
Indian Space Research Programme, Disaster Management and Relief efforts.
(6.13.2)
 
The Committee felt R&D, especially in the areas of import substitution in terms of development of new materials as
well as new process technologies, should be accorded much higher weightage in the interest of impetus to Indian
Nuclear Programmes.
(6.13.3)
  
This apart, the Committee felt that since the MOU is a mutually agreed document on performance parameters, a focus

shift in the contribution of Government for this type of PSE is also imperative.  The performance parameters of the
Department of Atomic Energy in the MOU should emphasis on more tangible factors like facilitating more in enabling
the company in recovering dues from SEB. 
(6.13.4)
 
The Committee also felt that MOUs should contain weightage for energy efficiency and resource efficiency efforts as
they also are to liable to reflect in the Balance Sheet of the Company under the Companies Act.
(6.13.5)
The Committee also felt that since the unit is operating in a strategic sector, it is imperative that it has a sound policy for
retention and upgradation of skills of its Human Resource.  This is more than imperative for a unit like NPCIL having
regard to its strategic contribution to India’s defence and infrastructure sector. It is therefore felt that the weightage for
HRD should also be higher.  At the same time the excellent expertise and human resource base should also be exported
in the form participation in safety audit teams constituted by IAEC, mutual inspection teams etc
(6.13.6)
            Also higher weightage should be accorded in the MOU for safety parameters besides, developing fail safe
technologies and excellent safety record and also the environment of high improbabity of risk.  
(6.13.7)
 
 Ecological and environmentally sustainable operation is also a vital area of concern for Nuclear Power.  Weightage to
this should also be accorded appropriately.
(6.13.8)
 
            As regards introduction of systems upgradation like Extra Resource Planning etc, the Committee observed that
the NPCIL is having its own LAN systems and felt little need for a performance enhancing systems application like
ERP.  In this context, it is the considered view of the Committee that NPCIL, which is working in high tech sector,
needs to be alert to organizational decays and take remedial measures through process reengineering of its work
systems. Hence, MOU weight should also be accorded for this appropriately.
(6.13.9)
 
            The Committee feels that considering the self-reliant manner in which nuclear power has been developed,
Government should provide higher financial allocation and resources for the growth of Nuclear power.

IL BACKGROUND OF MOU SYSTEM

2.1 The Department of Public Enterprises in its Background Note on the MoU system stated that the
MoU system was introduced as a major policy initiative by the Central Government as an important tool
to improve the performance of the Central Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs). The New Industrial Policy
of 1991 laid greater emphasis on the MoU system requiring all PSEs to be brought under the ambit of
the MoU system. Beginning with four PSEs in 1987-88, the MoU system has now been extended to a
large number of PSEs. By 2000-2001, 108 PSEs had signed the MoUs.

2.2 It was stated that the main objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of the
PSEs by imparting increased autonomy and accountability and to provide a method of evaluation of the
performance of the managements of the PSEs in an objective and transparent manner. Further, the
objective of providing clarity of goals to be achieved by PSEs is another dimension of the MoU system.

2.3. The Committee has noted that there is a High Power Committee (HPC) at the apex level, headed
by the Cabinet Secretary which is basically a policy making body for the MoUs. This HPC consists of
Secretaries of all nodal Departments of Government such as Finance, Expenditure, Planning
Commission and Programme Implementation, etc. The HPC undertakes the evaluation of the
performance of the PSEs and in addition the HPC also provides a forum to resolve inter-ministerial
issues.

2.4 To assist HPC in this task and also to provide the technical inputs and to finalise the MoUs, there
is an Advisory Body called Adhoc Task Force (ATF), it was stated. The members of the ATF are drawn
from various fields having vast experience in their areas and include retired Secretaries, Chief
Secretaries, top experts in different disciplines like finance, management, science and technology, and
prominent academicians. This body provides neutrality and objectivity to the MoU system.

2.5 The Department has also informed that under the present set up there is a small MoU Division
under the Department of Public Enterprises, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, which
co-ordinates the entire exercise of finalizing the MoUs in respect of all the PSEs numbering 108. In
addition to finalizing the MoUs, the MoU Division is also responsible for the evaluation of performance
of PSEs, both on the basis of the provisional as well as the audited results.

http://164. 100.24. 167/book2/reports/indus/83rdreport.htm 1/27/05


83rd Report Page 5 of 15

2.6 Explaining about the process of preparing MoUs, the Department have stated that the MoU
process starts with the issuing of guidelines by the DPE to the PSEs/Administrative Ministries for
drafting the MoUs. The PSEs prepare their MoUs on the basis of these guidelines. These draft MoUs
are then discussed with the Administrative Ministries and in the Boards of the PSEs. They are then
submitted to the DPE. DPE prepares background papers and its comments on each draft MoU keeping
in view the past performance of the PSE, its future potential, the industry scenario and the economic
environment of the PSE, it was added. It was further stated that these draft MoUs are discussed in the
MoU negotiation meetings where the ATF members, managements of the PSE, officials from the
Administrative Ministries and the representatives from nodal Government Agencies like Ministry of
Finance, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation and Planning Commission are also
present. The MoUs and the targets are finalised in these meetings through mutual discussions.

EXPORT CREDIT GUARANTEE CORPORATION
_OF INDIA LIMITED (ECGC)

L PROFILE

1.1 Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. (ECGC) was set up in 1957 by the
Government of India to support and strengthen the export promotion efforts of the country. The
corporation provides insurance cover to exporters against non-receipt of the payment for their exports
due to commercial and political risks. Export Credit Insurance seeks to create a favorable climate in
which exporters get timely and liberal facilities from banks. For this purpose, the corporation issues
policies and guarantees. The Registered and Corporate/Head Office of the corporation is located at
Mumbai. There are five regional offices at Mumbai, Chennai, Bangalore, Kolkata and New Delhi and 26
branches are also located in various cities in the country.

1.2... ECGC offers various policies which include standard policies, specific policies, financial
guarantee, transfer guarantee, overseas investment etc. The corporation has designed following five
types of standard policies to provide cover for shipments made on short-term credit :

Shipments (Comprehensive Risks) Policy — to cover both commercial and political risks from the date of

shipment.
Shipments (Political Risk) Policy — to cover only political risk from the date of shipment.

Small Exporters Policy — to cover both commercial and political risks or only political risk from the date
of shipment for the use of Small Exporters.

Contract (comprehensive Risks) Policy- to cover both commercial and political risks from the date of
contract.

Contracts (Political Risks) Policy — to cover both commercial and political risks from the date of
contract.

1.3 Specific policies are offered to provide continuous cover on the shipments of raw material,

http://164. 100.24. 167/book2/reports/indus/83rdreport.htm 1/27/05


83rd Report Page 6 of 15

consumer goods and consumer durables for which credit period does not exceed 180 days. Contracts for
export of capital goods or tumkey projects or construction works or rendering services abroad are not of
a repetitive nature. Such transactions are therefore insured by ECGC on a case - to — case basis under

specific policies.

1.4. Inorder to encourage banks to give adequate credit and other facilities for exports and protect
them from losses on account of their lending to exporters, ECGC provides financial guarantees which
include packing credit guarantee, export, production, finance guarantee, post-shipment export credit
guarantee, export performance guarantee, and export finance (overseas lending) guarantee. The
company also provides transfer guarantee, overseas investment insurance etc.

Il MISSION OF THE COMPANY
To support the Indian Export Industry by providing cost effective insurance and trade related

services to meet the needs of the Indian export market.

tm. OBJECTIVES OF THE COMPANY
To encourage, facilitate and develop trade between India and other countries.

To provide adequate export credit insurance cover, comparable to similar covers available to exporters
in other countries so that Indian exporters would be able to save themselves from losses that may arise
due to credit risks both commercial and political and also be in a position to maximize their export

business.

To provide the banks in India with export credit guarantee with a view to enable them to extend
adequate credit facilities to the Indian exporters both in pre-shipment and post-shipment stages.

To provide investment insurance to Indian investors undertaking investments in foreign countries

To operate the various schemes in such a manner that the Corporation would generate enough surpluses
to enable it to meet any losses that may result from unforeseen political situations.

To introduce new product lines so as to diversify into trade related services.
TV. | MOU OF ECGC FOR THE YEAR 2002-02

4.1 In the MOU meeting held to finalize the MOU of ECGC for the year 2002-03, the issues
relating to the opening up of insurance sector and its implications for ECGC were discussed in detail. It
was noted that ECGC would face competition in the near future and the company should be geared to
meet the same. It was agreed to introduce an criteria of preparation of strategic plan by the company in
the year which would define its new role and activities in the new changed environment. It was also
noted that with the registration of ECGC with IRDA, the position with respect to determination of rates
of premium was unclear. The company was planning to improve its image, ensure better communication
with clients, and undertake customer surveys and speedy settlement of claims.

4.2 Inthe MOU of ECGC, instead of the usual profitability parameters the financial criteria of Gross
surplus of business income over expenditure before tax, Gross margin,. other income before tax and Net
profit/Net worth (excluding reserves for unexpired risks) has been incorporated. Efficiency parameters
such as Treasury management, Recovery management, Reduction of Administrative Expenses,
Factoring, commerce, Outsourcing, Introduction of new products, Time taken for various work
processes and undertaking market surveys have also been added in the MOU.

V. Discussions with the management of Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC)

5.1 The Sub-Committee interacted with the management of ECGC at Mumbai. The CMD Shri
P.M.A. Hakeem gave a brief account of the work being done by ECGC. He informed the Sub-
Committee about the role played by ECGC towards the promotion of exports. Dr. Ramaiah, the
convenor enquired about the performance of ECGC on the MOU parameters to which Shri Hakeem
gave a detailed account of the performance targets achieved by ECGC. The Sub-Committee was also
informed about the losses incurred by ECGC on account of high value claims in 1991 on account of
Iraqi projects due to the gulf war. ECGC had now wiped out all the losses carried since 1991 and was
expected to declare a net profit before tax of Rs.75 crores for 2001-02. The Sub-Committee was also
informed of the corporate plan of ECGC, which included customer specific products to suit the needs of
the customer. The CMD also informed that ECGC had been enhancing its presence by expanding its
existing distribution channels by opening new branches, satellite centres and special promotion
agencies. Besides ECGC is also endeavoring to upgrade the knowledge, skill and expertise of its
manpower through regular training programmes. The Sub-Committee was also informed that ECGC had
introduced Maturity factoring for exporters since 17 April 2002. The CMD was asked to spell out the
future plan of ECGC in context of the liberalization of the Indian economy and in view of the opening of
the insurance sector within the purview of (Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority) IRDA.
The Sub-Committee was informed that ECGC will try to transform itself into a multi-product
organization from a single product organization so as to service the requirements of a large number of
customers and give a fillip to its business.

5.2 With respect to the financial position of the company, the Sub-Committee was informed that
against a capital base of Rs.415 crores as on date, the total exposure in terms of maximum liability
undertaken by ECGC is Rs. 40,000 crores. The annual premium income has grown from Rs.89.51 crores
in 1991-92 to Rs.330.45 crore in 2001-02 showing a growth of 269 percent . On asked whether ECGC
is assuming risks disproportionate to its capital base, the Committee was informed that the Government
had agreed to provide a further sum of Rs. 25 crores towards the paid up capital of ECGC during the
current year to raise it from the present level of Rs. 415 crores to Rs. 440 crores.

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE

6.1 The Committee is of the view that ECGC should expand the range of its activities to cater to
medium and small-scale exporters. The Committee recommends that ECGC should endeavour towards
specialization based on customer segmentation based on customer size, which has become a necessity in
the present circumstances.

6.2 The Committee after examining the performance of ECGC within the MOU parameters is of the
opinion that weightage should be given to the role played by ECGC in providing impetus to exports in
the small-scale sector. The Committee feels that the SSI sector makes a marked presence in the export

शा. NATIONAL FILM DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION (NEDC)

PROFILE
National Film Development Corporation Ltd. (NFDC) is a Public Sector Enterprise set up in

1975 under the companies Act, 1956.The company was restructured during 1980 by the merger of the
erstwhile Indian Motion Picture Export Corporation (IMPEC) and Film Finance Corporation (FFC) and
the company emerged as Central Agency to promote good cinema in the country. Over the years, NFDC
has provided a wide range of services essential to the integrated growth of Indian cinema Besides
producing and financing films NFDC exports Indian films all over the world and imports commercial
films, Tele-films and serials for distribution and exhibition in the country. Other technical services
provided by NFDC include recording and dubbing, production equipment hiring, subtitling of films,
video duplication, video production, postproduction etc.

VUI. MISSION OF THE COMPANY
To plan and promote an integrated and efficient development of film industry and to be a leader
in fostering excellence in cinema and to develop state of the art infrastructure as well as quality products

in the audio-visual and related fields

Ix. OBJECTIVES
Generation of revenue of Rs. 90.00 crores through the activities mentioned at serial nos. (a) to (e)

below :-
Distribution of Indian and Foreign films through various channels such as theatres and television to
ensure its wider reach.

(b) Promotion of Indian film and television software abroad, through exports by
participation in various international film markets and in other ways.

(c) Import and development of state-of-art pre-production and post- production technical
infrastructure such as camera, editing and recording facilities required by the film industry in Chennai,
Kolkata and Mumbai and hiring out of these facilities.

(d) A beginning to be made in providing appraisals services for the film industry.
(e) To ensure sustained financial appraisal services.
Financing/Producing of about 11 quality films.
Promotion of culture and understanding through film media by organizing foreign and Indian film
weeks in collaboration with Film Societies/State Film Development corporations in India and abroad.
Promotion of social security and welfare measures for needy Cine/Artists of yester years through
Cine Artistes Welfare Fund Of India - the Trust set up by the Corporation.

XII. OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee was of the opinion that in today’s world the impact of mass media is tremendous.
However, commercial considerations should not be the sole criteria for production of films. The
Committee strongly feels that films, which are socially relevant, must get preference in NFDC.

The Committee during the course of deliberations was of the opinion that NFDC should play a more
active role towards the popularization of Indian Cinema at the international level. The Committee
recommends that NFDC should provide support to both Indian films and Indian Directors to enable
them to get international exposure and success.

The Committee is of the considered opinion that the film festivals being organized by NFDC are mainly
held in major metropolitan cities. The Committee recommends that film festivals should be held in
smaller towns so as to propagate and promote Indian cinema and to provide wider audience.

The Committee feels that NFDC should help in promoting regional films so as to enable them to get all
India viewer ship. The Committee recommends that NFDC should help in the distribution/exhibition of
regional films by providing Hindi/English subtitles.

The Committee is of the opinion that Indian Cinema cannot remain isolated from the global cinema and
hence steps to bring good quality foreign cinema must be made. The Committee recommends that
NFDC should bring in good quality foreign cinema to India.

The Committee was informed that resource constraint has been a major factor hampering the growth of
NFDC. The Committee feels that with the grant of Industry status to the film industry financial
institutions can finance the production of quality films The Committee strongly recommends that
government should take up the matter with the financial institutions so that more loans are extended
NFDC.

setting up seven lakh micro enterp rises during the Eight Five Year  Plan (1993-97), through industry, 
services and business routes. The scheme was operated in urban ar eas only during 1993-94, and in both

educated unemployed youth have benefited from th e scheme. The PMRY is continuing in the Tenth
Plan period.

1.4    The Committee observes that the target (2.20 lakh beneficiaries) set for PMRY is too low to have
any significant impact on the creati on of employment opportunities in the country. This issue weighted
on the Committee's discussion with of ficials of State Government, Mini stry of Agro & Rural Industries
during its visit to Andhra Pradesh, Kamataka, Kerala. The Committee no ted that the target fixed each
year for PMRY has remained st atic during the last three year s i.e. for 2000-01, 2001-02 and 2002-03 
only 2.20 lakh persons were to be c overed under PMRY scheme. This figure, when divided between the
states and thereafter, among districts of each state, is like a drop. Th is figure is too minuscule to have
any noticeable impact on the unemployment scenario in a country of millions. 
  
1.5    The Ministry of Small Scale Industries, with whom the matter was taken up explained that the 
fixing of target was based on two aspects: - 
(a)
    Basic Target which is fixed, and is based on th e State's population as in 1991. This target is 
given by the Planning Commissi on, and is based on the employm ent potential and the numbe r
of unemployed registered with Employment Excha nge. An annual. target of 2.2 lakhs is given
for 2002-03, on an all India basis. This is communicated in March every year, for the next year.

tile target under PMRY which are as under:- 
  
(a)  Banks complained that there is generall y delay in communicating PMRY targets to them,
which results in delay in grounding of the unit. Also, selection of beneficiaries is done only on
specific dates. The delay in comm unicating target of the banks le ads to delay in sanctioning o f
loans and subsequent disbursal of loans to the beneficiaries. Target is communicated in two
installments, which results in delay in its implementation.

unviable. Autorickshaws, photocopy shops, STD booths etc were cite d as examples. Banks
hesitate to sanction loans for activities of simi lar nature as these activities reach a saturation
point which is a major reason to the failure of the scheme. 
  
(c)  Most beneficiaries go in for trade and business activities. 
  
(d)  Percentage of overdues to total loans is 67 per cent, which is a matter of great concern. 
  
(e)  Absconding entrepreneurs who divert funds and close shop are also a matter of concern. 
  
(f)   From the entrepreneurs' side, request for change in activ ity results in delay in getting
approvals. 
  
(g)  Marketing of products is a problem area which entrepreneurs find difficult to surmount.

and Kerala may not be sufficie nt for sustenance of the sc heme, they should provide cnough
encouragement to banks to improve their participation.

mostly for service and business in Kerala. Certain activities like auto rickshaws have become saturated.
Applications for industries sector are very few due to reasons like labour problems power and extensive
investment required in infrastructure like land, building etc. 
  
4.5    The Committee recommends th at each region, particularly at th e District and Bl ock level should
identify viable activities and prepare project profiles  to help the borrower and the bank to select viable
projects. DIC and banks should meet regularly in wo rkshops to identify viab le and feasible vocations
and prepare project profiles. This ha s to be done at Dist rict and State level at  least once a year. The
agencies involved in implementation of the programme should participate in such programmes. 
  
4.6    The Committee notes that the beneficiaries are selected from th e age group of 18-35 years. The 
lower age limit requires to be increased to bring more mature youth to the scheme, .the Committee feels.

4.7    The Committee observes that  though the ceiling on project co st under PMRY has been increased
from Rs.1 Lakh to Rs.2 Lakhs with effect from 199 9-2000; for activities other than business, no 
perceptible increase in the amount of the average loan disbursed is  observed. This may indicate that
either there is a predominance of business activities in the cases sanctioned, or hanks have taken a
routine target-oriented approach in  the implementation of the scheme with little care for the actual
requirement of funds for setting up micro-enterpris es. There is concern that  activities are being unde r 
financed which lead to their una vailability and their misuse ri ght from the very beginning. The
Committee, therefore, advise that Model Project Profiles should be prepar ed in every district on
successful activities and banks could release the financing, according to these model profiles. 
  
MARKETING OF PRODUCTS 
4.8    The entrepreneurs find it very  difficult to sell their products in present days' stiff competition. The
Committee, therefore, observes that  permanent sales outlets should be  set up at Block/ Taluk/ District
levels. The Government may provide  infrastructure, including space and staff for running such sales
outlets. 
  
PUBLICITY 
4.9    The Committee finds that  not enough has been done to popular ize the scheme. The Committee
observes that all possible measures should be taken to ensure adequate publicity to the scheme to create
greater awareness in order to invite  applications from elig ible candidates in greater numbers. This will,
in turn, ensure a wider choice during selection of candidates. Fu rther, the Green Channel (Single
Window) system introduced at the dist rict level should be made more effective in assisting more and
more beneficiaries to come forward for starting micro-enterprises. 
  
SUBSIDY 
4.10  In order to attract more and more educated youth to the scheme, the Committee feels 
.     Subsidy ceiling of Rs.7500 be raised to Rs.15,OOO subject to a minimum of 15 per cent. 
.     The ceiling on income (R s.40,OOO) may be enhanced to Rs.50,OOO to Rs.60,O OO so as to
enlarge the selection zone. 
  
CHANGING THE MINDSET OF BANKS 
  
4.11  Frequent review meetings by DIC, along with supporting bankers to take stock of the assisted
projects, may go a long way in imp roving the working of the micro enterprises and enable the banks
borrowers to take corrective steps at the earliest stage wh erever required. This is  expected to improve
the success rate of the assisted projects. 
  
TRAINING TO ENTERPRENEURS 
  
4.12 It is borne out by experience that the success rate is  higher when the applic ant possesses required
training on the vocation prior to starting the enterpri se. Necessary training inputs should be given to the
prospective applicants before sponsoring the a pplications. Besides, DIC and other governmental
agencies may also be associate for imparting trai ning at the pre-application stage. The modules fo r 
training need to be reviewed and revised periodically to suit the requirement of new entrepreneurs and in
keeping with the market scenario. 
  
4.13 The Committee finds that although at tempts were made to achieve quantitative targets in the case
of PMRY, no serious effort was made  to achieve qualitative targets. Entrepreneurs have to face many
hurdles like power connec tions, frequent inspections, lack of infrastructure, while embarking on an
enterprise. The scheme is not a smooth for a beginner. Moreover, th ere are other schemes like REGP
which offer more incentives/concessions/subsid
y to the entrepreneurs and prove to be more allurin g to

them. In view of the these constr aints, the PMRY scheme needs to  be given a new orientation and
provided with more incentives so as  to bring the ma jority of rural populance and weaker section of the
society into the ambit of the sc heme and raise their economic c ondition and bring them into the
mainstream of the nation. Only by taking suitable initiatives to modify the scheme in such away as so to
make it sustainable a nd attractive, and by taki ng effective steps to popul arize the scheme, bette r
recovery performance, if can be made effective. 
  
4.14 The Committee recommends that Districts recordin g better recovery performance should be 
targeted for better coverage under the scheme. 
  
RECOVERY IN ANDHRA PRADESH, KARNATAKA AND KERALA 
  
4.15 It may be observed that recovery performance of the States has remained ei ther static or has been
showing a decreasing trend as  in the case of Kerala . Three out of the five State in the region, Andhra
Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala have  already enacted Revenue Recove ry Acts notifying PMRY dues at
par with Land- Revenue dues. Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka have also posted special Tehsildars in the
districts for recovery of loans under the Government sponsored programme. 
  
4.16  Central Government have laid emphasis on ag ro and village industries by creating a separate
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industrie s. To give a meaningful impetus to Agro and Rural Industries, the
Committee recommends setting up of  Centre -State forum on A&RI where under the Officers of the 
Central Govt. would meet the Stat e Industry Deptt., District Industr ies Centre, industry associations,
entrepreneurs, and banks from time  to time to get feed back about  the credit flow, infrastructural
facilities, and other difficulties faced by the Agro and Rural Industries, and formulate possible solutions.
The Committee hope that the Centra l and State Government should jo in hands in bringing more and
more people under the ambit of the Agro and Rural Industries.

REPORT
 
1.Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited (HSCL) is an offshoot of the Construction Division of Steel Authority 
of India Ltd. ( SAIL). The company was incorporated in 1964 with the prime objective of creating in Public Sector an
organisation capable of-taking-up   the construction of  modern  Steel Plants in the country. HSCL has executed works
in Steel Plants right from inception till commissioning, viz, Bokaro Steel plant, Vizag Steel Plant, Salem Steel Plant and
was  associated  with the expansion and modernisation activities of Bhilai Steel Plant, Durgapur Steel Plant, IISCO
(Burnpur)  as  also Bhadravati Steel Plant.  With the decline  in traditional work-order , the company  diversified its
activities  in  other sectors like  power , coal, oil and  gas and also  infrastructural facilities like  roads/highways,
bridges, dams, underground-communication and transport system besides  industrial and  township  complexes
involving  high degree of planning, coordination and modern sophisticated techniques. The Company gained experience
in the areas like civil works of plant building, structural fabrication and erection in industrial plants, and erection of
Equipment in the Steel Plants. As SAIL expanded its activities, activities of HSCL also expanded.  Apart from activities
in SAIL, the company expanded its activities in other areas, like civil works for buildings, other than SAIL, Dam
Construction'. Bridge construction, coal handling plants, road construction, stadium complexes, school buildings and
industrial townships etc. The company also gained experience in planning & coordination in steel & non-steel sectors.
1.2       The authorized capital of the company has been raised from Rs.20.00 crore to Rs.150.00 crore on approval of 
Government of India through the financial restructuring-cum-financial assistance package sanctioned to the company. 
Similarly, the paid  up  capital  has also been increased from Rs.20.00 crore to rs.117.10 crore.
1.3       The Ministry of Steel  informed the Sub -Committee that  HSCL suffered   in 1970s primarily   due to two
reasons . The first factor was the sudden  increase in work force between 1970-79 from 4,100 to 26,537.  Of this,
Bokaro unit alone   accounted for 12,600.  This  was due to the  crisis created when a large number of public sector and
private  companies engaged by Bokaro Steel   failed and left their  work sites leaving behind  their workforce.  Due to
pressure, both from the Government and from the steel plants.  HSCL  had to take over these works along with the
workforce, in order to  complete the works within the   stipulated time.  The other major factor responsible for the
company's decline was the lack of   substantial activity in the  steel sector.   The works awarded to HSLCL by the steel
plants  after 1974 were  not adequate  to sustain the additional recurring liabilities, mainly due to increase wage bills on
account of statutory hikes including  revision of pay and increase in the number of workforce.  As a result of the above
factors,   the company began to incur continuous losses from 1978-79 onwards (except 1985-86) and  as on 31.3.1999
the accumulated loss stood at Rs.1383.28 crore.  Another  factor  which  also contributed to the downgrading of the 
company is the huge  loss suffered by HSCL on Libyan works, undertaken under  Government  of India  protocol,  due
to reasons beyond the control of the  company .
 
1.4       The Committee notes that the reasons as placed  by the Ministry of Steel, for the suffering of  HSCL.  The
Committee is of the  opinion  that  lack of vision for  human resource management and  lack of a concrete policy  led to
and sudden increase in work force in HSCL.  The Committee further  opines  that HSCL's present suffering is due to
error of judgment and some elements were beyond  the  control of   management   and Government due to prevailing 
circumstances, lack of managerial vision and manpower policy added to the woes  of HSCL.

2.2.      The Committee, while taking note of the current financial performance of HSCL  expresses its concern over its
pathetic conditions,  and is of the view  that  HSCL  needs  improvement for  better financial   performance.  HSCL 
requires a  new vision, new managerial  will and effective strategy for the  continuance  of  its existence.
3.         FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE -CUM-RESTRUCTURING PACKAGE
3.1       With a view to bail out the company from its financial crisis, a comprehensive financial restructuring proposal
was approved by Government of India/CCEA in  9
th July, 1999.  The revival  package provided  several financial
assistance/exemptions  which, inter-alia, included :-
Conversion of plan loans  of Rs.97.10 crore as on 31.3.99 into equity
Grant of moratorium on repayment  of and interest holiday on all Government  of India    loans upto 31.3.99 for 10
years.
Waiver of interest accrued and outstanding on all GOI loans as on 31.3.99 amounting to around Rs.975.17 crore
Non-plan loan of  Rs.79.33 crore during 1999-2000  for payment of statutory dues with moratorium on repayment and
interest holiday for five years subject to a review at the end of  five years.
Exemption of corporate tax in 1999-2000 on  account of windfall profit due to waiver of interest on loans.
Continuance of Government  guarantee of Rs.92.00  crore, Rs12.00 crore  cash credit  and  Rs.80.00 crore bank
guarantee  facilities, with waiver of guarantee  commission of one per cent .
It is expected that HSCL will rationalise its manpower through VRS scheme and necessary funds for the same will be 
raised from banks.  The Government will provide guarantee and full interest subsidy  for raising loan of Rs.318.36
crore   during the  three  years  i.e. 1999 -2000 to 2001-02 for separating  2000 employees per year.
 
3.2       The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government for approving the  financial restructuring
proposal.  Considering the  fact that resources are limited the  sanctioning    of revival  package  having financial
implication is a  considered decision of the Government.  Committee also appreciates the Ministry of Steel for its
consistent    efforts in persuading the Ministry of Finance for  giving   revival package  to  HSCL.   The  Committee
notes the provisions  of revival package for  HSCL.
4.         Implementation of status of revival package
4.1       As regards the status of  implementation of  financial-cum-assistance  restructuring  package, the  Sub-
Committee was  informed by  the Ministry of Steel that action has already  been taken on   point (i) to (iv).  In respect 
of the issue  regarding (v) exemption from payments of corporate tax on  account  profit   due to waiver of interest on

Committee further  hopes that  consequent upon the  separation of  7,106  employees and reduction in the wage bill, the

5.2       The Committee observes that financial assistance-cum-restructuring package  as proposed by the Ministry of
Steel and so approved by the Government was not as  comprehensive so as to mitigate the accumulated loss and total 
liability of HSCL.  The company continues to rein in adverse financial scenario and disadvantages in  general because
implementation of the revival package would  respond  only  if approved  measures are  taken in time for total  and
comprehensive restructuring of the company.  HSCL  needs total  overhauling  and complete and comprehensive 
restructuring in one  go as partial  package and  delayed implementation  defeats   the whole  idea, approach and  action.
5.3       At present, the company has 5997 skilled technical and non-technical personnel on its roll.  The expenditure
towards salary  and wages in 2001-02 is estimated to be about Rs.63 crore against Rs.146.09 crore in 1998-99.  The
actual loss of Rs.172.55 crore in  2000-01 was expected to come down to Rs.133 crore in 2001-02.  The  company
cannot stand on its own with wage  and statutory dues accumulating  to around Rs.205 crore as on 1.2.02 .   A proposal
has been put up to the Finance Ministry  by the Administrative Ministry for favourable consideration.  It is a harsh fact
that with gradual reduction in margin due to fierce   competition in the  present   market economy situation, the
company can not sustain the salary burden of 6000 employees at the turnover level of Rs.275.00 crore.  In view of the
above, the  company proposes to obtain Government guarantee for a further loan of Rs.250.00 crore to separate another
5000 employees.  This would enable the company to manage with a manpower figure of around 1000 at an annual
expenditure of  about 12 crore towards salary and wages.
5.4       The Committee is of the view that once the comprehensive restructuring package is effectively implemented
HSCL  would acquire  sufficient   resilience   and synergy to work even against fierce competition.  The Committee
recommends that HSCL management should strive in this regard. 
5.5       The Sub-Committee wanted to know the reasons as to why, despite the implementation of Financial Assistance
cum Restructuring package as sought by the Ministry of Steel in tandem with HSCL management and as approved by
Government in July, 1999, the accumulated loss of HSCL stood at Rs. 532 crore as on March 2000, and the expected
loss for the year 2000-2001 was Rs.65 crore. The HSCL management stated that the loss of Rs. 532 crore as on
31.3.2000 and another Rs.65 crore as on 31.3.2001 is mainly attributable to the insurmountable factors which include:-
Turnover could not be raised to the level required as per the restructuring proposal; 
Lack of work orders from Steel Plants due to continuing decline in Steel Industry;
Recession in construction Industry;
 Delay in getting loan for VRS;
Under-utilisation and idling of manpower and resources at Steel Plants.
5.6       The Committee is constrained to express its concern over the fact that financial assistance given for 
restructuring  package  could not be implemented in the  expected   manner and the outcome    thereof   is not  as
expected.   The Committee notes the  reasons  for failure of revival package,  although it is not fully envisaged with the
reasons for  failure  of  revival package  as advocated by the Ministry of Steel.  For the  revival of the company, HSCL
management has to procure work order despite ups and downs in Steel Industry and HSCL management  should not
face  much  difficulties as Government   is giving  due importance  to the construction sector.  The committee  is  of the 
view that optimum utilisation   of manpower and  resources at the  disposal of company is the responsibility of HSCL
management.

6.         Reasons for  partial failure of  Financial Assistance -cum- restructuring package
6.1       The Ministry of Steel  informed the Sub-Committee that  the Restructuring package could not yield the desired
result and advocated  the under mentioned detailed reasons for the partial failure of the restructuring package: -
Delay of about eleven months by commercial bank in the sanction and disbursement of the first phase of loan for VRS
amounting to Rs.210 Crore, forcing the company to carry idle wages.   In the revival plan it was envisaged to separate
2000 employees per year beginning with 1999-2000 but the loan amount was only disbursed in June, 2000 due to late
sanction. As a result, the actual separation under VRS could be effected only thereafter.
The projections in terms of profit & loss as contained in revival package were made with regard to the prevailing market
condition at that time. Since then, the market condition have shown a down turn and even big companies like SAIL have
been incurring losses.
Most of the works undertaken by HSCL are being sub-contracted primarily because of the age profile of its employee
and also the difficulties faced in their redeployment on work sites which are scattered all over India. Most of the receipts
of HSCL are passed on as payments to Sub contractor, thereby leaving a very marginal amount for utilisation towards
meeting overheads like salaries /wages etc.
HSCL has diversified its operations in the non-steel sector as jobs from the steel sector had virtually not coming up. The
margins in the diversified areas are very low, and this  means that HSCL would continue to incur losses.
HSCL has been replacing its  obsolete equipment in order to execute the works efficiently at site. During the years
1999-2000 and 2000-2001 equipments for an amount of Rs.35 lakhs and Rs.2.38 crore respectively were purchased.
Further in 2000-01, order for one excavator cum loader for Bokaro Unit for Rs.71 lakhs have been placed during the
year.
 
6.2       The Committee,  while taking note of the detailed reasons for partial failure of  Financial Assistance
restructuring package, is constrained to express its concern.  The Committee  is of the view that HSCL  management
could  have well  managed and controlled  the problems being faced by  HSCL. The Committee views that replacement
of obsolete equipment in HSCL  should have  positive  impact on the operational efficiency of company  rather than  
deterring   the implementation of revival package.  Moreover, HSCL management should chalk out  a strategy for better
margin of profit. The Committee opines that HSCL management while implementing VRS should keep in mind the age 
profile in the company  so as to retain capable and   efficient  the work  force  to undertake  the job.
 
6.3       The Sub-Committee wanted to know the reasons for delay of about eleven months by Commercial Bank in the
sanction and disbursement of the First Phase of the loan for VRS to Rs.210 crore and steps which were taken by HSCL
management to avoid the delay.  The management stated  that immediately after receiving the communication for
approval of Financial Restructuring-cum-Financial Assistance Package of HSCL, SBI, LHO, Patna, was contacted for
consideration of sanction of VRS Loan.  Since initially there was no positive response from the Banks, a high level
committee consisting of CMD, D(F), Executive Director, HSCL and Joint Secretary, Ministry of Steel visited Sr.
Officials of SBI, at their central office at Mumbai and held discussions at the highest level.  Subsequently SBI Capital
Market was assigned the job of syndication of VRS Loan on 3
rd September 1999.  Finally, SBI  LHO, Patna
communicated the sanction of VRS Loan for Rs.209.82 crore on 25th March, 2000 and the amount was drawn on 2nd
June, 2000.  The main reasons for delay in sanctioning and disbursement of the fund by SBI as informed by Ministry of
Steel , are mentioned below ;-

7.0       HSCL becoming a sub-contracting company
7.1       Replying to the Sub-Committee's query regarding HSCL becoming a sub-contracting company from a
construction company resultant and the possibility of sustenance of company under changed circumstances, the
management stated that the company has to resort to sub-contracting to augment the order book position in the face of
stiff competition from the construction sector.  It also has to offset difficulties like severe cash crunch to deposit
EMD/SD etc. and funds for procurement of raw materials and other inputs.  Sub-contracting is also necessitated due to
the fact that shifting manpower and other resources from steel plants to short duration projects is not only expensive but
also invites social and other local resistance.  Moreover, the age profile of the employees is also a deterrent in carrying
out the works departmentally.  Low margins due to competition and inadequacy of related expertise and skill are also
strong factors compelling adoption of sub-contracting system.
7.2       The HSCL management clarified that the company has neither become, nor has any plans to become out and out
a sub-contracting company.  It has a rich team of experienced engineers, workers, technicians and a strong fleet of
construction equipments, as its backbone.  In most cases, the company executes the jobs giving maximum possible
departmental inputs combining with it the strengths of the sub-contractors.  The extent of departmental inputs varies
according to location and nature of work.  As of now, the downward trend has been witnessed and therefore, given the
difficult circumstances enveloping the Company, the process is expected to remain the way it is for some more time. 
Till then, the primary concern of the company would be the payment of salary and wages to its employees as well as
liquidation of all other liabilities.  Once out of this predicament, the company's performance is bound to increase
through better utilization of equipments, supervision, design, procurement and monitoring besides direct execution as
much as possible.  Under the changed scenario and market economy, the system of sub-contracting (with maximum
departmental inputs) cannot be altogether discarded.  The execution arrangement, as elaborated above, is practical and
sustainable, if the liabilities reduce. 
7.3       The Committee understands the  compelling  circumstances under which HSCL has to adopt the system of  sub-
contracting  business pattern but   it is also an open secret that sub-contracting   gives low margin for HSCL than if the
work done by the company itself.  The  Committee  is of the view  that VRS  offer  by HSCL  to its employees would
take care of keeping with itself the workforce consisting of  productive age profile and  willing to undertake
work/assignment from whatever concern its coming.  The Committee feels that  direct undertaking of work by HSCL
staff would give larger margin to HSCL and thus opening scope for profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better
that the  system of sub-Contracting  is replaced by direct involvement of HSCL employees,  sooner than later.
8.0       Work Order position of HSCL

9.3       Since inception and over the years, majority of the resources and infrastructural facilities had been built up in
PSU Steel Plants.  However, the continuing decline in the steel sector during the last several years has cast a shadow of
uncertainty on the question of sustenance of the company.  During the earlier years, steel plant projects were being
awarded to HSCL on nomination basis.  As a time progressed, the special status of the company with SAIL Steel Plants,
for the construction which the company was framed, got eroded. With the introduction of "Internal award Procedure" by
which  HSCL are exposed to unreasonable competition.  This makes bagging jobs in steel plants further more difficult. 
Inspite of the scope of jobs of AMR, operation maintenance, waste disposal, slag processing and scrap recovery in the
steel plants, HSCL's role has been marginalized .
 
9.4       The Committee is of the view that  HSCL deserves a better deal in SAIL with Government  mediation, therefore
the Committee recommends  that  all the project as well as  AMR and operational jobs, within the execution capacity of
HSCL, should be offered on nomination on priority basis to HSCL.  This would enable the company to utilise its
infrastructure, set up over the years at SAIL plants and  meet  the expenses of the company. Award procedure  of SAIL  
should be relaxed suitably   for preferential treatment   to HSCL.  The  company may have  long term
arrangement/understanding   with SAIL on the basis of quantum of job  assured for award.   The Committee further
recommends  that a certain portion of the construction jobs in the Infrastructural sector be assigned to HSCL  on 
nomination basis,  at   least during  the initial  years of planned revival.  Purchase preference  to PSUs should be  strictly
adhered to.  Presently the PSUs/Government Department   are not  uniformly following the system.  The dismal balance
sheets of the company, for several years now, have made customers apprehensive in pre-qualifying HSCL for their
prospects.  Judging  the merit  of the situation, respective Administrative Ministries may issue necessary directives not
to disqualify HSCL for quoting, based on the financial performance of last  few years. HSCL should be granted
relaxation in registration formalities with Government   Departments for  taking up work. HSCL should be exempted
from submitting EMD for taking up work with Government departments and PSUs. HSCL's  experience in construction 
of roads in the integrated steel plants should be  considered   as qualifying criterion for High way work and matter may
be taken up  with the  Ministry of Road Transport and  Highways.

expected to become viable only is the wages and salaries is around 10% of the turnover.  It may be seen that the
projected expenses on salaries and wages can accommodate employment of a maximum of 1000 employees in the
company.
 
15.3     The Committee is of the view that HSCL management   should  make on all  out efforts for  achieving the targets
as projected by HSCL  management for the next  three years.  The  Committee is of the view that  HSCL management  
would  not face any  difficulty  in achieving  the  target in view  of these   fact  that second  revival package for HSCL
have been approved  by the Government.
Sanction of  revival package for HSCL
16.1     The Ministry of Steel  in its communication  vide  No.H.11014(5)2002-Parl. dated  23.7.2002 has informed the
Committee that  the Ministry of Finance have agreed to provide  relief  by approving increase in    Government  of India
guarantee  by Rs.250 crore to HSCL to raise further loans from banks for separation of around 5000 employees  under
VRS, along with  provision for interest subsidy. However, the Ministry of Finance  have agreed   for  non -plan
assistance for only Rs.89.44 crore.  Since  this part   assistance  by Ministry  of Finance is not  sufficient to meet the
requirement  of the  company, the Ministry of Steel   has  again taken up  the  with the Ministry of Finance for grant of
full financial assistance i.e.  Grant  of non-plan loan of Rs.182.28 crore to enable HSCL to pay salary and wages
amounting to Rs.122.58 crore and  statutory dues amounting  to Rs.59.70  crore outstanding as on  31
st March, 2001, the
Committee was informed .  The Ministry of Steel   has taken  up the   matter  with the Ministry of Finance  for grant of
non-plan  assistance of  Rs.125.17 crore to enable the company  to discharge its liabilities towards payment of arrears of 
wages and salaries of its employees.
16.2     The Committee  is pleased to note that  the Ministry of Finance  has given due consideration  to  the proposal of
Ministry of Steel for providing Government of India guarantee  for raising fund for  rationalisation  of manpower in
HSCL .  The Committee hopes that the revival package, as sanctioned by the Government, should be implemented
without delay and HSCL management would take step for separation of surplus employees  i.e. 5000 under VRS  within
a time frame.
 
The Committee, however,  is  of the view that  the Ministry of Finance  should consider  the proposal of  the Ministry of
Steel for grant of  non-plan assistance of Rs.125.17 crore to enable HSCL   to discharge its liabilities towards payment
of arrears of wages and salaries of its employees.  The Committee is of the opinion that once a comprehensive package
for revival of  HSCL is sanctioned in one go  the company would be able to come out  of red.
16.4     The Committee has been  informed that  an amount of Rs.89.44 crore have been  released to HSCL for  making
payment of outstanding dues to its  retired and separated employees as an interim measures.
16.5     The Committee hopes that HSCL would be  able to  make payments of  outstanding dues to its  retired and
separated employees without delay.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE
COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
 
The Committee notes that the reasons as placed  by the Ministry of Steel, for the suffering of  HSCL.  The Committee is
of the  opinion  that  lack of vision for  human resource management and  lack of a concrete policy  led to and sudden
increase in work force in HSCL.  The Committee further  opines  that HSCL's present suffering is due to error of
judgment and some elements were beyond  the  control of   management   and Government due to prevailing 
circumstances, lack of managerial vision and manpower policy added to the woes  of HSCL.
 
( Para 1.4)
 
The Committee, while taking note of the current financial performance of HSCL  expresses its concern over its pathetic
conditions,  and is of the view  that  HSCL  needs  improvement for  better financial   performance.  HSCL  requires a 
new vision, new managerial  will and effective strategy for the  continuance  of  its existence.
( Para : 2.2)
 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government for approving the  financial restructuring proposal. 
Considering the  fact that resources are limited the  sanctioning    of revival  package  having financial implication is a 
considered decision of the Government.  Committee also appreciates the Ministry of Steel for its consistent    efforts in
persuading the Ministry of Finance for  giving   revival package  to  HSCL.   The  Committee notes the provisions  of
revival package for  HSCL.
 ( Para 3.2)
 
Implementation status
 The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of Steel has taken action  on all provisions contained in the  revival
package.  The Committee hopes that efforts  of the Ministry of Steel in  persuading   the Department of Revenue  for
exempt  of  corporate  tax for HSCL would have a positive impact on the financial performance of HSCL.  The
Committee further  hopes that  consequent upon the  separation of  7,106  employees and reduction in the wage bill, the
financial ratio of the company  would further improve.
( Para 4.2)
 
The Committee understands that it is but natural that the accumulated loss of the company would come down once the
Government  grants waiver of interest Government loans, so far the same is a book-entry and it hardly has any reflection
on the actual financial performance  of the company.
 ( Para 4.4)
 
The Committee is happy to note the  savings on the specified  overheads due to  measures undertaken by HSCL 
management to rationalise administrative expenditure.   The Committee hopes that the efforts to rationalise
administrative  expenditure would continue.
( Para 4.8)
 
The Committee observes that financial assistance-cum-restructuring package  as proposed by the Ministry of Steel and
so approved by the Government was not as  comprehensive so as to mitigate the accumulated loss and total  liability of
HSCL.  The company continues to rein in adverse financial scenario and disadvantages in  general because
implementation of the revival package would  respond  only  if approved  measures are  taken in time for total  and
comprehensive restructuring of the company.  HSCL  needs total  overhauling  and complete and comprehensive 
restructuring in one  go as partial  package and  delayed implementation  defeats   the whole  idea, approach and  action.
 ( Para 5.2)
 
The Committee is of the view that once the comprehensive restructuring package is effectively implemented HSCL 
would   acquire  sufficient  resilience   and synergy to work even against fierce competition.  The Committee
recommends that HSCL management should strive in this regard. 
 
( Para 5.4)

failure  of  revival package  as advocated by the Ministry of Steel.  For the  revival of the company, HSCL management
has to procure work order despite ups and downs in Steel Industry and HSCL management  should not face  much 
difficulties as Government   is giving  due importance  to the construction sector.  The committee  is  of the  view that
optimum utilisation   of manpower and  resources at the  disposal of company is the responsibility of HSCL
management.
 ( Para 5.6)
 
The committee expresses its concern over the gap in the  actual turnover of the company vis-a-vis  the turnover
envisaged in  the  financial  restructuring proposal .  HSCL management should have made  an all out efforts  to achieve

( Para 5.8)
 
 
The Committee is of the view that the HSCL management  should have  undertaken  necessary steps  to rationalize 
expenditure toward contract payment.
( Para 5.10)

package, is constrained to express its concern.  The Committee  is of the view that HSCL  management could  have
well  managed and controlled  the problems being faced by  HSCL. The Committee views that replacement of obsolete
equipment in HSCL  should have  positive  impact on the operational efficiency of company  rather than   deterring   the
implementation of revival package.  Moreover, HSCL management should chalk out  a strategy for better margin of
profit. The Committee opines that HSCL management while implementing VRS should keep in mind the age  profile in

salaries given to HSCL employee during the   span of  eleventh months.  The Committee opines that idle wages and

System of  Sub-Contracting  Business Pattern
 
The Committee understands the  compelling  circumstances under which HSCL has to adopt the system of  sub-
contracting  business pattern but   it is also an open secret that sub-contracting   gives low margin for HSCL than if the
work done by the company itself.  The  Committee  is of the view  that VRS  offer  by HSCL  to its employees would
take care of keeping with itself the workforce consisting of  productive age profile and  willing to undertake
work/assignment from whatever concern its coming.  The Committee feels that  direct undertaking of work by HSCL
staff would give larger margin to HSCL and thus opening scope for profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better
that the  system of sub-Contracting  is replaced by direct involvement of HSCL employees,  sooner than later.
( Para  7.3 )
 
The Committee, while recognising  the special relationship of HSCL with SAIL, appreciates the role of  HSCL in the
modernisation of  SAIL's PSUs and hopes that SAIL  would  continue  to award  work order   to HSCL on priority  basis
, keeping  in view that   SAIL owes to   HSCL's deep rooted  problems  i.e.  surplus manpower  from Bokaro  were

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorized
by the Committee, hereby present this Eighty-sixth Report on Performance Review of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation
Ltd. (MSTC).
2.      The Committee on Industry constituted Sub-Committee for Ministry of Steel to examine the Performance Review
of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd. (MSTC). The Sub-Committee visited Kolkata on 17th to 20th July, 2001 and
interacted with the Management of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd. (MSTC).
3.      The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 14th March, 2002 heard the Secretary, Ministry of Steel and official of
MSTC. The Report has been prepared on the basis of on the spot-study by the Sub-Committee-I for the Ministry of Steel
of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry and interaction with the Secretary, Ministry of
Steel and officials of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd. (MSTC).

REPORT
         MSTC Limited (formerly known as Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd.) was incorporated as a Public Limited
Company under the Companies Act, 1956 on 9 th September, 1964. The status of the company underwent change in
February, 1974 to that of a subsidiary of Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL). In the year 1982-83, the corporation
was converted into a Government of India Company transferring the shares of SAIL to the President of India. It was the
Canalizing Agency for import of Carbon Steel Melting’s Scrap, Sponge Iron, Hot Briquette Iron and re-rolled scrap till
February, 1992. It was also the canalizing agency for import of ships for breaking till August, 1991. Presently, the
company undertakes disposal of ferrous and non-ferrous scrap arising from integrated steel plants under SAIL/RINL
etc. and disposal of scrap, surplus stores, etc. from other public sector undertakings and Government departments and
also import of ferrous and non-ferrous scarp, coke, finished steel and petroleum products. MSTC is the only Central
PSU under the Ministry of Steel to issue bonus shares.

3.1.0Domestic Marketing
3.1.1While a subsidiary of SAIL, MSTC started acting as selling agent of IISCO, RSP, BSL for disposal of their scrap
arising and thus started its Domestic Marketing activity. In 1993, after being de-linked from SAIL, MSTC extended its
activities to other PSUs, Government departments etc. The objective of DM is to maximize availability of indigenous
scrap by including the principals to mobilize and sell their scrap arisings/rejected/ condemned/surplus/spares/capital
equipments etc. so that the same can be recycled. The disposal action is taken in such a manner that the maximum
possible price is realized in totally transparent manner by selling the materials through open tenders, public auctions etc.
This activity was given importance only after decanalisation. The annual volume of business that was Rs.210 crore in
1992-93 reached at Rs.600 crore in 2000-2001.
