  INTRODUCTION
          I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this Ninetieth Report on Sickness in SSI Sector in the city of Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh.
2.       The Committee, in this context, heard the oral evidence of SSI Associations on 4th June, 2002.
3.       The Committee in its meeting held on 9th August, 2002 considered and adopted the Report.
NEW DELHI;
August 9, 2002
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
                                                                      Chairman,
              Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry.
REPORT
BACKGROUND
          Situated on the banks of the river Ganga, Kanpur stands as one of North India's major industrial centres with its
own historical, religious and commercial importance. The city, which was once described as Manchester of the East, is
one of the biggest producers of textile and leather products in Uttar Pradesh. These are exported in bulk from here.
About 50 tonnes of air cargo is generated from leather products only. Apart from leather and textile industries, fertilizer,
chemicals, two wheelers, soaps, pan masala, hosiery and engineering industries are also operating in the city.
1.1     The city hosts the world famous Lal Imli woollen factory, which was once the pride of the State. Besides, many
big companies such as LML Ltd., Kothari Products, Coca Cola, Pepsi, Duncans Industries Ltd. (Fertilizer factory),
Rotomac, Nerolac, Hindustan Lever, Ashok Masale, Goldie Spices, Mirza Tanners, Super House, BIC, NTC, GCMMF
(Amul) etc. have their offices/plants at Kanpur. The stockyards of HAL and SAIL are also located in the city. A large
number of ordnance factories and defence establishments such as DMSRDE, Small Arms Factory, Field Gun Factory
and Parachute Factory are also located in Kanpur. Gas Authority of India Ltd., NTPC, and perfume industries of
Kannauj are very close to Kanpur. A Software Technology Park is also being developed here. The city also hosts the
offices of the Directorate of Industries and Directorate of Handloom to look after these industries.
1.2     About 50 years ago, Kanpur was at second place in the country after Calcutta in terms of industrialisation.
However, in course of time, the city could not maintain its glory due to the closure of a number of industrial units
mainly comprising of textiles, iron and steel, engineering goods, etc. The famous industries Lal Imli Elgin Mills and
almost all the units of J.K. Group have been lying closed since long due to industrial downturn and lack of
infrastructural facilities particularly shortage of power, lack of technological upgradation and industrial unrest. Yet in
the State of Uttar Pradesh, Kanpur still holds an important place in terms of concentration of industries at one place.
STATUS  OF  SMALL  SCALE  INDUSTRIAL  UNITS  IN  KANPUR
2.       Certain special characteristics, which set the SSI sector apart in the Indian industrial environment, also hold good
for the small-scale industrial units operating in Kanpur. These include the decentralised nature of the sector, low capital
intensity, use of poor technology, making use of locally available resources only and its unsuitability for rural areas.
Study of the Subject by the Sub-Committee for the Ministry of Small Scale Industries
2.1     The above Sub-Committee decided to study the sickness of SSI sector in the city of Kanpur. The 
Sub-Committee comprised the following Members :
                 1.  Prof. M.M. Agarwal (RS) - Convenor
                 2.  Shri P. Rajendran (LS)
                 3.  Kunwar Sarv Raj Singh (LS)
                 4.  Shri Ramanand Singh (LS)
                 5.  Dr. Faguni Ram (RS)

90th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/90threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:19:49]
                 6.  Shri Ram Raghunath Chaudhary (LS)
`                7.  Dr. Abrar Ahmed (RS)
                 8.  Shrimati Sumitra Mahajan (RS)
                 9.  Shri Talib Hussain (LS)
               10.  Shri Dayabhai Patel (LS)
          The Sub-Committee visited Kanpur and heard the SSI associations on 9.10.2001. Again, the 
Sub-Committee heard select association in New Delhi on 4th June, 2002. The Sub-Committee heard the following SSI
Association in New Delhi :
                 1.  Indian Paints Association
                 2.  UP Hosiery Association
                 3.  UP Small Scale Soap Industries Association
                 4.  Panki Industries Association
                 5.  Associated Chamber of Commerce and Industry
Inter-active Session with the SSI Associations
2.2     During the course of the interactive session, the associations attributed reasons of sickness of SSI units to the
following factors :
Labour Problem
2.3     The associations brought it to the notice of the Committee that the Union Finance Minister had assured that units
employing less than one thousand persons would not be brought under the ambit of labour laws, but in reality, when
these units are required to resize their manpower, they are not able to do it as the employees go in for arbitration where
dates of hearing are fixed six months after filing the application. When labour is given some rights, they start
misbehaving with the management. Management of SSI units spend a lot of time in solving the problems posed by the
labourers. In Kanpur 90 per cent of SSI units have become sick due to leadership of labour. There is no power in the
hands of the management to discipline the labour.
          Wherever the statutory dues were paid in the industry, sickness started to surface and whenever workers were
made permanent, they stopped doing work and started misbehaviour with the management. Labour reforms should,
therefore, be done in a way so that the constraints coming in the way of running units could be removed. Hire and Fire
system may be one of the options which can be considered by the Government.
Erratic Power Supply
2.4     In Uttar Pradesh there is a daily power cut of four hours. As a result, only 60 per cent of production capacity can
be achieved. Four hours of total working hours are wasted as non-productive hours. Four hours' power cut is a daily
affair but sometimes it lasts for 10-12 hours, thus crippling the SSI units. State Power Corporation has absolute
authority in the matter of supplying of power. They do not listen to the problems of the SSI units. There should be a
State-Level Committee under the Chairmanship of a Judge, which should hear both sides and give decision which
should be mandatory.
          The Associations have suggested that like Telephone Department, State Power Body should publish a booklet
indicating contact numbers of officers who can be contacted in case of any difficulty. The time taken in taking a
decision and giving effect to it in the Power Department should also be reduced to minimise the problems of SSI units.
Lack of Testing Facility
2.5     There is no provision for a testing facility in Kanpur for the paint industry. Consequently, they have to go to
Kolkata for getting their products tested. To an enquiry the Association informed that IIT and CIGS do not have any

90th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/90threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:19:49]
provision for testing facilities for SSI units. These institutions cater to the needs of the defence sector only. Even if SSI
sector gets any tests done at these institutions, the test results are not accepted by other organisations like Railways, etc.
The Associations, therefore, requested for providing a testing facility for the paint industry.
Absence of Revival Route for the Sick Units
2.6     The Associations informed that when large industries fall sick, they could be revived through the revival package
given by the Bureau of Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR). But when a small sector industry becomes sick,
it has no route for revival. In case there is any revival route, the SSIs should be told about how to go about it.
Working Capital, Bank Loan without Collateral Security
2.7     Associations informed that SIDBI is making available loan without collateral security, but when the SSIs go to
any bank, the latter informed them that they have no information about such a system. All the banks should be informed
that loan without collateral security should be made available.
          The SSIs procure land, construct buildings/shed and purchase machinery on their own and thereafter seek loan
either from the market or from banks. When their turnover increases, their working capital requirement also increase.
They are trapped due to non-release of loan from banks.
Lack of Adoption of New Technologies
2.8     Adoption of new technologies is not taking place in the SSI sector and most of them are using obsolete
technology. Awareness about the new technology is limited to a limited circle only.
Lack of Quality Awareness resulting in poor products and high cost of production
2.9     Before embarking upon a particular industry, entrepreneurs are not aware about the marketability of their
products. Also, they use obsolete technology for production, manufacture poor quality products at high cost, and
compete with each other. Big industries on the other hand, with their better quality products and reasonable prices,
snatch away the market from the SSIs.
No Guideline about how to get bank loans
2.10   SSIs are totally at the mercy of the bank managers. If the manager is good and efficient, the SSIs get all assistance
and loan. Where the bank managers are indifferent, one has to pay a number of visits to the bank for obtaining relevant
forms. Even after obtaining and filling in forms, loans are not easily available as the bank officials  are wary of giving
loans, as they are not sure about the viability of the project. A guideline should be circulated to the SSIs to educate them
about how to get bank loans and bank officers should also be trained as to how to help the SSIs in getting loans.
Absence of proper Mechanism for Recovery of Bank Loan
2.11   Banks have no mechanism to recover loans. State Finance Corporations have the right under the Provision of
Arrears of Land Revenue to sell the closed unit to another unit to recover the amount of loan. In case of banks, the
matter goes to the Debt Recovery Tribunal and the condition of machines purchased by the sick units becomes worse
due to non-use. To obviate the situation, the banks should be given the right to sell the defaulter unit. This would
encourage the banks to give loans, as there would be a way to recover the loan.
No Mechanism to Access the Sickness of SSIs
2.12   Even if an industry falls sick, it does not mean that it will not survive. If the proper aid is given to the industry at
the initial stage of sickness, it can survive. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has given a guideline for assessing the
sickness of SSI but it is on paper only. The banks and Financial Institutions (FIs) are not adhering to it. It should be
mandatory for the banks/Financial Institutions to adhere to the RBI guidelines regarding assessment of sickness of
industries. There should be an ombudsman with whom complaints against banks/Financial Institutions can be registered.
2.13   A number of Committees on SSIs had been formed but the Government does not monitor implementation of their
recommendations. Similarly, RBI guidelines are there for credit flow and rehabilitation of sick industries, but there is no
mechanism to monitor their implementation. The banks and FIs are not ready to talk to industry associations. They want

90th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/90threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:19:49]
to talk to borrowers only. Some mechanism should be evolved on a reasonable basis to hear the grievances of SSIs with
regard to non-implementation of the RBI guidelines by the individual banks.
Non-cooperation of Telecom Sector
2.14   Poor telecom network in semi-urban areas sometimes prove to be a hindrance for SSI units. A little
communication gap between the supplier and the client due to absence of proper telecommunication system may result
in business loss.
No Centre for Development of Cotton and Textile
2.15   Hosiery industry in Kanpur is linked with cotton and textile but there is no centre for Uttar Pradesh to develop
cotton and textile. Hosiery industry has to go all the way to Tirupur for development purpose. A process and product
development centre should be established at Kanpur to help the SSIs in the matter of technology. This will give hope to
the closed cotton and textile mills.
Industrial Unrest and Minimum Wages
2.16   Industrial unrest and wages are inter-linked. If the industry is using skilled labour, it cannot be engaged on
minimum wages. Wages are determined by demand and supply. Skilled workers will go to an industry where they get
higher wages. If the industry sticks to the stipulated minimum wages, it will give rise to industrial unrest, which will
hamper working of the industry. Government should make a fresh survey to define minimum wages.
Non-release of payments to SSIs by Buyers
2.17   Public Sector Undertakings and other large industries buy from SSIs on credit basis and the credit period varies
from three to six months. But SSIs are not able to realise the payment from such buyers and thus their money remains
blocked for a long period. The Delayed Payments Act, which is supposed to resolve the issue, proved to be ineffective.
Government should suitably amend the Act to make it more effective.
Employees Provident Fund and Employees State Insurance Corporation Act
2.18   Some deductions are made from the salaries of the labourers on account of Provident Fund. But when the
labourers change one unit after another, in most cases they do not get their dues due to non-availability of records. It is,
therefore, suggested that the employees may be issued passbooks and entries relating to amount deducted from their
salaries may be entered in them. They would be able to receive their dues from the units from which they retire on this
factual basis.
          In the case of ESIC, the benefits go to the owner or director of the unit and not to workers. A policy should be
evolved so that workers get their benefit and owners pay the premium for the same.
Arrival of MNCs and Concession to Khadi Industries in Soap Industry
2.19   With the arrival of MNCs and concession given to Khadi industries, sickness in the soap industry commenced.
The methodology and size of manpower required for hand made soap industry is the same in both the SSI and Khadi
industries. But Khadi industries get concession while SSIs do not get any such relief. Kanpur had 150 soap factories in
SSI sector. Today, it has not more than 20, which are struggling to alive. Soap is made out of imported non-edible oil on
which 55 per cent import tax is paid by the industry. For the last one and a half year the rate of import duty has been
raised to the extent of 45 per cent. In Nepal, there is no import duty. They import duty-free non-edible oil, manufacture
finished product and re-export to the third country. While the manufacturing cost of Nepal soap is Rs. 16, the same is
manufactured in Kanpur at a cost of Rs. 24. To save the soap industry in Kanpur, the rate of import duty on non-edible
oil has to be reduced.
Basic Infrastructure
2.20   Industries are given sites at places where basic infrastructure like roads, communication, drainage etc. are not
provided. Industrial sites are allotted far away from the urban area where basic amenities like drinking water are not
available. No redressal measures have been taken by the Government despite the fact that this was brought to their
notice.

90th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/90threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:19:49]
Law and Order Situation
2.21   Due to power cut, anti-social elements are thriving in industrial areas. State policy authority expresses their
helplessness, as they do not have enough force to tackle the law and order situation there. The SSI branches of banks are
located outside the urban area of Kanpur. It is quite difficult to go to the SSI branch to deposit or collect money. Banks
should be located in safe areas.
Uniform Taxation
2.22   Four per cent taxation has been imposed on hosiery industry. Due to this, it has become sick. The rate of taxation
should be uniform throughout the country, and like other States, the taxation rate should be one per cent on this industry.
Pollution Control
2.23   Pollution control for the industries is necessary, but generally, problems keep on cropping up due to various
reasons. Therefore, in industrial areas where SSIs are situated as a cluster, facilities should be provided by the
administration for setting up of a common effluent treatment plant.
Purchase Preference
2.24   Government  institutions are not giving priority to SSIs in the matter of purchase of various items, Government
bodies are purchasing items from outside the State although the same items are available in the State at competitive
rates.
Representation of SSIs in Legislative and Municipal Bodies
2.25   In the absence of any representation of SSIs in the State Legislature and Municipal Corporations, the problems of
SSIs are not highlighted and even if these are highlighted, Government does not take them seriously. A provision for
representation of SSIs should, therefore, be made so that they are given an opportunity of being heard.
Exhibition of spare parts of Railways
2.26   Exhibitions of articles related to spare parts used in railways may be organised to revive the engineering units
which are on the verge of closure in the adjoining areas of Kanpur. This will inspire the revival of engineering industry.
Non-acceptance of smaller denomination notes by the banks
2.27   SSIs receive their payments in smaller denomination notes (like one, two or five) and coins. The banks do not
accept these currencies. SSIs have to suffer the loss of approximately five per cent (brokerage) in payment on the coins.
RBI should give clear guidelines to bank to accept all types of currencies.
INTERACTIVE  SESSION  WITH  THE  MINISTRY  OF  SSI  AND  BANKS
3.       During the interactive session with the representatives of Ministry of Small Scale Industries and banks, the
Committee was given the following clarifications :
3.1     Power cut : The power situation, that is, generation, distribution and supply all over the country has been a cause
of concern. The generation does not meet demand. Ministry of SSI often takes up the problems with the State
Government to bring about improvement of power supply in the industrial areas.
3.2     Labour Laws : The Ministry of SSI has brought the concern of the industry to the notice of the Labour Ministry
and they have taken certain initiatives. Certain aspects of the problem, which relate to the industry, are already under
consideration of the Labour Ministry.
3.3     Technology Upgradation : One of the reasons for sickness or failure is lack of information and obsolete
technology. For promoting technology in the industry, the following steps have been taken :
                 a.  Industries are encouraged to take ISO 9000 certification and for that purpose, every SSI unit is given a
financial incentive of Rs. 75,000.

90th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/90threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:19:49]
                 b.  A one time capital grant of 50 per cent is being given to SSI associations for developing and operating
their testing laboratories.
                 c.  Scheme for transfer of technology through cluster.
                 d.  Certain financial institutions of DCSSI are implementing credit linked capital subsidy scheme.
                 e.  Technology Upgradation/Modernisation Fund.
                  f.  Technology Upgradation Fund for textile units.
3.4     Dissemination of Information : Dissemination of information is done through three methods :
                 a.  The Ministry of SSI have identified 500 industry associations all over the country. Whenever a new
scheme is introduced, the Ministry reports it to all of them.
                 b.  The Ministry has created an interactive portal. All information is available on the Ministry's website.
                 c.  The Ministry organises orientation courses, seminars, workshops, etc. for the benefit of SSIs.
3.5     Revival route : The RBI had appointed a Committee to study the rehabilitation of sick industries. The Committee
made recommendations and RBI had issued circulars for bringing the companies in the SSI sector out of sickness. The
package, among other things, includes revised advances, which would be more liberal. It also recommended on how to
define the viability of a unit and what should be the monitoring mechanism. It has also a particular instruction for banks
to identify sickness at an early stage and provide relief and rehabilitation steps within six months of identification. The
Ministry, the RBI, financial institutions and banks can check the sickness properly in a reasonable period of time.
3.6     Cheap Imports from Nepal : A new agreement has been signed with Nepal in March 2002. This takes care of
most of the problems. The component of value addition of the goods which comes from Nepal and which are said to be
Nepalese goods are actually sent by other countries through Nepal. These goods would not be accepted and agreement
signed with Nepal is a major step in this direction.
3.7     Purchase Preference : The purchase preference policy to be given to the SSI sector by Government Departments
and offices is available in the form of a guideline only. The Ministry of SSI has received a number of representations in
this regard. The Office of Development Commissioner is looking into it. Unless and until a pattern on the line of the
USA is adopted, which has relevant legislation, it would not be effective.
3.8     Coordination at Centre and State Levels : In order to have a coordination with different departments of Central
Government and State Governments, financial institutions and banks, the Ministry of SSI would bring forward a
legislation to redress the difficulties posed to the SSIs due to variety of reasons. The Ministry has already taken up
issues relating to labour laws with the Ministry of Labour. They have also taken up the matter regarding amendment in
Partnership Act with the Law Ministry.
3.9     Credit Flow from banks : Shri N.S. Mishra, General Manager, Bank of Baroda informed that as a result of a
host of measures taken by the Government/RBI in the wake of globalisation and liberalisation of Indian economy to
increase the flow of credit to the SSI sector and facilitate higher growth, a good number of new SSI units have been
coming up regularly.
          However, due to infrastructural bottlenecks particularly shortage of power, the incidence of sickness is very high
in these small-scale industrial units.
          As per data made available by the industries associations, the present position of industrial units/SSI at Kanpur is
as under :
Total number of industrial units financed by Banks in Kanpur 8690
Out of which
 
Total number of sick units 5475
No. of sick units rehabilitated by banks 305

90th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/90threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:19:49]
3.10   Shri S.S. Kohli, President of Indian Banks Association, informed the Committee that 6-8 weeks are taken by the
SSI branch of the bank to scrutinise the loan application. If any application is to be rejected, the branch has to take the
permission of its regional office. In that way, the loan application can be rejected by the zonal office or head office. On
asking why banks are not giving receipt after accepting application, he said that he would place the matter before the
appropriate authority.
3.11   He also informed that as per recommendations of the Nayak Committee, the RBI has prescribed loans for the SSI
on turnover basis. If any unit had a turnover of Rs. 10 lakhs in the previous year and comes with a loan application with
a projected turnover of Rupees one crore in the current year, it cannot be treated as a basis for giving loan. The lending
bank has to see whether the unit's machinery has the capacity to raise the turnover from Rs. 10 lakhs to Rs. 1 crore.
These are the problems the banks have to overcome before sanctioning loan applications.
3.12   He further suggested that (i) SSIs should not bank upon traditional items. SSIs should modernise themselves and
explore new areas where they can invest money for a reasonable good return; (ii) the associations should guide their
members about areas where they may invest their money and also discuss with the workers of units about the modalities
as to how to increase the productivity in a cordial atmosphere; (iii) the Delayed Payment Act has not been implemented
in the true sense resulting in non-payment to SSIs by PSUs and other big industries; (iv) a solution is to be found to help
the SSIs in this regard. He added that financial data to be furnished by the SSIs for getting loans are sometimes
incomplete. Information about the source of margin money, who would be getting the money, what is basis of projected
the turnover etc. is not given. The information given by SSIs should also match their books of accounts to justify their
loan applications. These are the basic problems.
3.13   As regards the problems of branch managers in giving loans, Shri Kohli observed that the problems posed by the
audit and CVC etc. are in the uppermost mind of the managers while scrutinising the loan applications, and requested
the Committee to look into this problem.
3.14   The Committee observed that the C.D. ratio in U.P. is much below the desired level and it should be increased.
Shri A.V. Seresai, CGM, RBI informed the Committee that CD ratio in Uttar Pradesh is 47.37 and this was not a good
picture. He further informed that the State Government have been impressed upon the need to increase the CD ratio.

should address the issues illustrated in paras 2.2 to 2.27 of this report.

and measures have been formulated for the benefit of the SSI, while it appeared from the oral evidence tendered by the

that the Ministry should reach the grass-root level and for this purpose, it should hold regular orientation
courses, seminar, workshop etc. in Kanpur. The Committee hopes that this kind of action would enable the SSIs
to reap benefit of the schemes formulated for them by the Government of India.

REPORT
 
COIR INDUSTRY -AN OVERVIEW
 
1.0     Coconut cultivation in India is concentrated in Kerala, which accounts for 48.63 per cent of the total production. Historically, the coir
industry took root in Kerala because of the availability of skilled labour and natural facilities of retting of coconut husk.
 
1.1     The development of the coir industry has been in areas where there is concentration of coconut cultivation and availability of coconut husk.
The coir industry is of great importance to Kerala, where it is second only to agriculture as a source of employment. With the expansion of
coconut cultivation and the concerted efforts of the Coir Board and the respective State Governments, the coir industry is coming up in Tamil
Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal and Assam. Kerala is the largest producer of coconuts and its contribution is as much as
50.5 per cent of total production.
 
1.2     Indian coir is exquisite live-in style, hygiene products of traditional and modern design consisting of handmade and machinemade
materials. It is helping a million disadvantaged women to earn their livelihood. Coconut husk is a natural product from a renewable source.
 
1.3 At present, the coir industry is of great importance to coconut producing states in India as it contributes significantly to their economy. This is
because coconut husk, the raw-material for coir industry, is available in abundance as a by-product of coconut industry in regions of concentrated

cultivation. Increased utilization of coconut husks abundantly available in all coconut producing states in India provides scope for development of
coir industry, thus augmenting rural employment. The husk surrounding the seed of the coconut contains coco fibre, the raw material for coir
industry. Coir fibre extracted from the coconut husk is used commercially for the manufacture of a range of products with different end uses.
 
1.4     The coir manufacturing industry producing coir mats, mattings and other floor coverings, was started in India on factory basis over a
hundred yeras ago when the first factory was set up in Alleppey in 1859 by James Darragh, an adventurous Irish born American national.
Enterprising Indians later set up their own coir producing units.
 
1.5     The coir industry has the potential to provide employment at low investment per job, and a large number
of people from the socially and economically weaker sections of society depend on this industry. It is for this
reason that the establishment of coir industry in India gains added significance.
 
COIR BOARD
 
2.0     The Coir Board promotes and facilitates overall sustainable development of the coir industry in India. The Coir Board is an autonomous
organisation establised by the Government of India under the provisions of the Coir Industry Act, 1953 , for promoting the overall development
of the coir industry and upliftment of the living conditions of the workers engaged in this traditional cottage industry. The Coir Board started
functioning w.e.f. July, 1954 with a view to providing infrastructural facilities for carrying out various objectives as laid down in the Coir
Industry Act.
 
2.1     The Coir Board is responsible for sustainable development of the coir industry through research and development, modernisation, quality
improvement, human resource development, market promotion, environmental protection and welfare of all those who are engaged in this
industry. The functions of the Coir Board, as laid down under Section 10 of the Coir Industry Act are as under:
 
(a)
    Promoting exports of coir yarn and coir products and carrying on propaganda for that purpose;
 
(b)    Regulating under the supervision of the Central Government the production of husks, coir yard and products by registering coir spindles
and looms for manufacturing coir products as also manufacturers of coir products, licensing, exporters of coir, coir yarn and coir
products and taking such other appropriate steps as may be prescribed;
 
(c)    Undertaking. assisting or encouraging scientific, technological and economic research and maintaining and assisting in the maintenance
of one or more research institutes;
 
(d)    Collecting statistics from manufacturers of, and dealers in, coir products and from such other persons as may be prescribed, on any
matter relating to the coir industry, the publications of statistics so collected or portions thereof or extracts therefrom;
 
(e)    Fixing grade standards and arranging when necessary for inspection of coir fibre, coir yarn and coir products;
 
(f)     Improving the marketing of coconut husk, coir fibre, coir yarn and coir products in India and elsewhere and preventing unfair
competition;
 
(g)    Setting up or assisting in the setting up of factories for the producers of coir products with the aid of power;
 
(h)    Promoting co-operative organisation among producers of husks, coir fibre and coir yarn and manufacturers of coir products;
 
(i)      Ensuring remunerative returns to producers of husks, coir fibre and coir yarn and manufacturers of coir products;
 
(j)      Licensing of retting places and warehouses and otherwise regulating the stocking and seal of coir fibre, coir yard and coir products both
for the internal market and for export;
 
(k)    Advising on all matters relating to the development of the coir industry;
 
(l)      Such other matters as have been prescribed in the Act or rules made thereunder.
 
STUDY OF THE FUNCTIONING OF THE COIR BOARD BY THE SUB-COMMITTEE FOR THE
MINISTRY OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRY

consisted of the following Members:

3.1     The Sub-Committee visited the Head Quarters of the Coir Board at Cochin and its regional offices at Vishakhapatnam and Bangalore in
May, 2002. The Committee's findings and observations are dealt with in the
succeeding paragraphs.
 
COMMITTEES' FINDINGS, OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
 
4.0     The Committee, during the course of its .visit to Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala, found that the utilisation of coconut husk for the
production of coir in the country is very low. Hence, there is vast potential for setting up production of coir and coir products. It has also been
given to understand that production of coir fibre has been affected by disease, which reduces the size of the coconut husk, resulting in low yield
and inferior quality fibre. The Committee recommends that all out efforts should be made to check the disease so that the size of the husk remains
normal and yields good quality fibre.
 
4.1     Coir industry, by and large, remains a rural cottage industry, characterized by low productivity, penetration of technology, investments, low
level of managerial skills and reluctance to quickly modernise. The traditional method of fibre extraction and production involves drudgery, is
time consuming and less remunerative, resulting in low wages for all workers engaged in various coir-related activities.
 
4.2     The coir industry consists of two segments viz. white fibre sector and brown fibre sector. Brown coir fibre is extracted from unretted husk.
The white fibre, which is more suitable for the manufacture of coir yarn and value added products, faces severe shortage due to decline in natural
retting facilities. After separating of the nut, the husks are processed by various retting techniques, generally in ponds of brackish water, for three
to six months or in back waters or lagoons for 10 to 12 months for bacterial fermentation. The prospects of white fibre look bleak with the
pressure emanating from growing environmental consciousness. The Committee recommends that Government should explore ways and means
to solve the problem faced by the
white fibre manufacturers in the absence of proper retting facilities.
 
4.3     Extraction of fibre from husk leaves coir pith or coir dust as a solid waste. Extraction of 1 kg. fibre generates 2 kgs of coir pith. It takes up a
large amount of space and its disposal is a problem, although, of late, there are signs of booming export market far the product as it can be
converted into organic manure. The Committee recommends that coir industry should take the opportunity to exploit the untapped export market
and the Government should of the all assiatance to such exporters.
 
4.4     Post-fibre extraction activities are not picking up in the brown fibre sector though there have been positive signs of late. The private sector
is often slow or hesitant to invest in the sector, probably for want of awareness of the potential of this industry. Even the state governments of all
coconut-growing states in the non-traditional areas seems to be oblivious of the vast potential that the sector offers, particularly for employment
generation in .the rural areas at a comaparatively lower level of investment. A more serious problem is that of obtaining skilled workers who are
needed to undertake post-fibre value-added productions activities in the brown fibre sector. All coir development plans, to date, have highlighted
the inadequacy of skilled manpower as the single- most important reason for the tardy development of the coir industry in the brown coir
producing states. The Committee recommends that the government should set up offices of the Coir Board in all brown fibre producing states
and, in coordination with the State Governments, arrange awareness programmes and training programmes for the benefit of private
entrepreneurs and labourers.
 
4.5     The industry is spread far and wide in the coconut growing states in the country, barring a few natural clusters. Even in those clusters, the
industry is not well integrated to take advantage of the development and promotional efforts towards modernisation. The Committee recommends
that in all major coconut growing areas, clusters may be identified where coir industrial activities could be established. In these clusters coir
industrial infrastructure should be set up preferably in the private sector. Basic techno-economic feasibility/consultancy and be given by the Coir
Board for setting up such production infrastructure.
 
4.6     The method of production in vogue has not undergone any significant change over the years. The cost of production has been progressively
rising, rendering it non-competitive in the domestic and export markets. This needs to be looked into more urgently. Technological upgradation is
a sina qua non for the development of the coir industry. Eco-friendly process and production technologies, development of cost-effective and
efficient machinery with higher productivity, which reduces drudgery will have to be developed. Progress in the development of coir machinery
has been very tardy. R&D efforts in machinery development have not been receiving the attention that it deserves. The Committee recommends
that special efforts have to be made to identify the potential coir machinery manufacturers who can be supported with appropriate technology
transfer from any. available areas. This activity may be taken up as joint venture programmes with greater emphasis on private sector
participation ensuring faster commercialisation.
 
4.7     There is a lack of awareness in the potential markets of the country about the coir products and their inherent qualities. The present
marketing network is inadequate and needs to be enlarged. Some of the other problems that have been affecting the coir industry are poor quality
raw materials and end products, lack of product innovation, absence of clear strategy for guiding the direction of exports, inadequate export
promotion, higher freight charges, uncompetitive price structure, competition from synthetic products and other cheaper natural substitutes, etc.
 
4.8     The Committee recommends that a national level project may be evolved for creation of awareness about coir products, development of
market, production of new and diversified goods of mass
consumption and quality assurance. It is understood that some steps have already been taken to establish a Coir Trade Information Centre for
collection analysis, its dissemination of information. It should become one of the principal activities of the Coir Board in the changed

circumstances. This sector can develop through flow of information especially marketing and technology, which is possible through IT assisted
programmes.
 
4.9     Rubberised coir from Sri Lanka and coir geotextiles from Vietnam, cheaper coir products from Thailand and Philippines have taken a part
of the export share held by Indian coir products.
 
4.10   The target for export of coir producing and achievements made during the last three years are given below:

1999-2000 325.00 303.05 93.26

4.11   It is evident from the above that the gap between the target and its achievement is widening. The Committee recommends that a thrust may
be given to boost export of coir products and assistance of Export Credit Guarantee Corporation may be sought in the matter. The Committee also
recommends that possibility of mutual cooperation in possible areas between India and other neighbouring coir producing countries may be
explored.
 
4.12   In order to overcome the problems outlined above, the Committee feels that the Government should aim at rapid modernisation for the
overall sustainable development of the coir industry, focusing on research and development, quality improvement, human resource development,
better marketing of products and welfare support to the needy, particularly the less-privileged group like women coir workers who constitute
more than 80 per cent of the work force.
 
4.13   The Committee stresses the need for greater emphasis on the involvement of the private sector as well as the concerned state government.
The Coir Board should also take advantage of programmes under other ministries for this sector.
 
4.14   In non-traditional areas where there is a dearth of skilled manpower, particularly traditional skill, the focus must be on production of valued
added goods through modernisation, involving rapid mechanization wherever possible. The Committee recommends that the Coir Board, in
coordination with State Governments should make an endeavour to undertake more sponsored R&D projects in association with reputed agencies
in both the public and private sectors.
 
4.15   Another area which needs immediate attention is manpower development and capacity buildings, as no development can be implemented
without trained and experienced personnel. The Committee feels that appropriate manpower development programme for skill up-gradation in
various fields, especially in non-traditional areas, is to be devised. Efforts for upgradation of the skill of artisans and technical/ managerial
personnel required for the industry are to be organized in coordination with NGOs, cooperative societies and other state government institutions.
State level training institutions should also be revitalized to enable them to undertake HRD-related activities.
 
4. 16 At present, there is a great demand for eco-friendly products throughout the world. Coir is an friendly product and there is an urgent need to
promote both the traditional as well as new products like coir geo-textile, coir pith, garden articles, coir wood substitute and rubberized coir.
Promotion of export market for coir and coir products is of vital importance for the growth of Indian coir industry. There should also be an
attempt to develop the brand image for the Indian coir, which should instantly evoke a sense of unique craftsmanship and assured quality.
 
4.17   A major area for development is the use of coir geo textiles in erosion control applications, and its use as agro mulch. A technology-based
promotion is required for the promotion of coir geotextiles. The Committee desires that initially demonstration projects for the use of coir
geotextiles may be taken up in different parts of the country through different departments like Agriculture, Forest, PWD, Irrigation, etc. A
National Coir Geo-textiles Technology Mission for popularisation of coir geotextiles may be launched with support from the Central and the
concerned State Governments. This would help conserve precious soil, while enabling the coir industry to grow.
 
4.18   In view of this, the focus henceforth should be on increasing coir husk utilisation, modernisation, capacity building through the
involvement of the private sector and State Government, promotion of coir through multi fibre products, improvement in production processes,
extension of coir activities in non- traditional, areas. The Committee, therefore, recommends that financial assistance for technology upgradation,
revitalisation and augmentation of training centres especially in areas where coir is yet to penetrate should be given. Such assistance should also
be given for cluster development programmes and marketing both for internal consumption and export.
 
4.19   The first and the foremost need is better institutional support through the active involvement of the concerned State Governments, specially
in the non-traditional areas, to undertake concerted and focussed measures for the development of the coir industry. The Committee recommends
that each of the State Governments may be advised to set up a separate cell for the coir industry in their respective departments of industry,
preferably under the SSI sector. The District Industries Centre or the District Rural Development Agencies of the concerned districts may be
made the nodal agency for the development of coir where there is coconut cultivation, and entrusted with the responsibility of imparting training,
enterpreneurship development, assistance in getting micro credits, and organising the workers into Self Help Groups for production and
marketing. The technical inputs may be provided be the Coir Board in extending training, especially in the production of value-added goods and
in getting trade information.

         Every State capital should have at least one outlet of the Coir Board and exhibitions may be held
periodically in all cities and small towns of the states for awareness as well as marketing purpose.
 
4.20   The cooperative structure in the coir sector is extremely weak. Their productivity is low and commercial viability is also generally poor.
The Committee recommends that specific projects may be taken up for restructuring the coir cooperative societies in all states with the help of the
National Cooperative Development Corporation, for which whole-hearted support of the concerned State Governments' has to be solicited.
 
4.21   The emerging trend in the global arena points to the fact that development of mluti-fibre products has a better future. It is understood that it
is in this context a suggestion has been made to set up a Natural Hard Fibre Development Board with a pre-eminent position for the coir sector.
The Committee recommends that a policy decision may be taken to make this concept come true.
 
4.22   The Committee was informed that the Coir Board has been implementing a project entitled Technology Transfer, Modernisation and
Capacity Building in Indian Coir Sector with funding from UNDP. Under the project, the Board has identified six coir clusters in Tamil Nadu,
Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala. The project is at the half-way stage. The Committee expects that on completion of the project, based on
experience, a replicable strategy for overall development of the industry could be formulated.
 
4.23   The Committee was disturbed by the understaffing of the regional offices of the Coir Board at Visakhapatnam, Bangalore, Pollachi and
Delhi. The Committee was informed that the regional office at Visakhapatnam comprised of nine employees, one regional officer and other
subordinate staff. With this staff, the regional office was incapable of reaching out to the vast area which fell within its purview. The regional
office was handicapped in providing training and cover such a large area in the absence of adequate manpower. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that arrangements should be made to equip the regional offices with sufficient manpower so as to enable it to cater to needs of
remote areas like the North-East states and Jharkhand etc.
 
4.24   The Committee also observes that existing training centres in Andhra Pradesh are unable to sustain themselves as the State Government is
not able to cater to their financial needs. Their functioning runs into rough weather for want of adequate financial support. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Government of India should provide them with sufficient funds for their smooth running.
 
4.25   The Committee came to know that dehusking is not being properly done in Andhra Pradesh. Only a small portion of coconut fibre is being
utilised due to lack of skilled labour. The Committee felt that there was need for more utilisation of husk in Andhra Pradesh. The Committee
recommends that more awareness progr.ammes should be launched in Andhra Pradesh so that coir is not wasted there.
 
5.0     The total annual turnover of coir industry in India is estimated at Rs.1300 crores. In view of the need for improvements and significance of
this industry, the coir sector essentially requires substantial investments. For various reasons the private sectors have not found this sector
attractive enough. In order to attract private investmcnt, the inherent strengths of the coir sector should be made palpably visible through
modernisation, demonstration of successful projects, provision of infrastructural facilities and efficient supportive services. This is possible only
through adequate public funding.
 
5.1     The total outlay proposed by the Coir Board during the Ninth Plan Period (for Plan S&T and Plan General) was Rs. 149 Crore while the
amount sanctioned was Rs.104.14 Crore and, finally, funds to the tune of Rs.56.39 Crore was released. For Plan cooperativisation, which is
implemented by the State Governments and Union Territories (a fund which is directely received by State Governments from the Government of
India) the Coir Board proposed an outlay of Rs.32.75 Crore, while Rs. 11 ,86 Crore was sanctioned and, finally, Rs.2.91 Crore was released. The
Committee also notes that the budget for the Coir Board is only Rs.17. 9 Crore. The Committee feels that there is a need to provide more funds to
the Coir Board to strengthen the coir sector. The Committee recommends the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries should work out a financial
package for the coir sector to enable it to meet the challenges of economic liberalisation and progressive withdrawal of quantitative restrictions,
etc.
 
5.2     The Committee is constrained to note that in spite of producing exquisite and relatively cheaper products by the Coir industry, it has not
caught up with the consumers due to lack of publicity. In spite of immense export potential of the coir products, export market remains to be fully
tapped. The Committee desires that appropriate action may be taken to give a fillip to the much neglected coir industry and realize its export
potential.
 
5.3     Since the coir industry has the potential to provide employment at lo\v investment per job, and a large number of people from the socially
and economically weaker section of the society depend on this industry, the Committee impresses upon the Government the need to make every
effort to make the coir industry a viable one for the benefit of the rural population.

by the Committee, hereby present this Ninety-second Report on the Action Taken  on the recommendations contained in
the 73rd Report of the Department-- related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry on "Demand for Grants
(2002-03) of the Department of Public Enterprises".
2. The Committee examined and considered the Action Taken note on the recommendations contained in the
Committee's 73rd Report on Demand for Grants (2002-03) of the Department of Public Enterprises.
3. The Committee at its meeting held on 11th December, 2002 considered and adopted the report.
NEW DELHI; 
11 December, 2002
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
 Chairman,
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the Recommendations contained
in its 73rd Report of the Department-- related Parliamentry Standing Committee on Industry on the Demand for Grants
(2002-03) of the Department of Public Enterprises which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok
Sabha on the 14th May, 2002.  
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in the
Report. They have been categorized as follows:
        (i)       Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Government:-
                  Paras 2.4, 3.2, 4.2, 8.7, 8.9 and 8.12 (Chapter -- I).
        (ii)      Recommendations/Observations, which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the
Government's replies:-
                  Para 6.9 (Chapter -- II).
        (iii)       Recommendations/Observations, in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of  the
Government:-
                  Paras 5.4, 5.5, 5.9, 5.10, 6.2, 6.6, 6.10, 7.8, 7.10, 7.11, 7.13, 8.10, 8.16, 8.17,
                  (Chapter --III).
        (iv)     Recommendations/Observations, in respect of which replies of the Government have not been  received:-
                  Para 4.4 (Chapter -- IV).
3.  The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry of Heavy Industries has accepted its recommendations as
mentioned in Chapter -- I of the Report.
4.  In respect of the recommendations made in Paras 3.17 and 3.21 in Chapter -- II, the Committee is convinced with the
logic and explanation advocated by the Ministry of Heavy Industries and therefore does not want to pursue further.
5.  The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementations of recommendations contained in Chapter -- III
and therefore the Committee desires that the Ministry of Heavy Industries would furnish logical explanation in respect
of these recommendations.

  The Committee is happy to note that the MoU system has enabled the DPE to undertake objective assessment of
CPSEs. The Committee recommends for further strengthening of the MoU system and hopes it will be able to adopt
itself to the requirements of PSEs in a globalised economy.

Status of Navratna and Miniratna companies
RECOMMENDATION
  The Committee notes that Non-Official Directors for Navratna and Miniratna PSEs have benefited immensly due to
the status assigned to them. The Committee feels that the Department of Public Enteprises should undertake all possible
steps to introduce professionalism in these Public Sector Enterprises so that they are able to face challenges of changing
times and able to develop competitive edge.
Para 5.5

92nd Report of Committee on Industry

RECOMMENDATION
  The Committee, however, proposes to undertake a study to know how far Directors of MoU signing PSEs are given
sufficient power to enable them to take quick decisions in their business related matters and formation of joint venture
etc. in India and abroad.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
  Steps have already been taken for professionalising the Boards of Navratna and Miniratna PSEs. A Search Committee
was set up for selecting non-official part-time Directors for Navratna/Miniratna PSEs. The delegation of enhanced
financial powers to the Navratna and Miniratna PSEs is subject to the condition that the Boards of these PSEs are
professionalised by inducting at least 4 non-official Directors in the case of Navratnas and at least 3 non-official
Directors in the case of Miniratnas. These non-officials are eminent persons drawn from various disciplines like
technocrats, management experts and consultants, professional managers in industry and trade, etc.  Induction of non-
official professionals through the Search Committee mechanism is a countinuous process.
  The MoU system is based on the principle of enhanced autonomy and accountability. Accordingly, the Boards of MoU
signing PSEs enjoy certain financial and operational autonomy within the guidelines. As and when the Committee
desires to undertake the study, this Department will provide requisite assistance to coordinate it.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
  The Department of Public Enterprises has informed about the steps taken about the professionalization of the Boards of
Navratna and Miniratna companies. But it has not stated how far they have been successful to face the challenges of
changing time. The Committee needs the detailed breakup of the composition of Boards of Navratna and Miniratna
companies to have an insight with regard to professionalization of Boards and how far they have played proactive role.

status of PSE and the administrative Ministries for the purpose. The Committee wishes that it may be apprised about the

Para 6.2
Counselling, Retraining/Redeployment, Setting up of New Centres/Addition of Nodal Agencies
RECOMMENDATION
The Committee feels that the initiatives taken by the DHI to counsel, retrain and redeploy the employees of CPSEs
are laudable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that greater focus on proper implementation and regular
monitoring of the above scheme is required to make it more effective at the ground level.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
DPE would strive for further improvement under the CRR Programme. For regular monitoring of the programme,
the Monitoring Cell set up under the CRR Programme has been in close touch with the Nodal Training Agencies and
Central PSUs for proper implementation and monitoring of the programme. Regular field visits have been made to the
Nodal Agencies and locations of the training imparted in order to closely watch and monitor the programme, have the
feed back from the beneficiaries and also to meet the Central PSUs in the surroundings so as to create a cohesive
environment for the CRR programme. Besides, at the local level provision has already been made for setting up of
Coordination Committee consisting of the Members from Central PSUs, Nodal Training Agencies and credit institutions
so that the issues can be discussed and sorted out locally.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
The Committee wishes to know number of visits have so far been made to the nodal agencies and locations of the
training and details of feedback received from the beneficiaries and results achieved after meeting the Central PSUs in
the surroundings. The Committee further wishes to know whether coordination Committee at local level consisting of
Members from Central PSUs, Nodal Training Agencies and credit institutions has since been formed, if so, at how many
places and results achieved therefrom.
Para 6.6
RECOMMENDATION
The Committee is of the opinion that with the increase in the number of employees opting for VRS, the programme
for retraining and redeployment of these employees requires tremendous technical expertise. The Committee has been
informed that training agencies have been identified throughout the country to rehabilitate workers who have retired
under the VRS scheme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Public Enterprises should
exercise greater monitoring over the working of these agencies and ensure that effective training depending on the
actual job market conditions is imparted.
ACTION  TAKEN  BY  THE  GOVERNMENT
Visualizing the professional/technical expertise required, the selection of the Nodal Training Agencies have been
made in such a way that it should cater to the need of the restructured employees. Both the Central PSUs as well as
Nodal Training Agencies, who are the key elements of the CRR programme have been advised to draw up the training
modules for 20 days/30 days/40 days in such a manner that should cater the individual needs of the rationalised
employees of CPSUs. They should also take into account the market opportunity available, the strength and weakness of
the trainees, the resources required for that particular project that the trainees would be taking up and the capacity of the
individual concerned etc. Besides, constant monitoring alongwith field visits by officers of Monitoring Cell, DPE are
made so as to have first hand feed  back from the beneficiaries and the difficulties/suggestion, if any are put into place
so as to bring further improvement in this programme. However, recommendations of the Committee have been noted.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
The Committee recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should play a proactive   role in the matter and
watch the quality of training programme, guide the trained persons in taking up projects in consultation with the Small
Industries Service Institutions and have meetings with the Credit Intitutions to facilitate availability of required funds.

Para 7.8
The Purchase Preference Policy
RECOMMENDATION
   The Committee is happy to note the extension in the Purchase Preference Policy upto 31
st March, 2004. However, the
Committee is very much concerned to note that some PSEs are not following the Purchase Preference Guidelines and
are not specifying this provision in their NITs. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Public
Enterprises should scrupulously monitor the compliance of the Purchase Preference Policy and all the administrative
Ministries/Departments should issue necessary instructions to the PSEs unde their jurisdiction to comply with the
Purchase Preference Policy.
ACTION  TAKEN  BY  THE  GOVERNMENT
Recommendations of the Committee on the compliance of the Purchase Preference Policy have been noted. As the
Committee is aware that DPE has already issued an OM dated 19
th November, 2001 to all administrative
Ministries/Departments and CPSUs for strict compliance of the policy. DPE has also issued another OM on 7.8.2002 to
all Ministries/Departments and Chief Executives of PSEs to follow the above OM in letter and spirit.
In view of the ERC recommendation to downsize the department, no headway has been made to set up a monitoring
cell in DPE due to shortage of trained and experienced manpower/officers. However, the same could be re-looked into.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
The Committee notes with dissatisfaction that there was delay of two and half months in issuing the circular to the
PSUs and administrative ministries. There are certain P.E.Ss, autonomous bodies who deliberately do not include
Purchase Preference clause in their Notice Inviting Tenders (NIT) and there is a possibility that these bodies might have
taken the opportunity not to include the said clause in their NIT during that period. Similarly those PSUs who could
have availed the Purchase Preference Policy during that period could not do so in the absence of the said circular. The
Committee feels that D.P.E. should not have taken so much time to issue the circular.
The Committee strongly recommends that Purchase Preference Policy should be extended for two and a half months
beyond 31.3.2004 to make good the loss, which took place due to departmental inaction.

Para 7.13
Inter P.S.U. Cooperation
RECOMMENDATION
The Committee is of the view that the very existance of several PSEs is at stake and if they do not bring in synergies
amongst themselves by resorting to inter-PSE cooperation, the possibity of their survival appears dim. The Committee,
therefore strongly recommends that strategic alliances may be made amongst PSEs in a mutually beneficial manner and
for that Department of Public Enterprises should be an initiative by devising suitable mechanisms on a priority basis.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that department of Public Enterprises should appoint a Task Force to devise a
mechanism early. 
ACTION  TAKEN  BY  THE  GOVERNMENT
This Department has already instructed all the PSEs to prepare their strategic plan outlining the road map for their
growth on a long-term basis. Forming a strategic tie ups and alliances is a part of the bussiness strategy and the
managements of the PSEs are in a better position to take a decision in this regard. Setting   up of task force in DPE may
not serve the purpose, however, the supporting role of Administrative Ministries will be crucial in this direction.

formulate an Auto Policy  in view of the ongoing liberalization of the economy and W.T.O. Obligations. In response to
the Committee's recommendations the Department of Heavy Industries in its Action Taken Note has informed the
Committee that Government of India has brought out an Auto Policy on 7th March, 2002.
3.1 The Chairman stated that the Committtee on Industry took up the Auto Policy for detailed discussion as the policy
laid down certain recommendations for the growth of the Industry. Since most of these recommendations required
actions by the Ministries other than the Department of Heavy Industries and so far  these recommendations had not been
translated into real  Government Policy. 
3.2 The Chairman apprised the Members that the Committee had already taken up the matter for discussion and in this
regard the Committee had held two meetings on 24 th June, and 16 th July, 2002. Based on the discussion held on 24 th
June, 2002 a  questionnaire was prepared and replies thereon was obtained from Department of Heavy Industries. In the
meeting held on 16th July, 2002 the Committee had interacted with Automotives Research Association of India (ARAI);
Society of India Automobiles Manufacturers (SIAM); Automotive Tyre Manufacturers Association (ATMA); and
Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA); Prozon Inc. (manufacture of Fuel saver). Apprising the
Members the details of discussion held in these two meetings, the Chairman spelt out the scope for discussion in Auto
Policy which inter-alia  included import of second hand imported cars; lack of testing facilities; foreign direct
investment, research and development; construction of bus-body building ; terminal life policy; lifting of quantitive
restriction; using spurious items and related 'e' mark issue; excise duty on tyre and concession on import tyre; ban on
used tyre; difficulties due to octroi on 5-6 States, switching over from tube tyre to tubeless tyre; encouragement to small
car industries; infrastructure import tariff; environmental aspects etc.
3.3 The Committee, thereafter, discussed in details the aims of Auto Policy which  aimed at to promote integrated,
phased, enduring and self-sustained growth of the Indian Automobile Industry. The Committee discussed also the
objective of Auto Policy which inter-alia include promotion  of a globally competitive automotive industry; Exalting
the sector as a lever of industrial growth and an employment; Establishment of an internatinal hub for manufacturing
small affordable passenger cars and key center for manufacturing Tractors   and Two wheelers in the world; Ensuring a
balanced transition to open trade at a minimal risk to the Indian Economy and local industry; Modernisation of the
industry by facilitating indigenous design, research and development; Steering up India's software industry into
automotive technology; Development of domestic safety and environmental standard at par with international standards;
assisting development of vehicles propelled by alternative energy sources.
4.         *                                                          *                                                                      *

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this Ninety-Third Report on the Action Taken by the Government on the
Recommendations contained in the 75th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry on Demends for Grants (2002-2003) pertaining to Ministry of Small Scale Industries.
2.      The 75th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry was presented to Rajya
Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 14th May, 2002.
3.      The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted the report at its
meeting held on the 11th December, 2002.
NEW DELHI ,
11 December, 2002;
         
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER 
Chairman,
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry.
REPORT
        The Ninety-Third Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
Recommendations contained in the 75 th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry on the Demands For Grants (2002-2003) pertaining to the Ministry of Small Scale Industries which was
presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 14th May, 2002.
2.     Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in the
Report. They have been categorized as follows:
        (i) Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Government:- Para 3.8, 4.5, 4.6, 5.3, 6.7, 7.5,
8.1, 8.2, 11.5, 11.6, 14.3, 15.1 (Chapter –I).
        (ii)    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government’s
replies:- Para 6.5, 10.2, 11.6, 11.7, 11.8, 17.1, 17.2, 13.3, 21.2 (Chapter–II).
        (iii)    Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the
Government:- Para 3.6, 3.7, 6.3, 6.4, 9.7, 11.2, 12.4, 12.5, 18.4, 19.3 (Chapter–III).
        (iv)   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government have not been received:-
Para 10.3, 10.4, 14.4, 16.2, 16.3, 20.3, 22.2, 23.2 (Chapter–IV).
        (v)   Observations/Recommendations at a Glance. (Chapter–V).
3.     The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries has accepted its recommendations
as mentioned in Chapter – I of the Report.
4.     In respect of the recommendations made in Chapter-II the Committee is convinced with the logic and explanation
advocated by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries and therefore does not want to pursue further.
5.     The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation of recommendations contained in Chapter-III
and therefore the Committee desires that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries would furnish logical explanation in
respect of these recommendations.
6.     In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry of Small Scale Industries has either furnished
the interim replies of couched its language in vague terms like the Ministries views have been conveyed to concerned
agencies therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries should furnish Action Taken Note
in respects of recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the
recommendations of the Committee.
7.     The details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
CHAPTER-I

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED
BY THE GOVERNMENT
WTO OBLIGATIONS
Para 3.8
Observation/Recommendation
        The Committee further observes that it is essential to create greater awareness about the obligations India has to
fulfil under the WTO regime and their impact on various sectors. There is a need to have adequate preparedness for
WTO compliance. The Committee recommends that regular interactions between the Government and SSIs should take
place for this purpose. Special cells with legal backup may be created and strengthened to deal with WTO related
problems of SSIs in concerned Government Department and industry associations.
Action Taken/Comments
        With a view to create awareness among the SSI units/Associations, etc. on WTO Agreements and their
implications, Ministry of SSI & ARI organized 28 one-day Sensitization Workshops all over the country. The
Ministry also organized 16 one-day workshops on Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) during 2001-2002 with
the assistance of WIPO and 16 Seminars all over the country to disseminate information to the SSI
Associations on Anti Dumping Procedures.
        A WTO cell in the office of DC (SSI) was set up on 15 th November, 1999 with the objective to keep abreast with
the recent developments in WTO, disseminate information to SSI units and their Associations, coordinate with other
Ministries and Departments, prepare the policy for SSIs in line with the WTO agreements, organize WTO Workshops
especially for SSI units at macro & micro level in the Small Scale Sector to enable the small/tiny sector to understand
the WTO agreements. With a view to assist the SSI Sector on legal matters a panel of legal experts on WTO matters has
been created at the Office of the DCSSI to assist the entrepreneurs in filing anti-dumping and IPR related cases.
RESTRUCTURING OF NATIONAL SMALL INDUSTRIES CORPORATION FOR DEVELOPMENT OF
SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
Para 4.5
Observation/Recommendation
        The Committee recommends that in response to challenges and opportunities arising out of globalisation, new
responsibilities envisaged for SIDO like gathering latest information regarding WTO Agreement, WTO sensitization
and strategy building programmes, anti-dumping proceedings, etc. need to receive priority consideration. In this context,
action for upgrading sub—sector specific schemes for technology transfer and exports need to be taken care of.
Appropriate HRD strategies need also to be paid attention. Government should work out restructuring of NSIC in the
light of suggestion made by M/s Ferguson and Co. (Consultant) to achieve the above objectives.
Action Taken/Comments
        This Ministry is getting sectoral studies conducted in areas having a strong SSI presence to formulate a pro-active
strategy and to fine-tune the existing policies and programmes. Five sectoral studies have already been undertaken with
UNDP assistance of US $ 20,000 on Hand tools, Medicinal Biotechnology, Glass and Ceramics, Bicycle parts and
Flavour and Fragrance. The Ministry also financially supports Industry Associations to develop monitoring mechanisms
on the performance of four selected product clusters in terms of growth, removal of QRs, surge in imports, etc. These
Associations/Clusters are CII-Food Processing and Machine tools; FISME – Shaneel; and Kishangarh Marble
Association – Marble respectively. The work on these projects has since been started.
        The Ministry has also formulated a “market Development Assistance for SSI Exporters” SSI-MDA Scheme to
enhance exports by the SSIs. Under the scheme financial assistance upto Rs. 1 lakh is given to SSI Associations for
initiating anti-dumping investigations.
        M/s A F. Ferguson & Co. were asked to prepare an operational plan keeping in mind the various activities of NSIC
as approved by the Ministry after discussion with the share holders. M/s A.F. Ferguson & Co. has since finalized the
operational plan which was submitted to this Ministry in July, 2002. The operational plan was put up to the Board of
Directors in their meeting held on August 2, 2002. After approval of Plan by the NSIC Board and Government, it will
be put in operation.
DEVELOPMENT OF CLUSTERS
Para 4.6

93rd Report of Committee on Industry
