3.35 The Committee expresses serious concern that the stocks of goods worth several hundred crores are lying locked and unused.
Perhaps this is why, KVIC has been experiencing working capital difficulties. If this state of affairs continues, KVIC will not only be
faced with resource crunch as the money remains locked up and stocks lying unsold but also lose customer base as there will be no takers
for the old stocks.
Comments
        The continuous efforts are being made to liquidate stocks which have reduced from Rs. 658 crores approximately in March, 2001 to
Rs. 579 crores in March, 2002.
3.36 The Committee recommends that KVIC should dispose of the old stock as early as possible even by providing heavy discounts and
recover money. KVIC may utilize the revenue earned on fresh inventory and recycle the money. KVIC should keep fresh inventory as
old inventory would not fetch much money.
Comments
        Rebate policy for the year 2002-03 has been announced. KVIC has been directed to take urgent remedial action to see that old stock
lying in the various godowns of KVIC and that of Khadi Institutions is reduced to minimum.
Review of stock build-up
Para 3.41
        The Committee recommends that CCPC should henceforth undertake periodical review of the stock build-up before approving the
quantities to be purchased. Further, responsibility for the lapses for allocating of funds and excess stocking of cotton on the part of
officials/non-officials should be fixed.
Comments
        The suggestion of the Committee has been noted and has already been communicated to KVIC for taking further necessary action.
Ministry has already asked KVIC to fix the responsibility for the lapses for allocating of funds and excess stocking of cotton on the
defaulting officials.
Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC)
Paras 4.2 & 4.3
4.2   The Committee observes that in spite of KVIC's repeated request over the years, funds flow to KVI institutions from banks under
ISEC is not up to the desired level. Analysis of ISECs issued by KVIC and actual funds made available by banks against the ISEC
indicates that in the recent past the gap in the ISEC value vis-a-vis fund provided by banks goes to be extent of 50%.
Comments
        The Ministry is in agreement with the observations of the Committee. Necessary action is being taken in this matter.
4.3   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India/RBI may take appropriate policy decision so that banks are
bound to honour the ISECs issued by the KVIC to its full extent.
Comments
        The matter has been taken up with the banks by the Ministry so that the recommendations of the Committee will be implemented by
KVIC and banks.
EXIM Policy - 2002
Para 5.5
        The five year EXIM policy announced on 1st April, 2002 seeks to enable Indian artisans, Cottage and Small Industries to venture
out overseas and adopt the world as their market. The new policy makes exports free, easy and possibly rewarding. This assumes special
significance especially when India ranks low in global competition given global slowdown and domestic recession. The EXIM policy is
comprehensive, encompassing agro sector, cottage and handicrafts and small scale sectors thus taking care of more than 80% of the
population living in rural areas.
Comments
        A draft scheme for export promotion of KVI products under the EXIM policy has been formulated which has been sent for vetting to
Finance Wing. It will be implemented very shortly.
Coir Products

Para 5.6
        The Committee therefore, recommends that in view of the importance of this sector, diversified forms of coir products and product
mix should be attempted. Research programmes should be undertaken by the Coir Board for improving the quality of the coir fibre, for
enhancing the export of coir products such as the green husk fibre produced in non traditional coir producing areas using "coirret". The
Committee also notes that the market for coir pith, a waste material of the coir industry converted into one of major export items in the
list of coir products, remains untapped and the potential for the export of coir pith is excellent. The Committee therefore, recommends
that all out efforts should be made to make pith export achieve its fullest potential.
Comments
        The recommendations have been noted for further action. However, in this connection it is stated that under the UNDP assisted
project, the Coir Board has entered into a collaborative project with the National Institute of Design, Ahmedabad for stratetgic Design
Intervention and product development for diversification of coir industry. As a part of this project blending coir with other natural fibres
like sisal, jute, banana, rami etc. and spin finer count yarn for making innovative products like vertical blinds, curtain materials etc. has
been undertaken. The Coir Board has already conducted workshops for training the representatives of the trade for blending coir fibre
with other natural fibres and to manufacture value added products out of it. For diversification of coir products, a project has been
undertaken in association with Indian Institute of Packaging, Mumbai for developing package material using coir fibre.
        As recommended by the Committee, the Board is taking efforts in association with the private sector for promoting export of coir
pith. Besides, the Coir Board has developed a fungal spawn viz. Pith Plus for converting coir pith into organic manure. The technology
for production of Coir Pith Organic Manure (C-POM) using Pith Plus is being popularized in the trade by organizing field demonstrations
in the selected coir production centers as a continuing plan programme. The Coir Board extends financial assistance to the entrepreneurs
for setting up coir pith processing units for which assistance to the tune of 25% of the capital investment on work shed and equipment
would be provided by the Coir Board subject to a ceiling of Rs. 1,00,000/-. These programmes are proposed to be continued during the
Tenth Plan period also.
Allocation Offund for Coir
Para 5.9
        The Committee observes that coir sector employs 5 lakh people and it has the potential of expanding its activities. Although the
funds allocation for the sector has been doubled in the Ninth Five Year Plan from what it was in the Eighth Five Year Plan, (Rs. 31 crores
during the Eighth Five Year Plan and Rs. 60 crores during the Ninth Five Year Plan), this sector is still under budgeted. There is further
scope for absorbing funds in this sector particularly in the non-traditional areas such as Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh,
Orissa, West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands where new products could be developed. The Committee therefore recommends that
the allocation for the coir industry should be revised so that attention can be focused on providing more employment opportunities in this
sector.
Comments
        Against the Plan allocation of Rs.31.00 crores during the Eighth Five Year Plan and Rs.60 crores during the Ninth Five Year Plan, a
higher allocation of Rs.115 crores has been made for the coir sector during the Tenth Five Year Plan.
Welfare Measures in Coir Industry
Para 5.11
        The Committee appreciates the measure for welfare for the people, especially women, engaged in the coir industry which remains
unorganized to a great extent. The Committee hopes that more such initiatives would be taken in near future for the benefit of large
number of people engaged in the industry.
Comments
        The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for future guidance.
Recovery Under PMRY
Para 6.9
        The Committee observes that the crux of the problem lies in the recovery scenario under PMRY which has been showing a
decreasing trend. If this sort of thing continues, there will be less funds available year by year to channelise for future schemes as the
money will be in short supply. A stage may come that the scheme may have to be closed down due to non-availability of funds. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that recovery of loans, which is a grey area in the present scenario, should be given more attention
and loopholes in this regard should be plugged so that the scheme may not be scuttled for want of funds in future and recycling of funds
may continue. The Chairman/Managing Directors - All India Scheduled Commercial Banks may be suitably advised by the RBI to

improve their recovery performance to recycle the funds and constitute recovery cells at Regional/Zonal Office level.
Comments
        The Chairman/Managing Directors, all Indian Scheduled Commercial Banks have been suitably advised by the RBI to improve the
recovery performance to re-cycle the funds and constitute 'Recovery Cell' and Regional/controlling office level, to improve further by
their Circular No. RPCD.SP.BC. 13/09.04.01/2000-01 dated 04.09.2000. On the advice of the RBI, Union Bank of India, Central Bank of
India, Dena Bank and Bank of India have constituted 'Recovery Cells' at Regional/Zonal Office levels. The RBI has further advised
banks to keep a close watch on the recovery of loan through better post-disbursement credit supervision vide  their Letter No.
RPCD.SP.BC. 34/09.04.01/2001-02 dated 19.10.2001. As per the report received from the RBI, the recovery for half year ending Sept.,
2001 has slightly improved and is 28.8 for the half year ending Sept., 2001. However, the observation of the Committee under Para 6.9
have again been communicated to the RBI for taking further necessary action vide Letter No. PMRY-P/PC/10(1)/2002 deted 16.07.02.
Achievement of Target under PMRY
Paras 6.10, 6.11, 6.12, and 6.13
6.10 The Committee futher observes that though the Government achieved in some measure quantitative target of the PMRY, no efforts
were made either by the Government or by other agencies to evaluate the qualitative achievement of the scheme. The beneficiaries
experienced difficulties in starting and running the venture. The major problem in starting the unit was in getting the loan. 50% of the
beneficiaries were affected by the delay in disbursement of the loan. This forced them to take loan from moneylenders at a very high rate
of interest and this had an adverse effect on their business. The beneficiaries reported that because of the financial delay they could not
reach their expectations. The beneficiaries of the category made default in payment of loan.
6.11 The Committee finds that shortage of funds for working capital is hindering the PMRY beneficiaries. They could not execute their
orders in time due to shortage of funds and for marketing capital requirements, they resort to private money lenders at a high rate of
interest resulting in the increased cost of production and short fall in profit margin.
6.12 The high cost of operation is another problem where 20% of the industries were affected by this and they could not compete in the
local market. Increase in the cost of spare parts are the main cost accelerating items and entrepreneurs could not repay the interest in time.
The entrepreneurs could not adjust themselves to the demand and supply mechanism of the market.
6.13 As regards the undue delay in giving loans by banks, the Committee impresses upon banks to avoid undue delay. The Committee
recommends that implementing banks should be advised by the RBI to sanction the applications within the prescribed time frame and
speedily dispose off the same to ensure that there is no inordinate gap between the sanction and disbursement of loan. DICs should play a
pro-active role in this regard. RBI's guidelines for disposing of applications under PMRY within the time period of thirty days must be
adhered to by banks.
Comments
        Banks have been advised by the RBI to dispose off applications upto a credit limit of Rs.25,000 within a fortnight and those for over
Rs.25,000/- within a 8-9 weeks vide  their Letter No. RPCD.SP.BC.303/09.04.01/1994-95 dated 1.8.94. The implementing banks have
been advised by the RBI to sanction the application within the prescribed time frame and speedily dispose off the same to ensure that
there is no inordinate gap between sanction and disbursement of loan vide  their Letter No. RPCD.SP.BC.34/09.04.01/1994-45 dated
19.10.01. The recommendations of the Committee as contained in its 74th Report have also been communicated to the RBI and to the
States/UTs vide Letter No. PMRY-P-PC/10(1)/2002 dated 16.07.02.
Power Connection under PMRY
Para 6.14
        Delay in getting power connection affected 30% of them in terms of production and marketing. Delay in getting delivery of assets
forced them to postpone the launch of their project eventually leading to addition to cost of the project. This upsets the success of the
project and may lead to more defaulters in future. Delay in power connection/power cut also affected their production and resulted in the
increased cost of production.
6.15 As regards, the delay in getting power connection, the Committee desires that Government should take suitable action in the matter
and impress upon the State Governments to deal such cases on priority basis.
Comments
        The observations of the Committee have been communicated to States/UTs vide this Office Letter No. PMRY-P/PC/10(1)/2002
dated 17.7.02

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF
THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries
Para 1.2
        The Committee welcomes the formation of the new Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries. It has satisfied the long-felt need for the
creation of a new Ministry which would look exclusively after the needs of this sector. This is expected to give a boost to the sector,
especially when our industries now face competition from global companies and find it hard to survive.
Comments
        No comments are required.
Constitution of KVIC
Para 3.2
        The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its 49th Report on Demands for Grants (2002-03)
pertaining to Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro and Rural Industries had expressed its concern at the inordinate delay in
reconstituting the Khadi and Village Industries Commission. The term of the previous Khadi and Village Industries Commission expired
in September, 1999 and since then the Commission had been non-existent which adversely affected the working of Khadi and Village
Industries. The Committee has been informed that the Commission has been reconstituted w.e.f. 2nd October, 2001. The Committee
welcomes the reconstitution of the Commission and hopes that the new Commission will be able to take care of the requirements of the
Khadi sector to make it self sustaining and vibrant.
Comments
        No comments are required.
Poor Quality and Design of Khadi Products
Para 3.37
        The Committee observes that poor quality and poor designs have resulted in poor sales and accumulation of large inventories. The
working cycle of production sales-cash-realization for Khadi is long and substantial funds are blocked as working capital for Khadi
institutions. This has adversely affected performance.
Comments
        The slump in Khadi performance was mainly attributed to the production of goods, which are not as per demand and taste of the
market. It was a fact that most of the Khadi producing institutions located in rural areas could not cope up with fast changing consumer
tastes particularly in cotton textile materials. This has to a large extent, resulted in the accumulation of inventory. One of the important
requirements in the above backdrop is the improvement in the quality and design of Khadi products. The Government of India is
implementing the Khadi package for Khadi and Village Industries programme which envisages better design development, quality
assurance standards etc. On implementation of such measures it is expected that the performance of Khadi sector would improve
considerably.
Employment Generation Under PMRY
Para 6.1
        The PMRY has emerged as a major Central Sector Scheme for employment generation among the educated unemployed youth, by
providing financial and other entrepreneurial development assistance in establishing self-employment ventures. Significant progress has
been achieved in the implementation of the scheme and as reported by the RBI, 7.748 lakh persons have been sanctioned loans under
PMRY, since its inception during the 8th Five Year Plan. The scheme is continuing in the 9th Five Year Plan. During the years 1997-98,
1998-99, 1999-2000 and 2000-01 loans have been sanctioned to 10.20 lakh persons. Further, 0.48 lakh persons have been sanctioned
loans during 2001-02 upto November, 2001. The anticipated target PMRY for 2002-03 is 2.2 lakh beneficiaries. The entrepreneurs
sanctioned loan under the scheme are provided stipendiary entrepreneurship, development training by various training institutions. The
period of training for industry sector is 5-20 working days and for service/business sector 7 to 10 working days. The training expenditure
admissible including stipend for industry sector is upto Rs.1,000/- per trainee and for service/business sector upto Rs.500/- per trainee.
The Central Government provides funds for training of beneficiaries and other entrepreneurial development activities in the form of
subsidy @ 5 per cent of project cost subject to a ceiling of Rs.15,000/- per beneficiary in respect of North Easterm States and Rs.7,500/-
per beneficiary for rest of the country. Besides this, funds are provided to the States/UTs for scheme operation.

Wardha Institute
Para 3.9
        The Committee welcomes this move as it aught to provide a great fillip to the sector. Simultaneously, the Committee notes that there
is no specific provision in the Budget for the required funds to implement the announcement of upgrading the Wardha Institute as a
National Institute named after Mahatma Gandhi. The Committee is of the opinion that there is a need for additional provision of at least
Rs.100 crores for the Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Rural Industrialisation, Wardha. This provision may be spread over a period of three
years.
Comments
        The Khadi and Village Industries Commission, Mumbai (KVIC), a statutory body under the administrative control of the Ministry of
Agro and Rural Industries has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and the IIT, Delhi in April, 2001 to implement a
three-year Project for revamping of the existing Jamnalal Bajaj Central Research Institute (JBCRI), Wardha and convert it into Mahatma
Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation (MGIRI). The duration of the Project is 3 years (May-2001 - April-2004). The total allocation
for the project is Rs. 8.35 crores. A total of Rs. 5.70 crores has so far been released to the KVIC under S&T including funds for the
implementation of this Project and the balance will be released in due course during the project period. It is hoped that the project will be
completed during the stipulated time-frame and within the total project outlay. There has not been any project cost revision-requiring
provision of Rs.100 crores. The project implementation is constantly under review to ensure that there are no slippages in the completion
of the project.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        Since this is an important national project, the Committee feels that it should be completed by April, 2004. The Committee
impresses upon the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries to keep on vigil on the progress of the project.
R&D for KVIC
Para 3.10
        The Committee observes that R&D is the need of the hour if industries are to compete globally and growth in the sector is to be
stimulated. The Committee, therefore, recommends that allocation for Research and Development for KVIC requires be increased. If
need be, joint collaboration with foreign firms may to be taken up.
Comments
        The Ministry is alive to the significance of R&D to promote global competitiveness of the indigenous industries. Therefore,
Government in its effort to strengthen Village Industries (VIs) for production of quality marketable goods, has been making substantial
funding to help organizations and entrepreneurs to promote their existing sphere of activities. But very little investment has gone into
research and development of support services infrastructure to promote and disseminate improved technology to increase productivity
and quality standards of goods produced in rural areas by the Village Industries.
        The inputs of S&T for Technology Upgradation, transfer of appropriate technology, quality assessment of associated inputs, Quality
Control/Assurance Mechanism of final products are some of the important areas where organizations like Khadi and Village Industries
Commission (KVIC), Mumbai under this Ministry, could play an important role either through its own infrastructure or using
infrastructure available elsewhere for the strengthening of Rural Industrialisation.
        In order to provide such inputs to the Village Industries sector in the country, Government has approved the following as part of the
Khadi Package announced in May, 2001:-
A.    Strengthening of the existing S&T/R&D infrastructure of the KVIC.
B.     To establish technical inter faces with the technical establishments in the country.
C.    Networking of Quality Testing/Certifying laboratories/Institutions in the country.
        Institutions have been selected by the Government for upgrading R&D facilities. As per the package announced by the Government

97th Report of Committee on Industry

of India, funds allotted under sector specific R&D will be utilized to the tune of Rs. 1550 lakhs over a three years period.
        Similarly, Technical Back-up Units (TBUs/Interfaces) covering the entire country at some S&T institutes will be set up. All these
units will form a network. The proposed Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation at Wardha will be the main node of this
network.
        In order to strengthen the quality assurance labs, the KVIC will enter into MoUs with existing laboratories recognized by the
National Accredition Board for Laboratories (NABL) which will cover both the public sector as well as private sector. KVIC products
will be standard sized according to BIS/AGMARK/FPO/ etc. Adequate budget provision will be made for strengthening of the quality
control laboratories.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        The strengthening of the existing S&T/R&D infrastructure of the KVIC was announced in May, 2001 but not much progress
has been made in the matter. The Committee recommends that this project should be completed in a definite time-frame.
JPRGY
Para 3.12
        While appreciating this initiative, the Committee expresses its concern that JPRGY should not meet the fate of NPRI (National
Programme for Rural Industrialisation as announced in the Budget for the financial year 1999-2000. The allocation of Rs.40 lakhs was
kept for the NPRI scheme in the BE 2001-02 which was reduced to nominal amount of Rs.1.00 lakh in the RE of that year. The scheme is
yet to take off. However, in the BE  2002-03 a provision of Rs. 90 lakhs has been made. The Committee, therefore impresses upon the
Ministry to review the progress of NPRI so that the earlier mistakes are not repeated by the administration.
Comments
        The scheme on NPRI was announced in the year 1999-2000 with a mission to set up 100 rural clusters every year. Office of the DC
(SSI) was made the coordinating agency of the programme. KVIC, SIDBI and NABARD are the major implementing agencies. No fund
was provided separately for the programme and it was felt that various Ministries/Departments were having their own programmes in this
area which could be coordinated and their synergies exploited for better impact.
        Efforts were made to firm up the scheme at the initial stage. A number of meetings were called in which all the agencies involved in
rural industrialization participated. A national level Steering Committee was constituted under the Chairmanship of Secretary (SSI &
ARI) to guide, implement and monitor the programme. Consequently, KVIC identified 50 clusters for development for each year, SIDBI
25 and NABARD 50 for a period of 5 years. So far, KVIC has launched the programme in 20 clusters, NABARD in 14 and SIDBI in 13.
The other clusters are also under consideration and preliminary/diagnostic studies are being conducted of these clusters. It was, however,
felt that some fund was required for certain gap filling exercises towards cluster intervention. Therefore, the Office of the DC (SSI)
launched a scheme on NPRI in the year 2001-02 to supplement the efforts of the various agencies. The amount provided in the scheme is
only Rs.5 lakhs per cluster. The purpose of financial assistance is to fill certain gaps in the development of clusters, and it does not
constitute the entire amount required for such development. As the scheme has been approved in the year 2001-02, it is expected to yield
results in the coming years.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee fails to understand as to why a scheme is announced by the Government without any budgetary provision. Ministry's
reply that no fund was provided separately for the programme and it was felt that various Ministries/Departments were having their own
programmes in this area which could be coordinated and their synergy exploited for their impact does not appear to be sound because this
Committee has its own experience that coordination among Central Ministries and Departments is a difficult preposition to achieve. The
Committee now expects that with the provision of funds the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would implement the programme.

sector, it is necessary to provide and offer products that match consumer preferences.
Comments

regard.

        The Committee welcomes the increase in the allocation for creating additional employment opportunities under REGP. The
programme can prove to be a major instrument in bringing about self-sufficiency for rural populace and in getting rid of unemployment
problems in a big way, if implemented by State KVI Boards in an effective manner. In order to implement the REGP/Margin Money

Para 6.2.7 BIRD GROUP OF COMPANIES

While the Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of Steel is supervising the
functioning of Bird Group of Companies but at then same time the Committee is of the opinion
that the Ministry of Steel should not act as a mute spectator when the performance of the
financially sick companies of Bird Group of Companies i.e. Bisra Stone lime Co, Ltd, (BSLC),

has declined due to improvement _ in the steel making technology but at the sametime the

dwindle further. This is sorry state of affairs. Out of a group of eight companies only four are

management lacks the required fund for VRS purpose and is at bay to find out the ways and
means to raise the same. Under the circumstances, the Committee feels that the Ministry of Steel
should come forward for rescuing MECON in time.

Recommendations    (Para 7.1.7)
 
MODERNISATION OF THE GEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee understands that in the wake of radical reforms in economic and mineral policies of the country, up-to-
date high quality database for optimum development of natural resources both on land and offshore, management of
natural hazards and protection of environment became essential. A quantum jump to the modernisation and technology
up gradation in all spheres of activity is prerequisite for the goal.
Action Taken
            The Department is giving full support to the modernization efforts and capacity building of GSI so that GSI is
geared to make available the high quality database for optimum development of natural resources both onland and off
shore.
 
Recommendations  (Para 7.1.8 )
EARTHQUAKE STUDIES BY THE GEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA       
After the devastating effect of the Gujarat earthquake, the Committee feels more emphasis should be given on the
earthquake studies to save human lives and property in the urban as well rural areas. The Committee recommends the
adequates funds may be made available to the G.S.I. for the purpose. The G.S.I. should also take the aid and assistance
of the experts available across the World.
Action Taken
GSI has given thrust to active fault mapping and microzonation studies of urban clusters, as a part of earthquake
studies towards deleneation of potential risk zones and mitigation of impact of disasters.  It is also collaborating with
Indian Metrological Department and participating in a Department of Science & Technology sponsored Indo-Italian
Collaborative Research Project for seismic studies.  Provision has been made for the procurement of the state-of-art
field location cum data collection equipments as a part of modernization programmes of Geological Survey of India .
Recommendations  ( Para 7.2.7 )

Non-Plan Loan to Mines PSUs
The Committee   is of the opinion that   non-plan loan is a necessary evil as it is   essential   for loss making PSUs to
maintain its  operation and   separation of surplus  work force and  sometimes even to meet the  cash loss, all depending 
upon the quantum of  loss being incurred by a  PSU.  Non-plan loan is an evil in the sense   that the amount of non-plan
loan gets added to the liability of the Company, which is always a burden on the Company.  The Committee notes that
during  2002-03  no non-plan loan has been allocated to mines PSUs, although rationalisation of manpower is being 
undertaken in almost  all mines PSUs.
Action Taken
            During the year 2002-03, no non-plan loan has been allocated to the PSUs under the Department of Mines.  The
position of non-plan loan given earlier to the PSUs is as follows:
(a)
                Hindustan Copper Ltd.

FINANCIAL RESTRUCTURING OF HINDUSTAN COPPER LTD.    
The Committee is pleased to note that as a result of implementation of VRS in HCL during last three years the wage
cost as percentage of turnover has come down   from 35.81% in 1999 -2000 to 22.98% in 2000-01 and turnover per
employee has increased from Rs. 3.30 lakh to Rs.5.11 lakh during the same period.
The Committee understands that HCL is sailing through adverse financial situation and is a loss making PSU, therefore,
the Committee is in agreement with the Department of Mines regarding incapacity of repayment of non-plan loan by
HCL. The Committee   feels that since the financial restructuring     of HCL is on the card the Department of Mines
should not delay any longer the submission of the proposal for conversion of non-plan loan   of Rs.440 crore   into grant
and the Government should not hesitate in clearing the proposal, as cleaner the balance sheet   of the Company larger
the possibility of a potential purchasers coming forward.

conversion of non-plan loan of Rs.440 crores into grant. Besides following measures have also been taken:-

                  Conversion of outstanding plan loan as on March 31, 2002, amounting to Rs.71.50 crore into equity to
improve the net worth of the Company.

(iii)               Extension of period of the Government guarantees already provided for raising working capital term loan
by a further 2 years or disinvestments which is earlier, in order to facilitate meeting the obligations for the
Secured Bond repayment.

mines PSUs are either have already been disinvested  i.e. BALCO  and HZL     or  are on the verge of disinvestment  as
in the  case of HCL  and NALCO and   due  to  on-going  liberalisation  process , the contribution of   mining sector  to
national exchequer would improve in the years to come.  The Committee hopes that the on-going  liberalisation process
should enhance the capabilities  of making  contribution of mining sector to the nation   and society in general.  In this
regard the  Committee  hopes that the Government would give due consideration towards  the contribution  made by
units of private  sector and PSUs in mining sector.
Action Taken
            Under the National Mineral Policy, 1993, 13 minerals hitherto reserved for exploitation by Public Sector were
thrown open for exploitation by Private Sector also and thereby provided a level playing field to private companies in
the mineral sector.  Thus entire mining sector is open for private investment including Foreign Direct
Investments(FDI).  A number of leading global mining companies have evinced interest in Indian mining sector
resulting in expected FDI inflow of Rs.3963 crores.  The National Mineral Policy, 1993 has also recognized the need for
encouraging private investment including FDI and state of art technology in the mineral sector and has therefore
contributed towards national exchequer and society in general.  Besides this, a number of amendments have been carried
out in the MMDR Act, 1957, MCR, 1960 and MCDR, 1988,  since 1994 to make Indian mining sector investor friendly
and hassle free.

Action Taken:
 
The National Mineral Policy, 1993, recognised the need for encouraging private investment including foreign
direct investment and state-of-the-art technology in mineral sector. Further , National Mineral Policy 1993 has  stressed 
that the Central  Government in consultation with the State Governments, shall continue to formulate the legal measures
for the regulation of mines and the development of mineral resources to ensure basic  uniformity  in mineral 
administration and to ensure that the development of mineral resources keeps pace, and is in consonance with the
national policy goals.
 
It is therefore evident that review of the policy and consequent amendment(s) in the Mines and Minerals
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and rules framed there under to cater to future demands is(are)  an ongoing
process, and can not be a one time exercise.
 
 For a structured  and institutionalized review of the policies and procedures affecting the mining and the mineral
sector and for all matters connected or incidental thereto, the Mineral Advisory Council has been constituted by the
Government. The Hon’ble Minister for Coal and Mines is the Chairman of the Council. The Council has balanced
representation from State Governments, Industry Associations , Experts in mining sector as well as Members of
Parliament. The Mineral Advisory Council inter alia reviews the status of implementation of the National Mineral
Policy, advises the Government on mineral policy and legislation and the status of the mining and the mineral sector,
including inter alia  all the issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its Report.
 
After the National Mineral Policy was announced, Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957
has been amended in 1994 and 1999. After amendment in the Principal Act in 1999, the Mineral Concession Rules,
1960 have been amended on January 17,.2000, September 25,.2000,January 22,2000, and on January 11.,2002 .
Similarly, after 1999, the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules 1988 have been amended on 17.1.2000,
25.9.2000 and 11.1.2002.
The  amendments in the legislation have been extensively discussed prior to their enactment and honed as per
recommendations of the Mineral Advisory Council in its various meetings. As a recent example, minerals for which the
State Governments would be empowered to approve mining plans have been identified, time limits have been prescribed
for  conveying a decision on application(s) for mineral concessions and mining plans, and fees payable for various
applications under the rules have been revised as per recommendations of the Mineral Advisory Council.
 
            Two meetings of the Mineral Advisory Council have been held since 1999. In addition the Department of Mines
organized a Conference of State Ministers of Mining and Geology, as well as a Tripartite Meeting of the Central
Government, State Governments and Investors in the Mining Sector in 2001. These meetings also discussed inter alia
the issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry. The review of the National Mineral Policy
and the other issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee will therefore appropriately be listed for
discussion in the next meeting of the Mineral Advisory Committee.         
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
            The Committee expects  that the  Department of Mines  understands the concern  of Department related
Parliamentary  Standing Committee on Industry  and  therefore  appreciate its desire accordingly.  Interchanging and
intermingling  and  the functions of  Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee with  Mineral Advisory
Council  would not only be belittling and undermining the status of  this Committee   but also juxtaposing  the role   of
Mineral Advisory Council.    The Department of Mines placed  the issues identified  by the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry in the meetings of  Mineral Advisory Council  but deprived the Committee of the outcome of the
meetings and  discussion held.  The Committee recommends that the Department of Mines should  furnish the details of 
Action Taken in its Note and  apprise the Committee comprehensively.   The Committee recommends that  the
Department of Mines should forward the  minutes of the meeting of Mineral Advisory  Council  to this Committee
whenever  the Mineral Advisory Council discusses the issues identified by the Committee.

FOREIGN INVESTMENT IN MINING SECTOR
 The Committee appreciates  the  efforts made by the Department of Mines towards making the  mining sector more

Concession Rules.  These initiatives will accelerate the inflow of foreign investment in the mining sector.

9.3 (ii) The Committee finds that there is only a marginal increase of Rs. 50 lakh. 'n the 
Budget Estimates compared to last year budget estimates of 32 crores. Rs. 32.5 crores 
sought for in this current year Budget Estimates is to be spent for meeting expenses on two 
items, i.e., transport subsidy and establishment of Growth Centres. From the funds asked 
for under the Scheme, the Committee notes that adequate planning has not been done. The 
implementation is tardy. The backward areas in the country are in difficult terrain and Jack 
of basic infra!'.tructure. Concrete steps have, therefore. to be taken to motivate people to 

avail of the facilities and concessions under the Scheme. State Governments sometimes do 
not keep any provision for the purpose. The infrastructural deVelopment in the area for the 
establishment of Growth Centres is done by the Central Government only when the 
concerned State Government is ready to provide with the required funds. The entrepreneurs 
are caught in the cobweb of Central Government grant, State Government grant, loans from 
financial institutions and market borrowings. The entrepreneur finds extremely difficult and 
feels demotivated when he faces diffculties right from the acquisition of land, power supply, 
availability of water, etc. Many entrepreneurs have left midway their projects due to these 
factors and non-cooperation from different sections of Governmental machinery . The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that for the development of Growth Centres in the 
backward areas 'single window scheme' may be adopted as one of the motivating factors to 
willing entrepreneurs to establish industrial units in backward areas. The Committee would 
further recommend perfect coordination among the Central Government, concerned State 
Government and the financial institution· to make the Scheme successful. The Committee 
would, therefore, like that Government should give re-orientation to the programme and 
ensure its proper implementation. 
9.4. Administrative Expenditure: The Administrative expenditure under the Head '3451' 
indicates an amount of Rs. 5.37 crores for the Budget Estimates. Out of this 11 lakhs is a 
plan expenditure for computerisation and 5.26 crores is for non-plan expenditure on the 
salaries and other expenditure on the maintenance of the Department. The estimates do not 
indicate any perception of the Department for the re-deployment of its surplus personnel on 
account of the reduction of the work load of the Department due to delicencing and other 
steps taken under the new Industrial Policy. The performance Budget of the Department is 
also silent on the extent of the austerity measures taken to curtail non-plan expenditure. The 
staff in any Department should reflect the work load". and surplus staff, if found should be re­
deployed for better use. The Committee, therefore, recommends that an assessment of the 
surplus staff may be made for their re-deployment in other spheres of Governmental 
activity.

9.6 (ii) The Committee, therefore, finds that foreign investment and technical collabora­
tion has been approved in Industrial Sector relating to even Food Processing Industries to 
the tune of 8472.2 millions of rupees without any consideration for the growth of indigenous 
industries in this Sector. Food Processing Industry have to a large extent depend on the local 
ancillary small scale and village and cottage industries and thereby there is no safeguard for 
the survival and development of such industries. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that :-
fa) disinvestment by PSUs and the funds accrued on account of the disinvestment 
should be utilised for reviving, and restructuring of the sick PSUs. The demand for 
grants and performance budget are totally silent on this aspect; 
(b) foreign investments should be approved in areas where we are yet to develop the 
technical know-how and depend upon foreign technology, The Government should 
ensure that foreign investment is earmarked for industries in the export sector to 
boost up the export of our industrial production. It should not disturb and dislocate 
the existing industrial growth of the country in the long run. The foreign 
collaboration should be identified for industries where we are lagging behind in 
international market. The Committee regrets to note that the demand for grants for 
the Department of Heavy Largest Industry does not perceive this situation and no 
funds have been allocated to organise and regulate foreign investment in our 
industrial sector particularly in the PSUs which we have developed and grown over 
a period of several decades but for which the present infrastructure for further 
development could not have been there; 
(c) every effort should be made to ensure that all the eight· benches of Board for 
Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) are made functional and the cases of 
sick PSUs pending before them are disposed off expeditiously to minimise the drain 
on the public funds. The Demands for Grants of the Department and the 
Performance Budget do not reflect any concern on the depleted strength of the 
BIFR benches and the expenditure and efforts to be made by the Department to 
make them functional; 
(d) the details of disinvestments made by the Public Sector Undertakings, undertaking­
wise, should be compiled by the Department and the data relating to the sale prices 
of shares, undertaking-wise and the amount of money so collected and spent, 

undertaking-wise may be collected may be furnished to the Committee for further detailed 
examination in order to allay the misgivings in the minds of general publia that the shares 
were sold at throw away prices by some Public Sector Undertakings; and 
(e) concrete steps should be taken by the Department to ensure that foreign investors 
are not allowed to dump their unsold products in India to the detrement of 
indigenous industries. 
9.6 (iii) MUL Incidentally , the Committee finds that the CISF was providing security at 
Maruti Udyog Limited at Gurgaon since 1983. In June 1992, MUL became a non­
government company and it was felt by MUL that the continuance of CISF would probably 
not be possible. MUL looked for alternative arrangements. It was found that Group 4 
Securities India (P) Ltd. was the best. Group 4 Securities is an international security 
company with operations in 40 countries. It started operations in India in February 1990 and 
has six branches in India. After a period of familiarisation and training the Group 4 
contingent has taken over security responsibility for MUL plant w.e.f April 1, 1993. 
The Committee notes with regret that even in the matter of switching over the Security 
network, Maruti Udyog Limited had to opt for an international security company thereby 
opening the door to a multinational company for a job for which trained and adequate 
manpower and resources were available within the country, if it was a necessity to dispense 
with the security cover provided by CISF, local talent and manpower could have been 
engaged by Maruti Udyog.

The performance Budget of the Department is silent on the steps taken by it to check the

This is a scheme to benefit educated unemployed youth with low income families and 30%

9. 7 (ii) Small Scale Industries: A sum of Rs .• 190.40 crores has been provided in the 
Budget Estimates for 1993-94. The revised estimates of 1992-93 were to the tune of Rs. 
147.41 crores. The Development of Small Scale Industries is organised through Development 
Commissioner of Small Scale Industries of the Department. The Committee finds that on 
administration and maintenance of the office of the Development Commissioner an amount 
of Rs. 3.68 crores is provided in the Budget Estimates with a component of 3.10 crores as 
non-plan expenditure. Rs. 58 lakhs are only for plan expenditure on two items i.e. publicity 
for 40 lakhs and for modernisation of library for 18 lakhs in the Budget Estimates. 
Comparing the budget figures for an important item like training which is 3.41 crores with 
that of the expenditure on the maintenance of the office of Development Commissioner, it 
may be seen that expenditure priorities are not on sound lines. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that every step should be taken to regulate the expenditure on this item and 
the money thus saved may be earmarked for other developmental item(s) of the Small Scale 
Industries. 
9. 7 (iii) Khadi and Village Industries: Khadi and Village Industries have been earmarked a 
sum of Rs. 525.64 crores in the current year Budget Estimates compared to 352 crores in the 
last years revised estimates. The Khadi and Village Industries cover a vast majority of our 
population in different areas of the country and primarily cater to the needs of our 
economically weaker sections. The Khadi and Village Industries generate vast potential for 
local employment and if given correct direction and infrastructural support, Kha.di and 
Village Industries can be more helpful in our rural economy. The Committee, however, 
finds that inspite of budgetary support, Khadi and Village Industries have not been able to 
compete in the open market and stand on their legs. The reasons , therefore, have to be 
studied and perceptive planning is to be made to make a beginning so that Khadi and 
Village Industries become self-sufficient in their functioning in all respects. The Commit tee 
finds that no thought is given in the Demands for Grants and there is no expenditure on this 
account. The Committee therefore , recommends that the priorities of expenditure may be 

re-fixed and monetary allocation be made. The Committee further recommends that every 
effort should be made to ensure that Khadi and Village Industri es do not suffer from 
shortage of financial resources, lack of infrastructural support and bureaucratic red-tapi sm. It 
is essent ial that the problem of marketing of the finished goods is taken on top priority. The 
Government should issue instructions at least to their Departments that Khadi/Village/Small 
Scale Industries Products are purchased for their requirements on the pattern of encourage­
ment given for Handloom cloth. The other point the Committee emphasises that it should be 
made obligatory on the part of the establishments of such industrie s to pay minimum living 
wages to the employees. The Committee further recommends that concrete steps are to be 
taken to ensure for the general health and welfare of the workers. Co-operatives in the field 
are to be activised and finished goods are marketed for adequate return. The Committee is 
aware of the fact that rural masses are not gainfully employed throughout the year. Some 
programmes for motivating the rural masses to utilise their spare time in engaging 
themselves in such industries are to be devised. The Committee finds that though a sum of 
Rs. 525.54 crores has been earmarked in the Budget Estimates for this item yet no money 
has been allotted for motivating people and for awareness programm es on the role and the 
utility of Khadi and Village Industries to rural masses. The programme for training 
undertaken by the Department also lacks perception. The Committee opines that prog­
ramme for training should be so designed and chalked out so as to give on the spot training 
and guidance by mobile training personnel in the first instance to familiarise the rural masses 
about various projects/schemes under Khadi and Village Industrie s. The initial phase may 
inrer-alia include ground level information about project, equipment, finance and marketing 
facilities for finished products. Once this phase of training is completed and the masses are 
motivated and assured of additional revenue to the person or to the family then additional 
training programmes as envisaged by the Department in the Budget Estimates would yield 
positive results. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the thrust of the training 
programme should be reoriented and grouped into two phases as mentioned above. 
The Committee trusts that its observations and recommendations will receive serious 
considerat ion for implementation.

TENTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I the Chairman. Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry having been authorised 
by the Committee to present the report on its behalf present this TENTH REPORT of the Committee on the 
Demands for Grants for 1994-95 of the Ministry of Mines. 
2. The Committee at its meeting held on the 23rd March, 1994 considered relevant documents and papers 
received from the Ministry of Mines on the Demands for Grants for the year 1994-95 and held a general discussion 
thereon. 
3. The Committee also heard the oral evidence of the Secretary of the Ministry of Mines alon~~th the heads 
of the various PSUs falling under the jurisdiction of the Ministry on the Perforn1ance Budget in the Context of 
Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Mines. 
4. The Committee considered the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in two sittings and considered and 
adopted the Report at its sitting held on the 12th April, 1994. 
5. The Demand s for Grants of the Ministry for the year 1994-95 as presented arc as under:-

6. Taken into account the documents and other material made available to it and oral evidence tendered before 
it the Committee concludes as under :-
6.01 The Performance Budget of the Ministry of Mines for the year 1994-95 states that the Ministry is 
primarily responsible for the regulation and development of the mineral sector including the mining and 
metallurgy of all non ferrous metals both in private and public sectors but excluding Natural Gas , Petroleum 
coal and Atomic minerals. Mmeral resources are national assets. Conservation and planned exploitation of 
minerals are therefore, of prime importance to the national economy. Besides providing the basic inputs to 
domestic industry the mineral sector accounts for sizeable exports and foreign exchange earni ngs. Having 
regard to the extent and variety of mineral resources in the country there is great potential for rapid growth 
of this sector. It is the onus of the. Ministry of the Mines to develop this sector with utmost care and caution 
to enable this sector to compete with the contemporary globalisation in the internatio nal area. But the 
Committee finds that the entire mines and minerals sector is in doldrums. Large number of mines have either 
closed or at the brink of closure. The situation is very alarming particularl y in the States of Bihar , Andhra 
Pradesh , Rajasthan, Goa, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh etc. where a good number of Mines have closed dov·m. 
There is no provision in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the revival of closed Mines in the 
country. The Committee has not been told of any kind of package prepared by the Ministry for the reopening 
of closed mines in the country and make them viable. Rather the Committee has been told that the minerals 
belong to the State Governments. The onus of re-opening of closed mines is therefore the responsibility of 
the States and Ministry has washed its hands off by pointing out the responsibihty on the States ignoring 
the loss being caused to the nation due to the closure of mines throughout the country. The States faced with 
acute resource constraints and are unable to divert their attention towards the closed· mines. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government must also pay attention towards the closed/ 
closing mines throughout the country and prepare a comprehensive package for their revival in 
consultation with the State Governments concerned. There must be a perfect co-ordi nation between 

2 
the Governme nt and the Gove rnm ent of the States in thi s •·egard . The Governm ent should constitut e 
a tea m of experts to find out the causes of closure of mines and suggest the ways for their revival within 
a t ime frame. 
6.02 The Committee finds that there is lack of coordination between the Government and the Government 
of the States as far as regulating of mining is concerned. Responding to a query about the foreign investment 
in the mineral sector after the enactment of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) 
Amendment Act, 1994 the Secretary of Ministry of Mines states that the minerals belong to the State 
Governmen ts. All applicat ions have to be submitted by entrepreneurs to the concerned State Governments 
and it is they who have to give the prospecting licence or the mining lease as the case may be. The 
Government did not have precise information whether any State Government had received any formal 
proposa l and whether any foreign party has applied for any prospecting licence. The Committee finds it not 
convincing. After opening the mineral sector of the country for foreign investment and participation in order 
to accelerating i nflow of domestic and foreign capita l into the mineral sector the Governme nt has left the 
matter entirely to the State Governments. On such a vital issue there should have been a perfect 
understanding and coordination between the Central and State Governments. The Committ ee, ther efor e, 
recommends· that Governm ent must keep a watch on every foreign investment propo sal in the miner al 
sector and advi se the c once rn ed State Government to make best u se of such a propo sal with out 
compr omising nationa l interest and prioritie s and maintain the closest coordin ation with the State 
Govern ment in thi s regar d. If there are stron g sentiment s expr essed by the State Gove rnmen t, as far 
as possib le such sentiments should be respecte d. It is import ant th at compensation money reac hes the 
peo ple allocated to Geological Survey of India (GSI) in Major Head 2853. GS I plays a dominant role for 
the gro\\th of the Mineral sector of the country. According to the Perforn1ance Budget (1994- 95) of the 
Ministry GSI is responsible for collection. collation and dissemination of geological data and providing 
basic geologic~ I information essential for the successful implementation of practically are the developmen­
tal programmes of the count!). The investigation carried out by GSI contribute directly to the discovery and 
evaluation of mineral resources ensuring thereby the continued and steady supply of vital ra\\ materials to 
the core industrial sector . The results of investigation aid in the better understanding of the cmstal 
framework and the geological process with bearing on development in other as vital sectors such as 
agriculture, land use management, irrigation and power development. utilisation of water resources. 
development of transport and communication, educat ion and scientific management of environment. Thus 
survey and mapping and mineral exploration are the most important functions ofGSI for Mineral sector 
and geological process having bearing on other important sectors oft he country but the committee finds that 
out of the total allocation ofRs. 125.74% crores in BE 1994-95 only a sum ofRs. 11.20 crorcs has been 
earmarked for survey and mapping and Rs. 12.90 for mineral exploration. Thus a total sum ofRs. 25.10 
crores will be spent on the vital functions of Survey and mapping and Mineral exploration whereas more 
than Rs. I 00 crores will be spent on other purposes mainly administration etc. The committee, therefore, 
recommends that additional funds be allocated for such primary functio ns as survey and mapping and 
Mineral exploration of the GSI. Such Su rveys and exp lorat ion should conform to a precise ly ind icated 
time frame so that a check would be possib le on tangible res ults achieved. The Committee appreciates 
the gesture of the Government in increasing the resource Budgetary allocation to GSI as per its 
recommendations made in its Thjrd Report on the Demands for Grants of the Ministl) ' of Mines ( 1993-94 ). 
However, the Committee recommends that instead of allocating a substa ntial amou nt for other 
purposes to GSI more thr ust should be given for its basic work. T hough the GSI is achieving its 
ta r gets, additiona l resources will certain ly bring an improveme nt in basic work and the nat ion will 
be benefitted.

INTRODUCTION
I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee  on Industry,  having   been  
authorised  by the  Committee, hereby present this 100 th Report of  Sub-Committee-I for  Ministry of Steel and Mines (
of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry)  on  Performance Review  of  National Mineral
Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) which is under the administrative control of  Ministry of Steel .
2.The Committee on Industry constituted Sub-Committee-I for Ministry of Steel and Mines .  The Sub-Committee took
up the issue of Performance Review of National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC)). The Sub-
Committee visited Hyderabad  from 28th and 29th June , 2002 and interacted with the  management of National Mineral
Development Corporation Limited (NMDC). 
3.            The Report has been prepared on  the basis of   on the spot  study and  interaction with the    Secretary ,
Ministry of Steel and officials  of National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC).

REPORT
 
National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) , a Government of India Enterprise and  a “Mini
Ratna Category-I” Company was established  in the year 1958, in pursuance of Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 to
promote and undertake development of minerals (other than coal, oil and atomic minerals) in Public Sector. NMDC is
the largest producer and exporter of iron ore in this Country. Its exports are around 7 million tonnes of iron ore per
annum (through Minerals & Metals Trading Corporation Ltd - canalising agency). It has also exported about 1.7 MT of

iron ore directly to China in 2001-02. NMDC has earned approximately Rs.750 Crores during the year 2001-02 by way
of foreign exchange. NMDC has been consistently achieving the rating of “ Excellent” from the very first year of
signing the MoU viz 1991-92.  It was placed in the fourth rank amongst the MOU signing PSEs for the year 1991-92,
from which it moved to third rank in the year 1992-93.  For the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96, for NMDC’s
performance of excellence and the achievement of composite score of 1.00 in each of these years under the MOU
performance evaluation, NMDC has been placed as the ‘ Joint Top Rank PSE’ in the country. This unique achievement,
as the Joint Top Rank,   has been achieved continuously for three years in succession.  Again, in 1996-97, 1997-98,
1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 NMDC was adjudged “Excellent”, barring 1998-99 during which period there
was general recession.

profit of Rs.160.00 crore for 1999-2000 and upto Rs.234.00 crore for the year (2000-01)  and  in the current year   the
company might improve over the figure  of last year. 
 
1.3       In the same meeting CMD  of NMDC   Shri  P.R. Tripathi  added :-
 
“The Corporation was set up in 1958  with the sole objective of development of minerals resources of the country other
than coal, oil, natural gas and atomic minerals  and  chemicals.  Now, the NMDC’s activities are concentrated on mining
of  Iron Ore, limestone and diamonds.  Due to a very good team spirit, we have an excellent system of management in
the company.  We have been consistently making profits since 1990.   NMDC had been  paying a dividend of 20 per
cent, then it has been increased to 25 per cent on the capital of Rs,132 cores.  We have returned the whole amount that 
has been given to us by the Government.  The profit of the company is the highest in the Steel Ministry.  Last year we
had Rs.314 crores.  This year our profit is very good and in spite of very poor and difficult situation in the steel industry,
we have a very good turnover.  This is mainly because we are very well diversified.  45 per cent of our  products are 
very well  diversified.  45 per cent of our products are being exported and 55 per cent is being consumed by the
domestic market.   ISPAT, ESSAR, VIKRAM are  depending on our product.  VSP is our major customer.  We
maintain very cordial relations with all so  that we can flourish in our business.”
 
1.4       The Committee notes that NMDC had been setting new records of performance in the areas of production,
despatches of iron ore, production and sales of diamonds,  increased supplies to domestic consumers.  Thus, NMDC has
been consistently scaling new heights of achievements from year to year both in physical and financial terms including
foreign exchange earnings to the country.

              The Sub-Committee was informed that NMDC has the following Mission :-
 
“To emerge as global mining organization with international standards of excellence, rendering optimum
satisfaction to all its stake holders.”

satisfaction to all its state  holders. The Committee appreciates the vision and professionalism embodied in NMDC’s
Mission. The Committee  extends  its best wishes of NMDC for realization of mission.

3.3       In order to translate the Mission of the company into actual performance NMDC  has chalked out elaborate
macro and micro objectives. It is but natural that to be global player one has to outperform the others and for doing so
laying of clear-cut objective is the first and foremost requirement. So has done the NMDC.  NMDC has set the
objectives of increasing its turnover (to the tune of Rs.2000.00 crore by the year 2005), productivity, cost effectiveness
in the areas of Mining. NMDC has set the objectives  of obtaining growth by expanding the existing mines in self-
enterprise or joint venture, exploration of high value minerals and production of value added items, extending
consultancy services and impetus to HRD and adherence to safety norms. While noting  the macro and micro objectives
of NMDC, the Committee hopes that NMDC would have a resilient strategy and feasible plan and course of action to
achieve the set objectives.
 
4.0       MANAGEMENT BY OBJECTIVES (MBO)
 
4.1       Pertaining the sub-committee’s query as  to what extent NMDC management is guided by the principle of
Management by Objectives (MBO) and to what extent the efforts undertaken by the management helped in realizing the
Mission of the company, NMDC management stated that          NMDC is not functioning or guided by terminology of
Management By Objectives but follows a strategy for achieving it’s mission and objectives.  Since mission and
objectives are clear to most of the employees, all efforts are guided to achieve the mission through set objectives.  This
approach is definitely helping the Corporation which can be seen by constant increase of turn over. NMDC had a turn
over of Rs.281.98 crore in 1991-92 which has gone up to Rs.1272.39 crore in 2001-02. This was possible only due to
increase in iron ore production and its sale and also in the production and sale of diamonds.
 
4.2       The Committee is pleased to note that NMDC  follows a strategy for achieving its mission and objectives. By
application of the principle of Management by objective (MBO) the Committee meant  as to what extent the efforts of
management and  workers are  guided to achieve the mission through set objectives. However, the Committee expresses
its satisfaction that NMDC, for all its practical purposes, is guided by ‘management by objective’  (MBO) and not
`management by activities. (MBA).

7.0       FUTURE GROWTH PLANS
 
7.1       Furnishing the details of future business plan of the Corporation, the NMDC management state that in keeping
with the opening of economy, domestic mineral environment and the International scenario, NMDC is planning its
growth by selecting some of the high value minerals and metals, where NMDC by its expertise could play a leading role
in development of open cast mines and processing. NMDC today is producing around 15 million and selling around
18.0 million tonnes of Iron Ore, which is around 22% of the Indian Iron Ore Production.  Because of good quality of the
product, NMDC brand of Bailadila as well as Donimalai has a name in the export market and is also able to satisfy the
special requirement of domestic sponge iron market, specially in the gas based processes. Looking into the future
expansion of steel industry and India being geographically  located close to the steel markets in China, Thailand,
Malaysia, Indonesia and also the new emerging markets in western Asia of Dubai, Bahrain,  India has a very good
chance for establishing its presence because of good quality of Bailadila ore, which could substitute the pellets.  Thus,
NMDC stands a good chance of being leading Export-house in these special markets.  Taking the above into
consideration, NMDC has planned to increase its production capability from the existing 15 million tonnes to 30.7
million tonnes by 2009-10.   This increase is to be achieved by opening of the following Mines:

8.0       STATUS OF EQUIPMENTS AND TECHNOLOGY EMPLOYED IN NMDC
 
8.1       Iron ore Mining: NMDC Management is always in search of latest Mining technology and equipment.
Accordingly, higher capacity drills, shovels and dumpers have been deployed in various existing Mines. In new Mines
120 ton capacity Dumpers against 50 T Dumpers and 8 meter cube Shovels against 4.6 meter cube Shovels and single
pass Drills against multi pass Drills are being planned. Latest information technology is being adopted in OCSL Plant
like; PLC, CCTV etc. The modern technology will enhance the productivity of Mines and also will result in reduction in
cost.
 
8.2       Diamond Mining: Mechanised Diamond Mine at Majghawan had a capacity of 24,480 carats per year by
adopting jigging technology. By adopting latest heavy media separation and X-ray sorting machinery, capacity of the
Mine has been enhanced to 84000 carats per year.  During the year 2001-02 the Mine could achieve 81,100 carats of
production. This has resulted in reduction in cost of production.
 
8.3       NMDC has identified the ROMELT technology of Russia which can  make use of low grade iron ore slimes to
convert  into pig iron. The technology has not so far been commercially used and NMDC would be the first Company in
the world to use ROMELT technology on a commercial basis in Bailadila Sector at an estimated cost of Rs.300 crores
including Rs.20 crores as loan from Technical Development Board, Govt. of India.  The ROMELT SAIL India Ltd
(RSIL) will co-ordinate for transfer of technology from Russia.  Required land has been handed over by the
Government.  All the statutory clearances are obtained  and  construction has started.
 
8.4       The Committee hopes that NMDC management would make continuous efforts  to up grade the technology and
equipment capacity so as to increase the production which can result in better financial results.

10.0     COST COMPONENTS OF PRODUCTS PRODUCEDBY NMDC .
 
10.1     The main components of the cost of production are  Fixed Cost and  Variable Cost.
The fixed cost consists of salaries and wages, depreciation and office/ selling expenses. The fixed cost is being reduced
by introduction of multi-skilling concepts and by adoption of CCTV at OCSL Plants. The variable cost consists of
explosives, drill bits, tyre & tubes, spares and consumables. It also consists cost incurred towards royalty and
electricity. 
 
10.2     The cost of production at pit head is comparable with the International Mining Operations. NMDC has to incur
additional Railway freight and Port handling charges  before product reaches the consumer. The port charges and
Railway freight charges are not under the control of NMDC. It may be worth mentioning that the cost incurred in
Railway freight and port charges amounts to 60% of the cost and balance 40% cost is in the control of NMDC. This
situation creates difficulty for NMDC to compete in the  international market for iron ore. Unless efforts are made to
reduce the railway freight and port charges, it will be difficult for NMDC to sustain the progress of the Corporation. 
 
10.3     Continuous efforts are being made towards cost reduction through the various managerial controls such as
 
a.
       Bench Marking
b.      Incentive for maintaining electricity and diesel consumption targets adopted through the Memorandum of
Understanding reached between management and union.
c.       Standard Costing
d.      Continuous review of consumables and improvement in the same
 
10.4     The Committee is pleased to note that NMDC management has introduced the multi-skilling concept to reduced
the fixed cost .    The Committee also notes that various managerial controls measures are at work to reduce the cost of
production .  The Committee  desires that the Ministry of  Steel, in its Action Taken Note of the present Report, would
furnish  the detail as to what extent the cost reduction measure entailed tangible   result.

12.0     MOU RATING OF NMDC 
 
12.1     NMDC is one of the Public Sector Enterprises which has been signing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)
with the Government of India since 1991. At the beginning of each financial year, an agreement is reached to achieve
certain parameters such as production, sales, gross margin, ratio of net profit to capital employed, energy conservation,
R & D efforts, human resource development, project implementation etc. based on the past performance into account,
the growth need and the potential to achieve such levels of performance.  These achievements at the year end are
evaluated for the said parameters and the company gets ranked based on the evaluation score. NMDC has been
consistently achieving the rating of “ EXCELLENT” from the very first year of signing the MoU viz 1991-92.  It was
placed in the fourth rank amongst the MOU signing PSEs for the year 1991-92, from which it moved to third rank in the
year 1992-93.  For the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96, for NMDC’s performance of excellence and the
achievement of composite score of 1.00 in each of these years under the MOU performance evaluation, NMDC has
been placed as the ‘ Joint Top Rank PSE’ in the country. This has been a unique achievement as the Joint Top Rank  
has been achieved continuously for three years in succession.  Again, in 1996-97, 1997-98, 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and
2001-2002 NMDC was adjudged “EXCELLENT”, barring 1998-99 during which period there was general recession. 
NMDC had been setting new records of performance in the areas of production, despatches of iron ore, production and
sales of diamonds, profits, increased supplies to domestic consumers.  Thus, NMDC has been consistently scaling new
heights of achievements from year to year both in physical and financial terms including foreign exchange earnings to
the country.   For the year 2001-2002, the company has surpassed the MOU target of dispatches of 180 lakh tonnes of
iron ore by achieving 182.04 lakh tonnes. The company has achieved an ever highest profit before tax of Rs.320.15
crores during 2001-2002.
 
12.2     NMDC has achieved the "Excellent" rating during the last five years except in the year 1998-99 which was
"Very Good"due to recession in the international steel industry. DPE has awarded NMDC an award for Excellence in
the achievement of MOU Targets for the year 2000-01 and a certificate of Excellence in the achievement of MOU
Targets  for the year 1999-2000. The system of MOU has helped NMDC which is evident from the fact that for the last

objectives.  While ONGC is engaged mainly in exploration of oil and gas, MECL and GSI are engaged  in exploration
of minerals.  IBM is also engaged in exploration of minerals  and also a statutory body for conservation of minerals.  
NMDC is engaged in in- house exploration and exploitation of minerals.  A council of such mineral enterprises can only
be considered (which may include other minerals like coal, Copper, Zinc etc.) if they are engaged in exploration and
exploitation of various minerals  like other multi-nationals. However, except ONGC  and GAIL these organizations are
the members of Federation of Indian Mineral Industries (FIMI) for interactions connected with development of mineral

19.0     LEGAL FRAMEWORK  FOR GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT OF MINING         OPERATION.
 
19.1     To what extent the existing legal framework is conducive to the growth and development of mining operation.
Any suggestion on the part of NMDC management for legal reform in this regard is as follow:-
 
“Mineral industry is governed by certain statutory act and rules such  as  Mines and Mineral Development and
Regulation Act, Mineral Conservation and Development Rules,  Mineral Concession Rule, , Mines Act etc.  With the 
economic liberalization, a new National  Mineral Policy  was announced in 1993 in which 13  major minerals were
dereserved and also foreign investment in the mineral industry was encouraged.  With the existing change in the legal
frame work, State Governments have been empowered to grant and renew mining lease as  minerals are considered to
be property of  the  concerned States.  However, it is observed that State Govts. are imposing their own conditions in
granting of mining lease and this is causing hindrance in the systematic development of mineral industry.  State
Governments should be advised to  form uniform policy and grant mining/prospecting lease on first come first basis,
rather than tendering, asking  for  additional royalty etc.
 
19.2     Ministry of Mines in consultation with GSI & IBM identify mineral zones, which should be developed to meet
the country’s need and such mineral zones, which should be developed to meet the country’s need and such mineral
zones should be taken out from the purview of Forest Conservation Act. “
 
19.3     The Committee is anguished  to  note the  submission of NMDC management  that  State Govts. are imposing
their own conditions in granting of mining lease and this is causing hindrance in the systematic development of mineral
industry and asking  for sweet equity, additional royalty etc.
 
 
 
19.4     The Committee is of the view that  procedural hurdles and bureaucratic rest-redtapism  should not  come onto
the way of systematic development of mineral industry.
 
19.5     The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Steel should   approach the Department of Mines for
organizing  across the  table interaction of representatives of   mineral enterprises and  officials of state  Government  to
form uniform mineral policy as per the canons of National Mineral Policy 1993 and  sort out problems relating  to
granting of  mining/prospecting lease etc.    The Committee  feels that the Department of Mines should  issue direction 
to GSI and IBM for identification of `Exclusive Mineral Zones’ for systematic exploration and exploitation of  Mineral
resources.  Having been give due weightage  to environmental aspects, `exclusive Mineral zones may be taken out from
the  purview of forest   conservation Act.

21.0     'Pricing policy' of NMDC
 
21.1     NMDC is supplying iron ore in the domestic market as well as for export purposes.  The iron ore, which is
surplus to the domestic demand, is exported to countries like Japan, China and South Korea.  The main export of
NMDC’s ore is through MMTC as per the existing EXIM policy.  However, NMDC is also exporting small quantities of
iron ore directly based on the specific export license issued by the Ministry of Commerce / DGFT.
 
21.2     Export Prices ; The prices for export of iron ore are basically determined by the global demand and supply
position on year-to-year basis. The percentage increase/decrease in prices over the previous year is usually finalized
between the major exporters of iron ore like Australia and Brazil and major importers like Japan and European
countries.  The same percentage increase/decrease in prices is made applicable to the exports from India.  Consequently
the prices of NMDC iron ore is also decided on the same basis. 
           
21.3     Domestic Prices: The despatches to domestic market accounts for about 53% of the total dispatches of NMDC’s
iron ore.  The dispatches to domestic market are regulated in terms of long-term agreement signed by various domestic
customers.  The duration of the agreement is for a maximum period of 5 years.  Iron ore market has remained basically a
buyers market due to frequent and prolonged recessionary trends in the steel industry.  Therefore the fixed escalation in
prices is not the acceptable norm in the industry.  In terms of the long-term agreement the prices of iron ore are to be
settled each year by mutual discussions.  The mutual discussions to finalise the prices instills a sense of confidence
among the buyers that NMDC is sensitive to the customer’s needs.
 
21.4     The Board of Directors of NMDC delegated the powers for deciding the pricing through an internal committee
consisting of CMD, Director (Prdn), Director (Fin) and ED (Comml.) and authorizing CMD to take up action as deemed
necessary in this regard.
21.,5    In terms of the above decision of the Board, negotiations are held by NMDC with the parties concerned in the
beginning of the each financial year.  The negotiation are primarily based upon the “what the market can bear” criteria,
and the ground realities of steel sector.  The negotiation also to some extent take into consideration the global
demand/supply position and trends of iron ore prices in the international market. 
 
21.6     The prices so negotiated and finalized with the parties are put up for the information of the Board and adopted
for supplies during the relevant year.
