 21.11.0           NEED OF   AUTONOMY FOR  NMDC IN EXPORT PROMOTION I.E.                               
DIRECT EXPORT BY NMDC
 
 
 21.11.1 The export of iron ore produced by NMDC is canalized through MMTC Ltd. in terms of the existing EXIM
policy.  The iron ore which is surplus to the demand of domestic industry is offered for export.  The major chunk of
export is canalised through MMTC and balance uncommitted quantity is permitted for exports directly by NMDC
through special export license.  The inherent drawback of the system are as follows:
 
                        (i)      The licenses issued to NMDC for exports by DGFT do not permit export to major importers of Iron Ore
like Japan and South Korea which together accounts for about 40 - 45% of sea-borne trade.
 
                      (ii)      The licenses are for limited quantity with a validity period of two/three years.  Therefore it is not possible
for NMDC to enter into an agreement/MOU on long-term basis with foreign buyers.
 
                     (iii)      NMDC has to ensure the parity of foreign exchange realization on exports on product-to-product basis with
MMTC.  Thus NMDC is deprived the freedom to adjust the prices etc. depending upon the available
inventory levels vis-à-vis the demand pattern.
 
                    (iv)      The import license imposes the restriction on NMDC to export to Japan and South Korea but for other
countries both MMTC and NMDC will be trading the same product and the brand image of the NMDC
product will never be established.
 
                      (v)      Since NMDC gets permission for Direct Export on piece-meal basis, the foreign steel mills operators have
reservations to consider NMDC as a long-term reliable supplier of iron ore.
 
                    (vi)      Since the Export Licenses are for limited quantities, NMDC cannot offer the whole product mix comprising
of both lump ore and fine ore as required by end users.
 
21.11.2            Therefore in the best interest of exports, NMDC should have complete autonomy and be permitted to
export its iron ore without any restriction of quantity, quality or geographical location.  This will enable NMDC to
operate more like any commercial organization and take business decision, which are in its best interest
 
21.11.3            NMDC is meeting the domestic demand of iron ore to an extent of 55% and the remaining 45% only is
being sold out to international market.  As per the policy of the government iron ore is to be exported through canalising
agency i.e. MMTC. MMTC finds out market to iron ore with 65% Fe content and above, whereas NMDC has got more
quantity of iron ore lying at pit head with less than 65% Fe content for which international market is available, but not
explored by NMDC.   To take care of this product NMDC is requesting Commerce Ministry to allow NMDC to direct
export to the countries other than the purchasers from MMTC i.e. Japan, Pakistan and South Korea. NMDC has already
exported directly to its foreign buyers 1.27 lakh tonnes in 1999-00, 9.65 lakh tonnes in 2000-01and  17.12 lakh tonnes in

23.0     HUMAN RESOURCES MANAGEMENT
 
23.1     Keeping pace with the national policy on workers’ participation in industry, NMDC has made a remarkable
breakthrough in having various fora of joint consultation and workers’ participation since the 70s and it has become an

integral part of industrial relations structure in the Corporation.  The joint fora are playing a very important role in
achieving industrial peace and harmony as also in achieving production and productivity.  These fora have been winning
the confidence of both employer and workmen due to its impartiality, understanding and integrity.  The Joint Councils
set-up in a three-tier structure are:-
a.       Shop Councils (Covering each production /other areas in all Plants);
b.      Project Joint Council (Plant level, the Apex body at every plant/mine);
c.       Apex Joint Council (Corporate Level comprising representatives from all Units).
 
23.2     It would thus be seen that NMDC as a forerunner has constituted a Three-tier Participative Forum and the
arrangement has been successfully functioning for more than three decades.
           
23.3     In addition, NMDC has made an important breakthrough in persuading the different Unions working in its
production projects and other units to come under one umbrella  by formation of a Federation at All India level called
"All India NMDC Workers’ Federation (AINMDCWF)."  This has  been done in the year 1971 and this Federation has
helped in formation of a Bipartite Committee at the corporate level in which all the unions affiliated to the Federation
irrespective of their recognition by the labour machinery, affiliation to different  Central Trade Unions, participate as
one group.  This Bipartite Committee has been working very satisfactorily and all the wage settlements and other major
issues relating to job specifications, work atmosphere and other service matters are settled amicably during the
discussions in the Bipartite Committee .
 
23.4     NMDC does not have surplus manpower in any of the category as on date due to change in market scenerio i.e
globalisation.  NMDC has decided to concentrate only on its core activity  - exploration and exploitation of minerals. 
Non-core activities like school, transport, canteen, etc. are being off loaded.  While doing so the persons engaged are
being retrained for some other jobs, which are required for the core activities. This approach resulted in non-requirement
of VRS Scheme.
 
23.5     The Committee is happy is know that NMDC is operating with optimum manpower.  The deployment of 
manpower from non-core sector to  core sector i.e.   to exploration   and exploration of minerals  management, `right-
man  at right place in  right time’ leads to increased labour productivity, the Committee opines.
 
23.6     The Committee expresses its pleasure over NMDC’s efforts  of giving accordance  to the national policy of
workers   participation   in management.  NMDC’s three-tier –participation forum i.e. shop council, project joint-

precedent should  be followed by other PSUs and units in private sector , as industrial  peace and workers management

25.1  Inflated mileage on Kirandul-Kottavalasa line.
 
25.1.1.Railways have been charging freight on Kirandul-Kottavalasa line (SE Railway) by inflating the distance by 30%
NMDC has been representing for the removal of the same in view of the increased traffic handled on the line. The
inflation in distance on K-K line had been continuing since 1967. Initially it was 65.2% but with the traffic volume
increasing, this was reduced to 30% in 1981. This percentage of inflation has been continuing since then. In the last
eighteen years there has been significant increase in the traffic handled on K-K line originating iron ore movement has
gone up from 56.36 lakh tonnes in 1987-88 to 145 lakh tonnes in 2000-01. In addition, the line has been handling other
traffic particularly on account of the NALCO's alumina plant near Koraput. In addition to the budgetary increase in the
freight charges over the years since 1981, Railways had been revising the classification of iron ore upwards resulting in
further increasing in the freight charges. The classification of iron ore which was 110 in 1989-90 had increased to 120 in
1994-95 and 125 in 1999-2000. For the year 2001-02, the Railway freight in respect of iron ore has been further
increased by 3% over that of the previous year with the classification remaining unchanged at 120.
 
25.1.2  The reduction in inflated mileage would help both NMDC and other domestic customers like VSP, Essar Steel,
Ispat Industries Ltd and Vikram Ispat to improve their economy in the operations.
 
25.1.3  The Sub-Committee was informed  that the Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. is linked to  Balladilla Mines of NMDC
for sourcing its iron  ore  requirements.  The  Kothavalasa-Kirandul section (  KK Line) under  Waltair Division of S.E.
Railway measures a distance of 475 kms.  Out of this distance, 118 k.m. is  on the Eastern Ghat Section and the balance
distance is in the plains  or  plateau.  This was constructed at a  cost of Rs159 Crore. and  was  opened for traffic in 
November, 1968.  In the initial stages,  Railways levied freight charges by  inflating the distance by 65.2 percent  with
stipulation  that the freight should be levied  on discontinuous  mileage basis (i.e.)  out of  475 k.m., only 35 km (i.e.)
from Kothavalala to VSP  will be charged normal freight.  Upon a further review in  1981, the percentage of  inflation
on the total distance was reduced to 30 percent  with effect from 1.6.1981. VSP is opereating from 1989 and since then
the inflated freight charge is being levied.  VSP has  transported 463.91 lakh tonnes upto March, 2002 and paid a freight
of Rs.1634.34 crore .Had VSP paid normal freight  (i.e.)  Rs.1284 crore  paid upto 2001-02 , VSP would have saved

25.1.4  Railways claim that they use additional locos to the extent of two or  three to move iron ore as well as high
maintenance cost  due to steep gradients  which accounts only for about  1/4th  of the total distance i.e., 118 kms.   But 
the traffic of 6 MT was reached in 1988-89 and it has already  reached 14.5 MT in the year 2000-01  which is almost
two and half times more than what was originally envisaged to have a break-even.
 
25.1.5  Initially the KK line was being used for export of iron ore from, Bailadilla sector only.  However, with domestic
iron and steel   producers  like RINL, Essar  Steel & Ispat Industries started using  the same line and the  haulage of iron
ore on KK line increased rapidly.  It is expected that by  end of the  year 2002, it would be 16.3 million tonnes. 
 
25.1.6  During the last 10 years, VSP has been requesting in various coordination meetings held by Ministry of Steel or
by Ministry of Railways for the withdrawal of  these inflated freight charges.  Since 1995-96, withdrawal of this extra
freight  charge formed a part of the chapter on " assistance from the Government" in MOUs  signed with RINL.
 
25.1.7  In the meeting of  the Sub-Committee  held on 12
th September, 2001 on the subject of "Key Concern Areas of
Steel Industries and promotion of steel consumption in various sectors of economy ", the issue of inflated freight charge 
was  discussed in detailed.  Participating in discussion  Shri R.N. Malhotra, Chairman, Railway Board  expressed his
views :-
 
" On the questions of concessions, I would like to say that we are prepared to consider any request from any
manufacturer for certain concessions which will help them and which in turn would help the Railways.  But Sir, by
reducing our revenue, we cannot help anyone.  If they are prepared to give us  an undertaking that  if we  reduce the
freight on the KK Line by a certain percentage, they will be able to give us so much  of extra  traffic, we can consider
it."
 
25.1.8  Interjecting in the discussion, the Secretary, Ministry of Steel expressed   his opinion in following words:-
 
" The question that has been raised with regard to the KK Line related to movement of iron ore from Bailadilla,
which is used by the Vizag Steel Plant.  It has a very long history.    It is not really a question of incremental traffic.  The
operative issue here is that 65 per cent additional freight charge was put at a certain  point  of time because that line was
specifically created for the movement of iron ore from point A to point  B,  with an understanding that if the level of
freight crossed six million tonnes, this additionality would   be removed.  The  situation today is that, as against the 65
per cent  enhanced rate that was being charged, the  current enhanced rate is 30 per cent, and the traffic  generated on
that line, today,  12 tonnes. We can not have a persistent kind of an incremental situation going on.  We understand that
at a point of time, the line was constructed for captive use, and additional charges were levied in order to make it viable
for the Railways.  Once a certain threshold of traffic generation has been achieved, the incremental rate should not
apply.  That was the original understanding.  One cannot have a situation wherein because  there is an incremental rate,
in order to reduce it, you must have incremental traffic.  The fact  that rate was brought down from 65 per cent  to 35 per
cent and now to 30 per cent is, itself, a recognition of the  understanding on which this 65 per cent  was  charged.  Now,
as per that understanding, that additionally factor should now go.  This  is the issue that has to be examined.
 
25.1.9  Responding to the arguments of Secretary, the Chairman, Railway Board, added :-
 
            " The Additionally which was charged earlier was for several reasons.  The first reason was that because it was a
hilly area, with sharp edges and curves, the construction cost of rails was very high.  The second reason was that we had
put surcharge on  movement of any traffic on that line because of the fact that in place of one locomotive, which is
normally required on a  plain terrain, we had to put three locomotive in place .  So, the cost of operation also was very
high.   Also, the  electricity  bill for the  operational  of  this line is five times higher than what it would cost in the case
of   a line on the plain.  Now, how do we recover that cost ?  We cannot go on reducing our revenue, unless there is a
commitment on the part of the steel plants that they will be able to sell so much of extra steel and thus give us that much
of extra traffic.".

Scrap Trade Corporation  Limited (MSTC) and the same principle has  not been  applied in the case of NMDC.  As per
the existing system, Iron-Ore is to be exported through canalizing agency  i.e.  MMTC.  MMTC finds out market to Iron
ore with 65%  fe content and above whereas NMDC has got  more quantity of Iron Ore lying in  its pit head with less
than fifty-five percent Iron content for which international market  is available but the same is not explored by NMDC. 
Therefore, the Committee feels that, It would  be in the fitness of things that NMDC is given complete  autonomy in the
best – interest of the Company.  The Committee feels NMDC be allowed to direct export to the countries other than the
purchaser from MMTC  i.e. Japan, Pak and South Korea, NMDC has already exported directly to its foreign buyers 
1.27 lakh tones in 1999-2000, 9.65 lakh tones in 2000-01, and  thus experience  so gained, would proved handy to
NMDC in direct export of Iron-ore.
 
( Para : 21.11.4)
 
RECENT RECOVERY IN STEEL INDUSTRY AND FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE OF NMDC
 
The Committee understand that, since the Iron Ore is   an important and major  raw material for production of 
steel, it is  but natural , the existence  of inter-dependence  of steel production  and the quality of Iron –Ore  traded .  The
Committee is pleased to note that NMDC’s sales have a direct relation to production of  steel in the country. That is so,
because  Steel Scenario is gaining  momentum  and is recovering fast, which,  the Committee feels , would lead to
increase in NMDC’s sales.
( Para : 22.4)
 
HUMAN RESOURCES MANAGEMENT
 
The Committee is happy is know that NMDC is operating with optimum manpower.  The deployment of 
manpower from non-core sector to  core sector i.e.   to exploration   and exploration of minerals  management, `right-
man  at right place in  right time’ leads to increased labour productivity, the Committee opines.
( Para : 23.5)
 
            The Committee expresses its pleasure over NMDC’s  efferts  of giving accordance  to the national policy of
workers   participation   in management.  NMDC’s three-tier –participation forum i.e. shop  council, project joint-
council and Apex  joint council  is a  unique  `feature of worker’s  participation in decision making  process.  Such 
precedent  should  be followed by other PSUs and units in private sector , as industrial  peace and workers management
relation has a definite  bearing on the labour productivity.
 
( Para : 23.6)
 
SWOT (STRENGTH WEAKNESS OPPORTUNITIES AND THREATS) ANALYSIS OF NMDC.
 
The Committee  is of the opinion that SWOT analysis should act as an instrument  for boosting   the physical 
and financial performance further. NMDC management should keep on analysing and reviving its SWOT- chart as per

The Committee hopes that NMDC’s strength and make  efforts for taking  advantage of its strength i.e. excellent R&D

RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee noted that many of the Central PSEs are making losses due to their inability to face the competition, because of their obsolete
R&D, high cost of production, shortage of work orders, etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should
infuse capital, state of the art technology and entrepreneurship into potentially viable PSEs so as to make these ‘Modern Temples’ capable to face the
private sector MNCs in the consumer economy.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The strategies for strengthening and improving the potentially viable PSEs include:---
           1.    Revival of PSEs through BIFR.
           2.    Financial restructuring wherever appropriate.
           3.    Joint Venture formation to have continuous access to technology, finance and marketing.
           4.    Manpower rationalization.
        Out of 26 BIFR referred PSUs under the Department of Heavy Industry revival plans have been sanctioned by BIFR in case of 12 PSUs. These
involve cash infusion of Rs.654 crore by the Government besides financial restructuring of Rs.2106 crores. Apart from BIFR sanctioned revival
plans, Government has on its own, approved the financial restructuring in case of 7 other sick/loss making PSUs involving fresh infusion of funds to
the extent of Rs.531 crores and financial restructuring of Rs.1443 crores.
        In order to rationalize the manpower, Government have provided an amount of about Rs.1700 crores under Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)
for retiring about 70,000 employees of PSUs.
        Lagan Jute Machinery Co. Ltd. (LJMC), a subsidiary of Bharat Bhari Udyog Nigam Ltd. (BBUNL) and Belting division of Andrew Yule & Co.
Ltd. have already been converted into joint venture companies. Also in case of 30 PSUs of Department of Heavy Industry, the process of JV
formation/disinvestments has been initiated.
Para 2.6

assistance in the form of working capital, Non-plan loan, Government guarantee, etc. to PSEs which are potentially viable.

etc.) and VRS/VSS as non-plan loans. The funds released during the last three years are as follows:---

fully.

GUARANTEE FEE SUBSIDY
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is constrained to note that the Department of Heavy Industry has provided for the provision of guarantee fee subsidy to only four
PSEs in 2001-02 leaving most of the needy PSEs to face hardships in getting bank finance. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should provide guarantee fee subsidy to the needy PSEs for leveraging finance for sustaining their operations.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        It may be mentioned that Government has already given guarantees to number of PSEs under DHI for cash credit facilities from Banks/Financial
Institutions for meeting working capital requirements. The total sum guaranteed by the Government for various PSEs under DHI as on March 31,
2002 is Rs.1333.20 crore. The guarantee fee is only 1% of the guarantee given. The guarantee fee subsidy provided to Hindustan Cables Ltd., Burn
Standard Company Ltd. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd. And Heavy Engineering Corporation Ltd. Mentioned in the para was as per the approved
revival schemes of these PSEs. A new scheme was also introduced in 2000-01 for providing interest subsidy on bank finance to PSEs, for
implementation of VRS. As per this scheme, 50% of the interest due on funds raised through bonds for VRS is disbursed as interest subsidy to the
PSEs concerned, which is much higher than the guarantee fee subsidy. However, guarantee fee subsidy as approved by the Government in the revival
plans of the PSEs, will continue to be provided.
Para 6.6 ---- 6.7
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that under this new scheme introduced by DHI, more funds should be given to Richardson & Cruddas (R&C),
Tung Bhadra Steel Products Ltd. (TSPL), Triveni Structurals Ltd, Instrumentation Ltd, Burn Standard Company Ltd (BSCL) and Hindustan Cables
Ltd. (HCL). To so as to meet their demands to finance manpower rationalisation programme undertaken in these PSEs.
        The Committee further recommends that in case the amount earmarked is not sufficient for this purpose, the additional allocations may be
sought at RE stage.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        A Budget provision of Rs.10 crore was made in BE 2000-01 for interest subsidy on Bank Finance to PSEs for raising funds from
Banks/Financial Institutions for VRS in order to reduce the burden on the Companies. The initial response from the PSEs was not quite encouraging
as the scheme represented a marked departure from the prevailing practice of extending full budgetary support for VRS. Hence the provision was
reduced to Rs.1 crore at RE stage. Out of that provision of Rs.1 crore, only Rs.44.37 lakh could be utilized by one PSE viz., Richardson and Cruddas.
A budget provision per Rs. 20 crore was made in 2001-02 for this purpose. There was good response from the PSEs and a total amount of  Rs. 21.28

Para 20.1
ANDREW YULE & CO LTD. (AYCL)
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that the examination of the report of the Committee on AYCL group restructuring may be expedited so that
necessary group restructuring may take place at the earliest. The Committee in its earlier Report had recommended that the Government should find a
suitable joint-venture partner for the engineering and electrical division of the Company, keeping in view the success the Belting Division had
achieved. The Committee recommends that Department of Heavy Industry should continue its effort to locate a suitable joint venture partner for the
Company.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        Andrew Yule & Co. Ltd. (AYCL) appointed M/s. L.B. Jha & Company (LBJC) as Consultant for preparation of a detailed restructuring report in
respect of business activities for each of the operating divisions of the Company. After critical examinations of the alternative options such as, Joint
Venture, closure, subsidiarisation etc. the Consultant on its draft Report made a presentation to the Board of Directors at its meeting held on May 10,
2002. The final report on the subject is expected to be submitted by June 07, 2002.
        As decided by the Board of Directors as its meeting held on May 10, 2002, the Company is currently exploring the possibilities of Joint Venture
in respect of its Engineering Division. Depending upon the responses received on the above, and the final recommendation of LBJC, the Board of
Directors will decide on future course of action in respect of Engineering as well as Electrical Divisions of the Company.
        Government of India earlier in 1997 had approved spinning off the Engineering Division into Joint Venture. No eligible bids were received
through competitive bidding process. This was followed by the negotiated settlement route. However, the JV could not be materialized, as the
negotiation broke on the issue of number of manpower to be transferred to Joint Venture.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee notes the reply given by the Department of Heavy Industry. The Committee, however stresses that DHI should continue the
process of locating a suitable joint venture partner for Andrew Yule and Co. Ltd.

RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee has noted that the cess to improve R&D in Automotive Industry has been increased from Rs.10.00 crore to Rs.25.00 crores in
the budget estimates of 2002-03. However, the rate of cess has not been revised from 0.05% to 0.25% over and above the excise duty as earnestly

Ministry of Finance and resolve to save the automotive industry.

        This Department has been regularly holding dialogue with the Finance Ministry on the issue of enhancing the budget allocation of cess on
automobiles not only at the time of framing up of budget/revised estimates but has also been writing with regularity to Ministry of Finance on this
account. As a result of this constant and close persuasion, the Ministry of Finance has enhanced the cess fund allocation from Rs. 10 crores to Rs. 25

Para 4.7
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is constrained to note that the Indian Automotive Industry is spending only 0.2% of their sales turnover on R&D as against 3%
to 4% spent by most auto industries in the developed Countries. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should create a separate corpus
of funds to meet the emerging requirements of R&D of the auto industries.

sector. Since the incentives relate to tax rebate and tax break, which are the concerns of Ministry of Finance, the issue has been taken up with the
Ministry of Finance for giving the required incentives to the automotive industry. An Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) has also been set up to
coordinate implementation of the Auto Policy, steer resolution of Inter-Ministerial issues and to remove impediments which hinder desired growth of
the automobile industry in India. The Department has also simultaneously taken up the proposal made by the Committee with the Finance Ministry.

Para 9.8 – 9.10
PRICE PREFERENCE TO DOMESTIC INDUSTRY
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is concerned to note that the domestic manufacturers are not able to avail price preference of 15% for projects funded by
international agencies like World Bank, United Nations, Asian Development Bank etc. as imports on such projects is allowed at ‘nil’ duty as per
Notification No.85/99-customs dated July 6, 1999. The power projects for 10th and 11th Five Year Plans are being finalised. Some of these projects
may entail multilateral funding. Additional power projects of 60,000 MW during the 11 th plan period are likely to be finalised. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Customs Notification No. 85/99 – custom dated July 6, 1999 should be rescinded to enable domestic manufacturers to
effectively compete against foreign suppliers by taking advantage of 15% price preference provided in ICB tenders.
        The Committee views this issue very seriously since it has effected zero customs duty regime applicable to all goods imported to India for
execution of projects financed by the United Nations/World Bank or any other International Organisation. This amended custom duty structure has
adversely affected competitiveness of the domestic Capital Goods industries.
        The Committee, therefore, recommends that this anomaly needs to be rectified at the earliest possible. The Committee also recommends that if
need arises then the DHI should take up this issue with the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) to resolve the log jam. The Committee
further recommends that the unresolved matter may be placed before the Cabinet Committee to consider the matter de-novo.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        This matter has been discussed in the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee. They had constituted a separate Committee headed
by Revenue Secretary for making recommendations on this issue. They have since given their recommendations stating that World Bank guidelines
provide for giving preferential treatment to domestic bidders. Their recommendations were discussed in a meeting on 12.08.2002 by the Standing
Committee (Sub-Committee-III). Further action on these recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee for issue of clarifications is
being taken by the Department of Revenue.
Para 9.11
REFUND OF TERMINAL EXCISE DUTY TO DOMESTIC INDUSTRIES
RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee is concerned to note that the domestic manufacturers continue to suffer cost disadvantages such as sales tax, octroi, and high cost
of finance and infrastructure bottlenecks to the extent of 18-28% while competing with imports. At present custom duty on Coal Mining, Fertilizer
and Power projects is 5% basic custom duty+16% CVD and ‘nil’ SAD. Under this structure the domestic industry is unable to claim refund of excise
duty and become uncompetitive. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be no duty free import of projects and a minimum of 15%
basic custom duty + ‘nil’ CVD + 4% SAD be imposed to enable the domestic industry to become competitive without increasing the project cost.
ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
        The issue has already been taken up by DHI with Ministry of Finance vide D.O. letter No. 3(23)/99-PE.XI dated December 29,.2000. Hon’ble
Minister (HI & PE) vide D.O. letter dated December 23, 2000 has also taken up various issues including the above with Hon’ble Finance Minister
(copy enclosed) (Annexure-VII).

RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that while rationalizing the duty structure compatible with WTO guidelines, the Government should protect the
interests of the domestic paper industries.
        The Committee views the Government’s Policy of reducing customs duty from 35% to 30% as against the WTO bound rate of 40% as a major
threat for the domestic paper industries. The Committee conceives that the reduction in customs duty would definitely encourage import, which in

ad-valorem.

Subject : Issues relating to Capital Goods Industry
Dear Shri Yashwant Sinhaji,
        As you are aware the capital goods industry is witnessing an unprecedented demand recession, causing declining market prices and erosion in
domestic market share. Capital goods sector has witnessed a decline of 2.7% in April-Sept.2000 as compared to a growth of 5% in 1999-2000 and
11% in 1998-99.
2.     Some of the factors responsible for deceleration are slow down in investment, reduction in the custom duty on capital goods/project imports
from a high of 85% to 0-5%. Domestic manufacturers continue to suffer cost disadvantages such as sales tax, octroi, high cost of finance and

101st report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/101streport.htm[04-07-2016 12:23:55]
infrastructure bottlenecks to the extent of 18-28% while competing with imports.
3.     This situation is further aggravated by the issue of notification No.85/99 dated 6.7.99 which allows import of goods for the projects financed by
the United Nations, World Bank, Asian Development Bank and other International organizations at “Nil” duty. Due to this notification, domestic
manufacturers are not able to avail the price preference of 15% for projects funded by such agencies.
4.     You are aware that the capital goods sector has very strong backward and forward linkages. Therefore, it is necessary to provide support to give
the desired impetus to this industry for reversing the declining trend and sustain its growth. In this context, I have following suggestions for your
consideration -----
        l     Custom Duty on all capital goods should be brought to bound rate of WTO.
        l     In project imports, restructure this present duty structure by levying minimum basic custom duty of 15% + CVD equal to excise duty @ 8%
or lower and rescind notification No.85/99 dated 6.7.99.
        l     Restoration of Terminal Excise Duty (TED) to domestic suppliers to projects where the end product is not exciseable.
        With regards,
                                                                                                                              Yours sincerely,

CAPTIVE  FERTILIZER  BERTH  AT  ENNORE  PORT  TERMINAL  (EPT)
2.4       MFL is planning to shift its port operations to the newly developed Ennore Port Terminal from Chennai Port,
considering the long-term benefits for the company and to overcome the present problems of port congestion and port-
to-plant logistics.
2.5       In this backdrop, MFL is planning to set up a Captive Fertilizer Berth as a joint venture project to handle 2
million TPA of Dry bulk and Liquid cargo, made up of 1.5 million MT is dry bulk cargo comprising of Urea, MOP,
DAP and finished grades of fertilizer and 0.5 MT liquid cargo comprising of Phosphoric acid and Liquid ammonia.
Modern handling facilities like Unloading Systems, Bagging Systems and Transit Storage form part of the project.
2.6       MFL is in the process of engaging a consultant to select a suitable Joint Venture Partner, among 12 parties who
have evinced interest to participate in this Captive Fertilizer Berth Project.
CAPTIVE  POWER
2.7       MFL consumes around 130 million unit of electrical power per year drawn from TNEB grid and also from
captive generation. 8 Diesel Generators and 2 Gas Turbines generate 32.7 million units (25%) per year as captive power.
2.8       To tide over frequent power failure, under-frequency and voltage fluctuations of TNEB grid, MFL is seeking
alternate power capacity from outside supply sources other than TNEB.
2.9       MFL had preliminary discussion with Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) for participation in their
proposed Rs. 2837 crore Independent Power Plant (IPP) Project of 500 MW capacity.
2.10     In the meantime, MFL is holding negotiation with CPCL for wheeling 4 to 5 MW of surplus power from their
existing captive Power Plant facility.
2.11     The company did not pay dividend to its shareholders after 1992-93. It is running in losses. The loss was
contributed by shortfall in production of urea and NPK, reduction in contribution for NPK, higher specific consumption
of raw materials, steep exchange rate variation, monsoon failure resulting in lower sales, higher rebates and discounts
and higher interest cost.
2.12     The company's operations continue to be unprofitable. During April and May 2001, Ammonia plant load had to
be restricted due to high Ammonia inventory levels caused by poor off-take by downstream urea/NPL plants. Similarly,
urea plant was also operated at low levels as off-take of NPK for sale has been poor. The annual turnaround was taken
up on May 28, 2001 with a schedule to complete it on June 22, 2001. However, due to the unexpected developments,
the turnaround was extended and the company could come back to production stream in respect of NH
3 only on August
3, 2001. Keeping in view the advice given by urea reactor manufacturers, the company decided to get the urea reactor
inspected which was not envisaged in the original schedule. The inspection of reactor was a difficult job involving
erection of structure above the reactor with hoisting facility. Though an attempt was made to erect the structure while
the plant was in operation, enough progress could not be made due to unfavourable environmental conditions. After the
shut down of the plants, erection work was taken up and hoists were provided at the top level of about 60 mtrs. height to
life the reactor bundles, each weighing 36 T. Reactor B was inspected on July 18 and after attending to some minor
repairs was boxed up.
2.13     In contrast, the inspection of reactor 'A' revealed extensive damages. A quick assessment was made and
necessary action was initiated by the company to rectify the bundles. Notwithstanding all these constraints, the company
decided to start and run the Ammonia and Urea plants at around 50% load. The quality of Urea being produced now is
relatively better with temperature of the Prill hovering around 50
o Celsius, which are the main objectives of Urea Prill
Tower modifications, aimed and achieved by the company. The repair works to Reactor 'A' involve procurement of
imported materials, extensive welding and other specialized jobs, which has been entrusted on a turnkey basis to the
manufacturer M/s Nooter Fabricators Inc. USA to secure Guarantee Test Run of urea plant.

2.14     The acute water scarcity situation affected the Chennai City subsequent to failure of monsoon. The water supply
to the company has been restricted to 0.33 million gallon per day (MGD) as against the requirement of 2.5 MGD. There
is an apprehension that the present supply could be cut down further. This problem is being tackled by the company by
purchasing water at a lighter rate from Metro Water with a view to sustain production at a maximum possible level.
Thus even if there was no problem in Urea Reactor, Urea production had to be curtailed to 45% due to cut in raw water
supply. On the sales front also, the company had been affected due to adverse agro climatic conditions prevailing in the
entire marketing territory of the company viz. Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. In Andhra Pradesh and
Karnataka, drought like situation is prevailing and posing threat to company's marketing efforts. In these states, rainfall
has been only 73% of normal and sowing has been only 40%.
FINANCIAL  ASSISTANCE  CUM  CAPITAL  RESTRUCTURING  (FACR)
2.15     MFL has submitted original FACR proposal to Government of India during January 1999. Whereas the proposal
relating to FIs have been approved and implemented by them during April 1999, the proposal submitted to Government
of India has undergone several revisions till date. In view of the losses incurred during 2000-01 and continuing during
the current year 2001-02 MFL has requested for a revised FACR packages from Government of India and other
institutions, which have extended long term/short term assistance. In respect of FIs, the revised proposal inter-alia
included downward revision of interest rate with moratorium on principal and interest payment for 2 years. With regard
to Government of India loans, the proposal provides for waiver of interest amounting to Rs. 71 crores and downward
reduction of interest rate. Similarly, the revised FACR envisages lower interest on the working capital assistance
received from commercial banks. With a view to avoid company becoming sick, the FIs and Government of India are
working out a comprehensive package.
2.16     The Company has been taking up with various policy-making bodies about disadvantageous position in which
the company has been operating with costly feedstock like Naphtha on one hand and high capital-related charged on the
other hand (consequent to implementation of Revamp Project at the cost of around Rs. 601 crores). Accordingly, in
order to reduce the yawning gap between cost of production and realization, company has represented to Tariff
Commission to reckon industry related/MFL specific problems in the areas of :-
                  –  Assessment of capacity utilization and normative capacity utilization
                  –  Consumption norms
                  –  Interest on working capital
                  –  Selling and distribution expenses
                  –  Return on capital employed
                  –  PCS based on cost of bought (imported) urea and Naptha-based captive Ammonia used in NPK production
                  –  Compensation to cover cost of 90 days forward cover for exchange rate variation.
            The above, if considered favourable by the Government, will help the company in recovering certain costs
substantially.

The department should take a pro-active role in ensuring required level and quality of gas from Mumbai
High or other projects to ensure smooth operation of the plant. Thus it should be included in the
performance part of the Government.
                 2.  The unit has been generally performing well with MoU's rating appropriately reflecting the present level
of performance. Sub-Committee however, feels that this performing units MoU should be more futuristic
and motivative in structure to enable this unit compete in free trade, QRs removed regime.
                 3.  There is need for restructuring the MoU for the fertilizers industry PSUs.
                 4.  The paramount factor in such energy intensive industry is to ensure the energy efficiency is accorded
higher weightage.
                 5.  R&D should also be accorded higher weightage than the present weight of 1 and this should split into
process development, product development like products ensuring higher life cycle for soils etc. and
systems improvement like productivity enhancements, ERP, business process reengineering, vendor
development online packaging cost efficiencies etc.
                 6.  Environment aspect should also be accorded higher weight.
                 7.  HRD element should also accord weight for introduction of quality circles, operation of shop steward
systems, remedial provisions for occupational hazards etc.
                 8.  Safety parameters weight to be enhanced and restructured to include introduction of fail-sale operational
mechanisms.
                 9.  Instead present provision of timely submission of MoU, the said weight should be extended to statutory
compliances that shall inter alia include timely submission of MoU, compliances of statutory nature like
implementation of SC/ST reservation roaster, compliance with direction of Department of Company
Affairs, FICC Regulations timely holding of AGMs, and other statutory requirements.
               10.  An appropriate grading to bring out the units close linkages with their client namely farmer community
should also be accorded.                                                                                        (Para 3.5)
            The Committee is of the opinion that RCF is facing genuine problems, which has affected its performance. The

CHAPTER - I
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
           
Recommendation (Para 2.2 )
 
Financial Performance of HSCL
 
            The Committee, while taking note of the current financial performance of HSCL expresses its concern
over its pathetic condition, and is of the view that HSCL needs improvement for better financial performance. 
HSCL requires a new vision, new managerial will and effective strategy for the continuance of its existence.
           
Action Taken
 
The Ministry of Steel has noted the observation of the Committee.  The financial performance of the Company
improved during 2001-02 over the previous Financial Year  2000-2001.  Major parameters are indicated below:

This improvement is continuing  during the present Financial Year 2002-03 also.  The Company has engaged the
services of a consultant to prepare a strategic plan for its further operation and management.
 
Recommendation (Para 3.2)
 
Revival Package to HSCL
 
            The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government for approving the financial restructuring
proposal.  Considering the fact that resources are limited the sanctioning of revival package having financial implication
is a considered decision of the Government.  Committee also appreciates the Ministry of Steel for its consistent efforts
in persuading the Ministry of Finance for giving revival package to HSCL.  The Committee notes the provisions of

revival package for HSCL.
 
Action Taken
 
            The comment/observation of the Committee is noted.
 
Recommendation (Para 4.2. )
 
Implementation of   the provision of  revival package
 
            The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of Steel has taken action on all provisions contained in the
revival package.  The Committee hopes that efforts of the Ministry of Steel in persuading the Department of Revenue
for exempting of corporate tax for HSCL would have a positive impact on the financial performance of HSCL.  The
Committee further hopes that consequent upon the separation of 7,106 employees and reduction in the wage bill, the
financial ratio of the Company would further improve.
 
Action Taken
 
Consequent upon separation of 7373 employees during 2000-01 & 2001-02, expenditure towards Salary &
wages  has come down by Rs. 32.06 crore in 2001-02 over 2000-01. Further reduction in cost towards wages and
salaries is expected after implementation of a fresh VRS package.
 
            Exemption from payment of Corporate Tax in 1999-2000 is within the provision of Restructuring Package.  No
demand from Income Tax Department for payment of Corporate Tax has been received.
 
Recommendation (Para 4.8:)
 
Savings on the Specified Overheads
 
            The Committee is happy to note the savings on the specified overheads due to measures undertaken by HSCL
management to rationalise administrative expenditure.  The Committee hopes that the efforts to rationalise
administrative expenditure would continue.
 
Action Taken
 
All actions are being taken to reduce administrative expenditure.  During Financial Year 2001-02,
Administrative expenditure was reduced by Rs.17 crore over the previous Financial Year  2000-01.
 
Recommendation (Para 5.2) 
 
Financial Assistance-cum-restructuring package
 
            The Committee observes that financial assistance-cum-restructuring package as proposed by the Ministry of
Steel and so approved by the Government was not as comprehensive so as to mitigate the accumulated loss and total
liability of HSCL.  The Company continues to rein in adverse financial scenario and disadvantages in general because
implementation of the revival package would respond only if approved measures are taken in time for total and
comprehensive restructuring of the Company.  HSCL needs total overhauling and complete and comprehensive
restructuring in one go as partial package and delayed implementation defeats the whole idea, approach and action.
 
Action Taken
 
Subsequent to the Financial Restructuring Package, granted by Government of India during July, 99, a proposal
for further revival of the Company was submitted in June, 01 to the Finance Ministry by Ministry of Steel.

Details of the proposal are as under:-
 
1.                  Grant of non-plan assistance for settlement of outstanding salaries and other statutory liabilities amounting to
Rs.182.28 crore.
2.                  Increase the existing Government of India guarantee by Rs.250 crore to facilitate further loan from commercial
banks for separation of another 5000 employees.
 
The Ministry of Finance has sanctioned Rs. 89.44 crore towards outstanding salaries and other statutory
liabilities of separated employees.  The balance liability stands at Rs. 133 crore as on August 1,.2002.  Ministry
of Steel is examining the objections of Finance Ministry with regard to pay revision in the Company which is
coming in the way of Finance Ministry releasing adequate financial assistance to clear all dues towards
wages/salaries.
 
            Out of the required Rs.250 crore for VRS Rs.50 has already been drawn from Indian Overseas Bank  in

Rs.250 crore is raised for effecting VRS of 5000 employees.
 
            The Company has also engaged a consultant for preparing a strategic plan and a plan for organisational
restructuring.
 
Recommendation  (Para 5.4)
 
Sufficient resilience and synergy to work
 
The Committee is of the view that once the comprehensive restructuring package is effectively implemented
HSCL would acquire sufficient resilience and synergy to work even against fierce competition.  The Committee
recommends that HSCL management should strive in this regard.
 
Action Taken
 
HSCL Management has already renewed its thrust on the impending changes in strategies of Execution,
Marketing, Financial operation and all round development.  New areas of operation, such as, Power, Roads and Bridges,
Railway projects and repair, Airport development, Residential and Commercial Buildings etc. have been identified to
compensate for the decline in steel sector.  All the units will be made to function as separate profit centres for their
existence.  HRD will be a high thrust area.  Action is already on for computerization of project monitoring system at a
faster pace.  In addition as stated above a strategic plan and a plan for organisational restructuring is being prepared.
 
Recommendation ( Para 5.10)
 
Rationalisation  of  expenditure toward contract payment.
 
            The Committee is of the view that the HSCL management should have undertaken necessary steps to
rationalize expenditure toward contract payment.

            HSCL Management is taking all steps to reduce expenditure towards contract payment.  This is evident from the
fact that direct expenditure during 2001-02 has reduced to 82% from 92% in 2000-01.
 
Recommendation (Para 6.4) :
 
Delay  by Commercial bank in the sanction and disbursement of the first phase of loan to HSCL
 
The Committee is perturbed to note the delay of about eleven months by Commercial bank in the sanction and

104th Report of Committee on Industry

disbursement of the first phase of loan to HSCL to the tune of Rs. 210  crore for VRS purpose on the plea of adverse
financial fundamentals of HSCL.  The delay in sanctioning of loan of HSCL have rather adversely affected the so called
financial fundamental  of HSCL during that span of eleven moths in the form of payment of wage and salaries given to
HSCL employees during the span of eleventh months.  The Committee opines that idle wages and salaries given to
HSCL employees during said eleven months is a criminal wastage of money so far as the financial state of the Company
is concerned and the matter needs to be inquired into.
 
Action Taken
 
Reasons for delay in sanction of 1 st phase loan by SBI have already been explained.  HSCL Management has
tried to compensate for the delay by stepping up the VRS process.  Against the directive of separating 6000 employees

CHAPTER –II
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE
 
Recommendation (Para 4.4)
 
Accumulated loss of the Company
 
            The Committee understands that it is but natural that the accumulated loss of the Company would come down
once the Government grants waiver of interest Government loans, so far the same is a book-entry and it hardly has any
reflection on the actual financial performance of the Company.

The comment/observation of the Committee is noted.
 
CHAPTER-III
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE HAS NOT
ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL.
                                   
Recommendation (Para 5.6 )
Failure of financial and  revival package
 
            The Committee is constrained to express its concern over the fact that financial assistance given for restructuring
package could not be implemented in the expected manner and the outcome thereof is not as expected.  The Committee
notes the reasons for failure of revival package, although it is not fully envisaged with the reasons for failure of revival
package as advocated by the Ministry of Steel.  For the revival of the Company HSCL management has to procure work
order despite ups and downs in steel industry and HSCL management should not face much difficulties as Government
is giving due importance to the construction sector.  The Committee is of the view that optimum utilisation of
manpower and resources at the disposal of Company is the responsibility of HSCL management.
      
Action Taken
 
Despite continued decline in steel industry, HSCL secured orders worth Rs.242 crore during 2001-02 as
compared to Rs.201 crore during 2000-01.  The target for 2002-03 has been set at Rs.300 crore.
 
            HSCL Management has already taken suitable actions to ensure that the physical performance of the Company
does not slide due to drastic reduction in manpower.  This is clearly evident from the fact that the Turnover increased

from Rs.243 crore in 2000-01 to Rs.258 crore in 2001-02.  However, effort is on to optimize utilisation of resources by
way of increase  in Turnover and Order booking.
 
Further Recommendation
 
            The Committee is of the view that since the Government is giving impetus to the construction sector and because
HSCL is engaged in the construction works, therefore, it should not be difficult for the HSCL management to procure
work order.  Moreover, the steel industry is up swinging, it is being  hoped that HSCL would be able to meet its target

Recommendation  (Para 5.8)
 
Gap in the actual turnover of the Company vis-à-vis the turnover envisaged in the financial restructuring
proposal.
 
            The Committee expresses its concern over the gap in the actual turnover of the Company vis-à-vis the turnover
envisaged in the financial restructuring proposal.  HSCL management should have made an all out efforts to achieve the
target as envisaged.
 
Action Taken
 
The observations of the Committee are noted.  The gap in turnover is largely  due to the slow down in the steel

Further Recommendation
 
The fact that HSCL is the only Public Sector Steel Construction Company, the Company should not have been
remained without work order, that is so, because,  Steel  PSUs were on the modernisation and expansion recourse. 
However, it is felt that  HSCL management would  chalk out  effective  course of action for procurement of work order
in future.
 
Partial failure of Financial Assistance restructuring package
Recommendation ( Para 6.2 )
 
The Committee, while taking note of the detailed reasons for partial failure of Financial Assistance restructuring
package, is constrained to express its concern.  The Committee is of the view that HSCL management could have well
managed and controlled the problems being faced by HSCL.  The Committee views that replacement of obsolete
equipment in HSCL should have positive impact on the operational efficiency of Company rather than deterring the
implementation of revival package.  Moreover, HSCL management should have chalked out a strategy for better margin

Action Taken
 
It is indicated at Para 5.10 that as a result of the steps taken by the management the direct cost has come down
which had a direct impact on reduction in losses.  Management’s  discretion is applied in regard to releasing on VRS

above,  as such, the scope of  maintaining  lower age profile of the employees on roll is limited.
 
Further recommendation
 
Since most of  the employees in HSCL  are in the age of group  of 52 and above and as such,  the scope of
maintaining   lower age   profile  of the  employees  on   the roll is limited, the HSCL management has  to apply to

104th Report of Committee on Industry

added  managerial  skill  as to how   re-orient    its  workforce  for making the same efficient and effective.   The 
Committee hopes that   the strategic plan  and restructuring plan where   a consultant has been engaged, would take care

Recommendation ( Para 7.3)
 
System of Sub-Contracting Business Pattern
           
            The Committee understands the compelling circumstances under which HSCL has to adopt the system of sub-
contracting business pattern but it is also an open secret that sub-contracting gives low margin for HSCL than if the
work done by the Company itself.  The Committee is of the view that VRS offer by HSCL to its employees would take
care of keeping with itself the workforce consisting of productive age profile and willing to undertake work/assignment
from whatever concern its coming.  The Committee feels that direct undertaking of work by HSCL staff would give
larger margin to HSCL and thus opening scope for profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better that the system of
sub-contracting is replaced by direct involvement of HSCL employees, sooner than later.
 
Action Taken
 
Subsequent to the separation of manpower in accordance with the provision of the Restructuring Proposal and
MOU with Ministry of Steel,  HSCL will be left out with only about 1000 employees on its rolls.  In such
circumstances, HSCL’s function will  be of supervisory nature only.  However, execution of contracts will be carried
out as per the approved procedures of the Company.  Adequate steps will be taken to optimize margins and use of
departmental inputs.
 
Further recommendation
 
            The Committee feels that  entrusting  HSCL merely  with the supervisory role  and continuing  with   the system

Ministry   with in the  Ministry  of Steel .  The Ministry of Steel is already playing the  supervisory role  over the steel

Committee on Industry) on  Modernisation, Restructuring  and Expansion Programme of Hindustan Zinc Ltd. (HZL) 
and  post disinvestment performance of  Hindustan  Zinc Ltd in the background of the shareholders agreement.  
Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL),  one of the leading producers of lead and zinc, was incorporated   in January 1968 as a
public sector Company after the take over of the erstwhile Metal Corporation of India Limited, to develop mining and
smelting capacities to meet the domestic demand of zinc and lead metals..   The authotrised share capital of HZL is Rs.

CHAPTER – V
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
1.            Management of Company Affairs
 
            The Committee notes the composition of the Board of  Directors of the Company which is expected to manage
the affairs of the company in accordance with the Articles of Association of the Company and The Companies Act
1956.  the Committee expects that new managements would ensure that no deviation is made in this regard.
 
2.         Special consent required from the Government
 
            The Committee notes the provisions identified in Schedule 4.5 of Shareholders Agreement (SHA) where special
consent is required from the Government for transecting the business pertaining of those items. The Committee
recommends that “Government Nominee Director” would actively participate in the meeting of Board of Director of the
Company and would keep the Government well informed the decision reached in the meeting.   The Governments
Nominee Director need to be vigilant and epitome of ensuring responsive and responsible management of affairs in the
Company.
 
3.            Adequate job opportunities for SC/ST physically handicapped persons
 

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

            The Committee is happy to note that the strategic partners recognizes that Government in relation to its
employment policies follows certain principles for the benefit of the members of the Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribes,
physically handicapped persons and other socially disadvantaged categories of the society.  The SP shall use its best
efforts to cause the Company to provide adequate job opportunities for such persons.  Further, in the event of any
reduction in the strength of the Employees of the Company, the SP shall use its best efforts to ensure that the physically
handicapped persons, Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribes are retrenched at the end.  The Committee hopes that the new
management would ensure the implementation of the provision inwards and deeds.
 
4.            Efficiency Vs Human Relation Approach
 
            The Committee is of the view that the new management would take every care for optimum utilization of
manpower by adopting the principle of placing a right man at right place in right time in such a way that company
affairs are managed in the efficient and effective manners and keeping in view endowment of human values and ethics.
 
5.            Keeping track with changing economic scenario
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that the new management should keep an eye to the changing economic
scenario at the national and International market and reorient its mission and objectives so as to improve its physical and
financial performance.  In demand driven economy it is essential that adequate attention is being given to market
research and reorient its production plan as per the demand of the market.   New management should keep on analyzing
the strength, weaknesses, opportunities and threats     of the company and chalked out future course of action as per the
requirement. 
 
 
6.         New management initiative for employee participation
 
            The Committee hopes that the joint consultative Committee (JCC) consist of nominees of workmen and
management would be functional in real terms and all efforts would be made for achieving organizational goals of
productivity, quality, cost management and good employee relation.
 
7.            Initiative in Inventory Management, Sales, Marketing and Finance
 
            The Committee notes that the initiative taken by the new management in the field of inventory management,
sales, marketing and finance and hopes that such initiative would lead to quick disposal of inventories, increment in
turnover and  sales and market share of HZL products and attainment of favorable financial ratios.
 
8.         Welfare amenities
 
            The Committee is happy to note that the welfare amenities which were available to nearby population of the
Units prior to disinvestment continue to be availed by them. The Committee hopes that   the new management will   
initiate renewed course of action for peripheral developments.  
 
9.            Environmental awareness and  sustainable development
 
              The Committee, while appreciating the initiative taken by the new management    for implementation of
environmental awareness  and sustainable development objectives recommends that the new management would
continue with  its concerted efforts.
 
10.            Disinvestment proceeds  for  spending  on social sector
 
            The Committee is of the considered view that   the Government should create a special fund to keep the  this
disinvestment proceed of  the company for spending on social sectors scheme with high appeal.

INTRODUCTION 
         I, the Chairman of  the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having 
been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred-Sixth Report on the Globalisation 
and capital goods industry pertaining to the Department of Public En terprises, Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises. 
2.      The Committee, in this context, held m eetings with various Minist ries and representatives o f
Industry Organisations on 16 th April, 8 th May, 25 th June, 12 th August and 27 th November, 2002 
respectively. 
3.      The Committee in its meeting held on 17th December, 2002 considered and adopted the Report.
 
  
CHAPTER – I 
INTRODUCTION 
         A new trend of global integration began to emerge all over the world in 1980s. This was facilitated
by the gradual integration of the world economics, which ensured free flow of capital and goods from
one country to another country. Foreign capital is now freely available to finance the large infrastructure
projects. Acceptance of WTO regime  by most of the countries has si nce led to a gradual abolition o f
quantitative restrictions and reduction duties and removal of restrictions on inter-country trade. 
1.1    In our context, the Industr ial Policy of 1991 starte d the process of de-lic ensing and except 18 
industries, licensing was withdrawn. The process of de-regul ation was aimed at en larging competition 
and allowing new firms to enter the market s. The market was opened up to domestic
entrepreneurs/industrialists, which as reserved for public sector unde rtakings, and foreign capital was
provided free entry up to 51% equity in high technol ogy areas. With the adve nt of globalization, when
World Bank-aided projects started to come to country, the lifting of import control and drastic reduction 
of import duties, competition from overseas posed a proble m to the domestic capital goods industry. It
has become difficult to stay in the race for this industry in the fa ce of stiff competition from the
multinational giants. 
1.2    Despite the tremendous odds even on date, there are examples of various domestic Indian
companies in sectors like automobi les, steel, engineering, etc. in both public and private sectors that
have successfully with stood the changes brought about by the liberalization of Indian economy; fo r
example Maruti cars are being exported and Tata have similar plans. TISCO has been recognized as one
of the least cost steel producers in the world and companies like IRCON, BHEL and L&T have been
successfully executing contracts abroad. These com panies have mana ged to meet the stiff com petition

the liberalization of Indian econom y. The impressive track record of  it calls for a special mention 
of its achievements. As a matter of fact, BHEL is a role model for other PSUs of Ministry of Heavy 
Industry. For, it has managed to stay in the race  despite the odds faced by  it as a result of stif f 
competition unleashed by the multina tional giants operating in its fi eld of specialization namely, 
manufacture of power plants. T hough BHEL has managed to sustain it s viability yet it is facing 
some unfair challenges. The abse nce of a level playing field vis-à-vis its multinational competitors 
has been posing stiff challenges to the company. This  is leading to an eve r-increasing pressure on 
its profitability. Despite this, the company has been constantly  upgrading its technology and has 
also been successful in acquiring state of the art technology used in HVDC  power projects. This 
reflects the commitments of the company as a whole to serve th e nation even when the odds are 
stacked against it. Therefor e, what this company requires is a li ttle help from th e Government in 
the form of suitable policy measures. In this re gard, the sub-committee draw s the attention of the 
Government to the issues of pr ice and purchase preference to BHEL, and import duty concessions 
to the foreign companies. Through  in some cases price and purchas e preference is granted to the 
PSUs, the positive results of this measure are negated by the import duty concessions extended to 
the foreign companies by the Government. These concessions and exempti ons are precisely the 
reasons for the playing field not be ing level for domestic companies or  for that matter PSUs as the 
bids offered by foreign players are much lower in comparison to the ones offered by PSUs. In other 
words, the competition is killed well before it begins. The Committee believes that the need of the 
hour is not to go back to the days of protectionism rather to provide  a level playing field to all the

policy of giving duty concessions to the foreign companies in as much as it leads to disadvantages to the
domestic companies especially the PSUs. It is the considered view  of the committee that foreign
companies should not be shown favour at the expense of domestic companies.”

3.        The amendment of Customs Notification N o. 85/99 dated 6.7.1999 was issued amending the 
earlier Notification No. 84/99 permitting imports at zero duty for projects funded by international
Organizations. With th e notification, the preference polic y under World Ba nk guideline has
automatically reduced to zero and adversely affected the domestic industry. The Committee consistently
followed up the matter and recommende d for corrective measures in its 36 th, 45th and 59th Reports and

matter. The World Bank issue is not only applicable  to Public Sector Undert akings but also to capital
goods industry in general. The Committee’s objective was to utilize it for the development of the
country. 
3.1      The Committee recalls that in the meetings held on 16 th April, 8th May and 25th June, 2002, The 
Ministries/Departments had expresse d their own reservations and concer ns but ultimately they realized
that if only they put their heads together they could resolve the i ssue. The Committee appreciates the
ministries and departments for their coordinated approach. 
3.2      Since globalization, the country is facing ma ny problems but at the sa me time the country cannot
go back. We have to see how to safeguard the country’s interest – both public and private sectors. 
3.3      Now, in view of the clarificatory notification issued by the Department of  Economic Affairs,

        At the outset, Convenor welcomed the Secretaries and ot her officers of the Ministries and

imports at zero customs duty agai nst World Bank/Asian Developmen t Bank's financed projects. The
Convenor summarised the view point s of CII and informed the commit tee that World Bank as well as
Asian Development Bank had been fi nancing various kinds of projects  for over two decades in India.
There was an established procedure for inviting tenders and for evaluating them. The primary features of
the guidelines were as follows: 
        (a)   International Competitive Bidding had to be followed; 
        (b)   Evaluation of tenders submitted by foreign bidders would be evaluated without including
customs duty; and 
        (c)   Price preference of 15% to domestic bidders was allowed with the stipulation that it would be
admissible if in the total package, there was value addition of 30% or  more and the price
preference was not more than applicable customs duty. 
2.     The Central Board of Excise and Customs Duty issued a notification No. 85/99 amending an earlier
customs notification exempting cust oms duty on import of goods for  ex ecution of projects financed by
loan or grant by World Bank, Asia n Development Bank or any othe r international organisation. The
World Bank had allowed 15%  Price Preference to dom estic bidders to offset  the domestic duty/levies
such as sales tax, octrois, etc. and certain disadvant ages due to inadequate infrastructure and higher cost
of finance. With zero customs duty from 6th Jul y, 1999 for direct import by pr oject authorities, the
effect of price preference of 15% had automatically been reduced to zero. Secretary, Ministry of Power,
Secretary, Department of Revenue, Director General of Foreign Trade raised the following objections: 
        (a)    World Bank/ADB had stopped fundi ng power generation projects in  India, the rescinding o f
the aforesaid customs notification had no practical significance; 
        (b)    If the domestic price preference was restored, the project cost would go up; and 
        (c)    If domestic price preference was restored, overseas bidders would not be interested in
competing for projects funded by the World Bank/ADB. 
3.     As regard point number 1 above, CMD, BHEL, drew attention to  the press report appearing in the
Financial Express dt. 7.5.2002 where Mini ster of Power was reported to ha ve stated that Government of
India would seek financial assi stance of around $ 4 billion from ADB for implementation of various
power projects. If this wa s true, domestic companies would be pla ced at a considerable disadvantage in
the absence of domestic price pref erence. Also, the power transmissi on sector continued to avail o f 
multilateral funding for its proj ects and domestic companies incl uding BHEL were already at a
disadvantage while bidding for these projects. In view of this, it would not be correct to conclude that
the issue had no practical significance. 
        In so far as point number two was concerne d, he stated that although the project cost may have the
potential of increasing to this ex tent, this may not happen in all cas es, as this would depend upon the
pricing strategies adopted by various bidders in specific projects. However, in the absence of domestic
price preference and the consequent  disadvantage suffered by domestic industry, it was likely that more
and more contracts would be w on by the overseas bidders who w ould quote their price in foreign
currencies. These companies would te nd to adopt a different pricing stra tegy in the absence of effective
competition from capable domestic companies. Also, as these projects got executed over a time frame of
3 to 4 years and given the propensity of the Indian ru pee to depreciate (past experience showed that, on

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
CHAPTER–I
LIQUIDATED DAMAGES – THE CONCEPT
            In a supply contract if there is a delay beyond the contractual delivery period in execution of supply, services,
erection and commissioning, the consignee may end up suffering actual or potential losses. Direct losses arising out of
the delay actual in nature that can be directly quantified like debt servicing etc. Potential losses are indirect losses like
opportunity costs, cost overrun of the project, time overrun of the project leading to inflation of project cost etc. The
losses tantamount to the damages suffered by the consignee and quantified unit of these damages are known as
Liquidated Damages.
2.         As per the standard terms of conditions of contracts internationally acclaimed the amount of liquidated damages
is generally ½% of the total value of the contract for every week of delay in supplies or other performance of the
contract plus any cost escalation that has taken place on account of any increase in taxes or imposition of fresh taxes, or
cost escalation of any raw material on account of this during the period of delay, cost escalation of labour due to any
new wage agreement, or imposition of any statutory conditions. However, the supplier will be entitled to any decrease in
cost on the above account of remission of taxes or withdrawal of taxes during the said period between stipulated
delivery period and the actual date of delivery.
3.         As per standard terms of conditions of supply contract generally also provide for force majeure clause meaning
unforeseen circumstances like legal injunctions, natural calamities, industrial action by workers etc. are reasons
attributable to the delay in supply or performance, the same is exempt from imposition of liquidated damages.
4.         The Sub-Committee-III for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises of Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry came to know about the effect of Liquidated Damages on the supplier
when it visited Bharat Heavy Plates and Vessels at Visakhapatnam (a subsidiary of BYNL) on 11th July, 2000. The
workers union as well as management of BHPV informed the Committee that due to delay in deliveries, Rs. 41 crores
had been held up with different units of the company which had created cash flow problems. Later on, after visiting

other units of Bharat Yantra Nigam it was revealed that all the subsidiaries of the holding company had problems on
account LDs imposed on them by their client companies. The matter came up before the Sub-Committee at its meeting
held on 9th November, 2000. The Convenor, after hearing the Secretaries, Department of Heavy Industry, and Ministry
of Petroleum and Natural Gas, about the present status of the outstanding issues of amounts of BYNL group of
companies withheld by various oil sector PSUS on account of LD and other disputed matters, directed the Secretary,
Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises to suitably take up the issue with the Ministry of Petroleum and
Natural Gas for advising the Oil PSUs to consider these cases favourably. The Committee also directed to follow it up
by personal visits by representatives of BYNL and their respective subsidiaries to the concerned Oil PSUs.
5.         Thereafter,  the Committee on Industry in its 44th Report present/laid on 21st December, 2000 recommended as
follows :
5.1       The Committee also came to know during its interaction with the workers and management of some PSUs that
due to non-delivery of final goods in schedule time, penalties have been imposed on them in the form of Liquidity
Damages (LD) which are proving a death knell for some of them.
5.2       The Department of Heavy Industry should take up the matter with the client PSUs for release of outstanding
amount locked-up on account of Liquidity Damages (LD) to such a possible extent, which can be released by the client
PSUs. This will be a helpful gesture to the PSUs who are having working capitalproblem.
5.3       The Ministry of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprise in their Action Taken Note informed that Government had
been taking up the matter with the concerned Ministries/Departments for release of withheld amount on account of LDs.
6.         This was reported to the House vide Committee's 60th report presented/laid on the 19th December, 2001. Since
the persuasive efforts of Department of Heavy Industry could not bear much fruit, 
Sub-Committee-III observed that these issues needed to be approached through a coordinated effort. The Committee
also felt that there was a lack of appreciation of concerns expressed by DHI in respect of the said issue by the other
Ministry. The Committee, therefore, decided to hear both the Department of Heavy Industry and the Ministry of
Petroleum and Natural Gas to find out a probable solution.
CHAPTER–II
MEETINGS HELD WITH THE MINISTRIES AND PSUS THEREUNDER
7.         The Committee held meetings on 17th April, 13th August and 4th December, 2002 on the issue. The
deliberations of the Committee are given below :
Meeting held on 17th April, 2002
7.1       At the outset, the Convenor welcomed the Secretaries of the Ministries of Heavy Industries and Public
Enterprises and Petroleum and Natural Gas, and representatives of various Central PSUs. The Convenor apprised the
Committee that the Committee had been pursuing the case of liquidated damages, which had been imposed by the client
PSUs on the supplier PSUs for non-adherence to the delivery schedule. There had been some problems among the
PSUs. These Liduidated Damages were imposed due to delay and as a result the money had been held up and the
supplier PSUs, specially the BYNL group of companies, had been facing working capital problem.
7.2       Secretary,  Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, informed the Committee that the engineering
industries were facing some problems as there had been no fresh investment in the economy. One of the main problems
had been the lack of working capital because the working capital limits had become irregular. The banks were not
willing to give further advance and the Government was also reluctant to issue fresh funds for the working capital. The
BYNL group of companies had a large measure of support from oil sector and the oil sector was one sector in the
economy where there had been some investment. About 50% of the turnover of these companies came from the oil
PSUs and generally oil sector PSUs also gave benefit of purchase preference to these companies. There had been delay
in execution of projects but in the recent past, these companies had assured that things had improved and some of those
delays or level of delays or the extent of delays that took place earlier, were not taking place now. The process of
disinvestments in all these companies was under way and in order to optimise the return to the Government, the
